en: Oṃ. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. That is full, this is full; from fullness, fullness issues forth.
Taking the fullness from the full, only fullness remains.
Oṃ, peace! Peace! Peace!
Oṃ. Salutations to Brahmā and the others, the founders of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), to the ancestral sages (vaṃśa-ṛṣi), and salutations to the gurus.
This is the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, beginning with the words "Uṣā vā aśvasya.

A brief commentary on it is now commenced for those desiring liberation from saṃsāra, so that they may attain the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self, which is the means for the cessation of the causes of saṃsāra.

This very knowledge of Brahman is denoted by the word *upaniṣad*, because it brings about the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence along with its cause for those intent upon it; for the roots *sad* (to perish) and *ṣad* (to dissolve) have that as their meaning. Because the book has that as its purpose, it too is called *upaniṣad*.
This work, consisting of six chapters, is called the *Āraṇyaka* because it is to be studied in the forest; it is called the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* because of its great size in terms of its extent.
The connection of this very text with the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is now stated.

This entire Veda is devoted solely to revealing the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired—means that are not known through perception or inference—because the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired are naturally sought by all persons.

Furthermore, regarding objects within the realm of the seen, since the knowledge of the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired is established through perception and inference alone, there is no need to seek scriptural authority (*āgama*).

Moreover, if there were no cognition of the existence of a self connected to other births, there could be no desire to attain the desired or avoid the undesired in those other births, according to the view of those who maintain that things arise from inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*).

Therefore, the scripture proceeds with reference to the existence of a self connected to other births, as well as the specific means for attaining what is desired and avoiding what is undesired in those other births.
Beginning with, "This doubt regarding one who has died—that some say it exists in humanity and others say it does not exist" (Ka.U.
1.1.20), it concludes with, "It must be perceived that it indeed exists" (Ka.U. 2.3.13).
13) Because such a definitive conclusion is seen in passages beginning with [the Upanishadic statement]:
“And as when one has met death” (KaU 2.2.6), and following the introduction, “Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body.”
And [it is said]: "Others follow the stump, according to their karma and according to their learning" (KaU 2.2.7).
And beginning with "He is self-luminous" (BṛU 4.3.9), [it continues]: "Knowledge and karma cling to him" (4.4.2).
2) And [it is said]: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, evil by evil action" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.2.13).
Furthermore, having begun with "I shall make him understand" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.15), [it continues] "consisting of consciousness" (2.1.16).
16) And thus [it is argued that] there exists a self distinct [from the aggregates], and that this is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If this is claimed, it is not so,
because we observe disagreements among proponents.

For if the existence of the self, which is connected to another body, were known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then neither the Materialists (*lokāyatika*) nor the Buddhists would be our adversaries by asserting "there is no self.
Indeed, no one disputes that a jar exists when it is an object of direct perception, such that one could say "the jar does not exist.
If it is argued that this is not so because one perceives a person in what is actually a post, we reply: no, for a dispute arises only after the post has been correctly identified.
The nihilists (vaināśikas), however, even when the cognition "I" arises, maintain that there is simply no existence of anything distinct from the body.
Therefore, because it differs from the object of perception, the existence of the self is not established through perception;
likewise, it is not established through inference either.

If it is argued that because scripture (śruti) indicates the existence of the self through indicative marks (liṅga), and because indicative marks fall within the scope of perception (pratyakṣa), [the self is thus perceptible], we say no; for the connection with a previous birth is not grasped by perception.

However, once the existence of the self is understood through scripture and through specific worldly indicative marks shown in the Veda, the Mīmāṃsakas and logicians (tārkika) who follow them [proceed accordingly].

And those who imagine that the marks of the notion of "I" (aham-pratyaya) are derived solely from their own intellects, rather than being Vedic, assert that the Self is both perceptible and inferable.

In every way, however, it is established that there exists a Self connected with other bodies; and for one who understands this and seeks the specific means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired in other bodies, the Karma-kāṇḍa was commenced to make those specific means known. It was not, however, to remove the ignorance regarding the Self—which is the cause of the desire to attain the desired and avoid the undesired, and which is characterized by the conceit of being an agent and an enjoyer—by means of the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman as the Self, which is the opposite of that [ignorance].

For as long as that [ignorance] is not removed, this [individual], impelled by innate defects such as passion and aversion toward the fruits of action, continues even by transgressing what is enjoined or prohibited by the scriptures;
thus, through mind, speech, and body, he predominantly accumulates actions designated as *adharma*, which accomplish seen and unseen undesirable results,
because of the superior force of his innate defects.
From that, there is downward movement as far as the stationary beings (*sthāvara*).

Sometimes, due to the superior force of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the scriptures, one accumulates through the mind and other faculties, for the most part, that which is called *dharma*, which is the means for achieving what is desired.
That is of two kinds: preceded by knowledge and that which is alone.
Among these, that which is alone has as its fruit the attainment of the world of the ancestors and so forth;
that which is preceded by knowledge has as its fruit the attainment of everything from the world of the gods up to the world of Brahmā.
And thus says the Śāstra: “One who sacrifices for the Self is better than one who sacrifices for the gods” (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa), and so forth;
and the Smṛti also states: “Vedic action is twofold” (Manu 12.88), and so forth.
And when dharma and adharma are equal, there is the attainment of the human state.

Thus, this course of transmigratory existence—beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary objects—is characterized by natural defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*), is produced by the means of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), and has name, form, and action as its substratum.
This very world, which exists in the form of effects and instruments, was previously unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) before its creation.

This transmigratory existence, created by ignorance like the sequence of seed and sprout, is characterized by the superimposition of action, agent, and fruit upon the Self; it is beginningless, endless, and a source of misfortune.

For one who has become detached from this [world], the Upaniṣad is commenced for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of Brahman—which is the opposite of that [worldly state]—in order to bring about the cessation of ignorance.
Now, the purpose of this knowledge connected with the Aśvamedha sacrifice is that those who have no entitlement to the Aśvamedha may still attain its fruit through this very knowledge.
As it is said: "Either by knowledge or by action," and "This indeed is the conqueror of worlds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.28).
[This is known] from such scriptural passages as these.
If it is argued that consciousness has only ritual action as its object, we say no;
for there is a scriptural statement of optionality: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and he who knows this [sacrifice] thus."

Because it is recorded in the section on knowledge (vidyā-prakaraṇa) and because its performance is seen in other rituals, it is understood that the attainment of its fruit results from this knowledge. Furthermore, among all rituals, the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is the supreme ritual, as it possesses the fruit of attaining both the collective and the individual; its mention here at the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman is for the purpose of demonstrating that all rituals fall within the sphere of saṃsāra.
Thus, he will show the fruit to consist in the state of hunger and death.
If it is argued that eternal things cannot have the state of being the fruit within the sphere of saṃsāra, we say no;
for there is a scriptural text summarizing the fruits of all actions,
and indeed, every action is connected with a wife.

Having shown that all actions are by their very nature motivated by desire through the passage, “May I have victory... this much indeed is desire” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17), [the text then states] regarding sons, ritual acts, and the lower knowledge: “The world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16).
16) Having thus shown the fruit, [the text] will conclude by summarizing the nature of the threefold food at the end: “This triad, indeed, is name, form, and action” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.1).
Thus, it is declared that the fruit of all actions is nothing but saṃsāra.
This very triad was then undifferentiated prior to its origination;
that same [triad] is again differentiated through the power of the karma of all living beings, like a tree from a seed.
This cyclic existence (saṃsāra), consisting of both differentiated and undifferentiated forms, is the domain of ignorance (avidyā).

Through ignorance alone, that which is superimposed as the nature of the self—consisting of action, agent, and fruit, and comprising the formed, the formless, and their latent impressions—is thus distinct from [the true Self].

Although it is non-dual, eternal, pure, enlightened, and free by nature, and consists of neither name nor form nor action, it nevertheless appears through the inversion of the distinctions between action, agent, and fruit.

Therefore, for one who is detached from this very nature of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit—which consists of the forms of means and ends—for the sake of removing ignorance, the seed of defects such as desire and the source of karma, just as one removes the cognition of a snake from a rope; [this instruction is given].
The knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is now commenced.
In that regard, first, for the sake of the knowledge of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), the passage beginning with "The dawn, verily, is the head of the horse" is presented.
Therein, a vision concerning the horse itself is stated, because of the preeminence of the horse.
And its preeminence is due to the fact that the sacrifice is named after it, and because it belongs to Prajāpati.
"The dawn, indeed, is the head of the sacrificial horse."
The sun is the eye, the wind the breath, and Vaiśvānara fire the open mouth of the sacrificial horse; the year is its body.

Heaven is its back, the intermediate space its belly, the earth its chest, the quarters its flanks, the intermediate directions its ribs, the seasons its limbs, the months and half-months its joints, days and nights its feet, the stars its bones, and the sky its flesh.
The undigested food is the sands; the rivers are the intestines; the liver and the lungs are the mountains; the plants and the trees are his body hairs.
His rising is the forepart; his setting is the hind part.
When he yawns, that is the lightning-flash.
What it shakes is the thundering;
what it urinates is the raining;
its voice is indeed speech. 1.1.1.
Regarding the word "uṣāḥ": *uṣāḥ* refers to the hour of Brahmā (*brāhma-muhūrta*).
The particle *vai* serves to indicate recollection; it causes one to recall the well-known time.
Because of the preeminence of the head;
and the head is the most important among the limbs of the body.
The connection is: "The head of the horse—of the sacrificial one, that is, of the one worthy of sacrifice—is Upā."

Since the animal, as a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), is to be consecrated, the views of Time and so forth are superimposed upon its head and other parts. Furthermore, its status as Prajāpati arises from the superimposition of the view of Prajāpati; thus, the superimposition of the views of Time, the World, and the Deity constitutes the making of the animal into Prajāpati.
For Prajāpati is of such a nature, like the fashioning of Viṣṇu and others upon an image;
and the sun is the eye because it is not separated from the head and because its presiding deity is the sun.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is wind (*vāyu*) by its very nature.
The opened mouth is the fire Vaiśvānara;
"Vaiśvānara" is a specific epithet for fire.
The fire named Vaiśvānara means "the opened mouth," because the mouth has Agni as its presiding deity. The year is the self;
the year consists of twelve months or thirteen months.
The self is the body;
and among the divisions of time, the year is the body and the self, according to the Vedic revelation: "For the self is the middle of these limbs.
The phrase "of the sacrificial horse" is repeated for the purpose of applying it throughout all [the subsequent sections].
The sky is the back because of the common quality of being elevated;

the intermediate space is the belly because of the common quality of being hollow; the earth is the *pājasya*—the term *pājasya* being derived from *pādasya* through a transposition of syllables—which means the place where the feet rest.

If it is argued that [the statement] "the four directions on both sides" is incorrect because of a numerical discrepancy between the sides and the directions—since the directions are connected to each side individually—[we reply]:
no, there is no fault, because it is established that [the horse] faces all directions; for the horse is connected to all directions by means of its two sides alone.
The intermediate directions, beginning with the south-east (āgneyī), are the ribs;
the seasons are the limbs, because they share the common characteristic of being parts of the year;
and days and nights are the foundations.

Because of the plural number, [the feet] are those belonging to Prajāpati, the gods, the ancestors, and humans; they are "supports" (pratiṣṭhāḥ), meaning "feet," because by means of them one stands firm.
For it is by means of these feet that the temporal self of the horse stands firm through days and nights.
The stars are his bones, due to the common quality of whiteness;
the sky is the clouds situated in the sky, because the intermediate space is said to be his belly,
and the flesh is so because of the common quality of being sprinkled with water and blood.
The *ūvadhyam* is the undigested food remaining in the stomach; the *sikatāḥ* (sands) are so called because of the common quality of having separated parts;
the *sindhavaḥ* (rivers) are the veins, which are the channels of the rectum, indicated by the plural number;
and the *yakṛt* (liver) and *klomānaḥ* (lungs) are the two pieces of flesh situated to the right and left below the heart.
The term *klomānaḥ* (lungs) always takes the plural form even when referring to a single organ. The mountains are so called because of their hardness and height;
the herbs are the small stationary plants, while the great trees are the *vanaspati*s; and the body hairs and head hairs are [the mountains] according to their respective correspondence.
Rising, that is, ascending, Savitṛ becomes the fore-part of the horse up until midday; the meaning is "above the navel.
Setting, that is, descending, he becomes the hind-part—the latter half—from midday onwards, due to the similarity between the front and back [of the horse and the sun's course].
When he yawns—that is, when he stretches his limbs, bending and tossing them about—that is his lightning-flash, because of the commonality with the opening of the clouds of the mouth.
When it shakes its limbs, that is "thundering," because of the commonality with the sound of roaring;
when it urinates, the horse "rains," because of the commonality with the act of sprinkling;
and its speech is indeed the sound itself—this is the speech of this horse.
The meaning is that there is no conceptual construction here. //1//
"Or 'day'":
the two cups called *mahiman*, made of gold and silver respectively, are placed before and behind the horse; this teaching refers to that.
— Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.2.
Day indeed was born as the first greatness after the horse;
its source was in the eastern ocean.
Night was born as the second greatness after it.
Its source is in the western ocean.
These two, indeed, as the two forms of greatness (mahiman), have come into being on both sides of the horse:
having become a steed (haya), it carried the gods; as a stallion (vājī), the Gandharvas; as a courser (arvan), the Asuras; and as a horse (aśva), human beings.
The ocean alone is its kin; the ocean is its source.
The day is the golden cup because of their common quality of brilliance.
How is it that "the greatness was born as a horse in front"?
Because the horse is Prajāpati.
For Prajāpati, characterized by the sun and other such features, is indicated by the day;
having indicated the horse, the golden Mahiman cup was produced, just as lightning flashes forth following a tree.
Of that cup, "in the eastern sea"—the word *samudra* [is used] with a change of grammatical case—[it is] the womb (*yoni*).
The word *yoni* refers to the place of depositing.
Likewise, the night (*rātrī*) shines (*rājate*), because of the similarity in color or the similarity in being inferior.
After this horse, from behind—that is, from the rear—*Mahiman* was born.
Its source is in the other ocean; its greatness is due to its vastness. For this is the manifestation of the horse: that two cups, one golden and one silver, are placed on both sides.
These two indeed, the two "magnitudes" (mahiman) known as *mahiman*, came into being on both sides of the horse, having come into being with the very characteristics previously described.
This repetition—that this horse is thus endowed with greatness—is for the purpose of praise.
Likewise, the passage beginning with "having become a steed" (*hayo bhūtvā*) is also solely for the purpose of praise.
The horse is "one who goes" (*hinoti*), meaning it possesses a distinguished movement;
or rather, it refers to a specific class of being.
It "carried the gods" (*devānavahat*), meaning it brought them to the state of divinity, because [the horse] is Prajāpati.
Or rather, he became the bearer of the gods;
however, being a vehicle does not constitute mere censure.
This is not a fault.
The capacity to be a vehicle is inherent to the horse;
because this is its inherent nature, the fact that the horse attains eminence through its connection with the gods and others is merely a form of praise.
Likewise, the *vājī* and other such terms denote specific species.
"Having become a stallion (*vājī*), he carried off the Gandharvas"—this is to be supplied [to the text].
Likewise, "having become a courser (*arvā*), [he carried off] the Asuras; having become a horse (*aśva*), [he carried off] human beings."
"The ocean indeed" refers to the Supreme Self; "bondage" means that in it one is bound.
"The ocean" is the source (*yoni*), the cause with respect to origination.
Thus, He is praised as being of pure origin and of pure abode.
According to the Vedic revelation, "The horse has its source in the waters," or rather, the ocean is well-known as its source. //2//
Thus ends the first Aśvamedha Brāhmaṇa in the first chapter. //1//
Now, the origin of the fire used for the horse sacrifice is described;
this account of its origin is intended as a praise, with the aim of explaining the vision concerning that very fire.
In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here.
This world was enveloped by death, which is hunger;
for hunger is indeed death.
He made that mind [his own], thinking, "May I have a self.
He moved about performing fervor; as he performed fervor, the waters were born from him.
"He indeed praised [the fire], thinking, 'May there be well-being (kaṃ) for me.
That is the very reason for the *arkya*'s name being *arka*.
Verily, well-being comes to him who thus knows this reason for the *arkya*'s name being *arka*. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.1)
*Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 1.2.1*: "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here.

Here, in this sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*), "nothing whatsoever"—that is, not even the slightest particularity differentiated by name and form—existed or came into being "in the beginning," prior to the creation of mind and the rest.
One might ask: could it have been a mere void? No, for the Śruti says, "There was nothing whatsoever here."
Neither the effect nor the cause existed [prior to the moment of arising];
for it is at the time of arising that the jar arises.
Therefore, the jar does not exist prior to its production.
[Objection: But surely it is not non-existent, because we perceive the lump of clay and so forth as its cause.
Only that which is not perceived is non-existent.
Let it be so for the effect, but not for the cause, because [the cause] is perceived;
for us, however, nothing at all is perceived prior to its production.
If non-apprehension were the reason for non-existence, then since neither cause nor effect is apprehended prior to the origination of the entire world, let there be the non-existence of everything.
This is not so, because of the Vedic revelation: "This was indeed enveloped by Death."
For if there had been nothing at all—that by which [the world] is covered and that which is covered—then he would not have said, "This was indeed covered by death.
Indeed, it is not the case that "the son of a barren woman is covered by a sky-flower.
Yet he says, "This was indeed covered by death."
Therefore, both that cause by which [the effect] was covered and that effect which was covered prior to its production existed;
this is because of the authority of scripture and because it is also inferable.
Furthermore, the existence of both cause and effect prior to production is inferred;
for it is observed that when a cause exists, an existing effect that is in the process of being produced arises, whereas such an effect is not observed when the cause is absent.
If it is argued that the existence of a cause for the world prior to its production is inferred just as the existence of the cause of a jar or similar objects is inferred,
and that even the cause of a jar or such things is non-existent because a jar cannot be produced without first destroying the lump of clay and so forth; [we reply:]...
Because clay and so forth are the causes;
for in those cases, clay, gold, and the like are the causes of the jar, the golden ornament, and so on,
and not the specific form of the lump.
Because [the effect] exists even in the absence of that [specific form].
For it is observed that even when the specific form of a lump is absent, the production of effects such as a jar or a necklace occurs from the mere causal substance, such as clay or gold.
Therefore, the specific form of a lump is not the cause of the jar, the necklace, or other such effects.

However, since a jar, a golden ornament, or the like does not arise in the absence of substances such as clay or gold, the substance— clay, gold, and so forth— is alone the cause, and not the specific form of the lump.
For every cause, in producing its effect, produces that other effect while causing the concealment of its own previously arisen effect.
Because it is contradictory for multiple effects to arise simultaneously from a single cause,
and because the destruction of a cause does not occur through the destruction of its prior effect;
therefore, the observation of the production of an effect upon the destruction of a lump of clay and so forth is no proof for the non-existence of the cause prior to the production [of the effect].

If it is argued that this is incorrect because clay and so forth do not exist apart from the lump and other such forms— if it is argued that it is illogical to claim that when the preceding effects such as the lump are destroyed, the cause such as the clay is not itself destroyed, but rather persists even in subsequent effects such as the jar,
because the cause such as the clay is not perceived apart from the lump, the jar, and so on?
No, for it is observed that when jars and the like are produced from causes such as clay, the latter persists even when the lump and other intermediate stages have ceased.
If it is argued that the perception of continuity is due to similarity and not to the persistence of the cause, we say no;

because since the very particles of clay and so forth present in the lump are directly perceived in the jar, it is illogical to postulate similarity and the like on the basis of a fallacious inference.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as a non-erroneous contradiction between perception and inference, because inference is preceded by perception; otherwise, it would follow that there could be no confidence whatsoever in any inference. Moreover, if everything were momentary, then even the cognition "this is that very same thing," which is being understood, would depend upon another cognition of that [object] for its own existence.

If that [cognition] also depends on another cognition of that [object], there would be an infinite regress; and because the cognition "this is similar to that" would also be false, there would be a total lack of confidence in all cases.
Furthermore, even for the two cognitions of "that" and "this," a relationship is untenable in the absence of an agent.
If it is argued that their relationship arises from similarity, no—
This is because it is logically impossible for two cognitions to be the objects of one another.
If they cannot be mutual objects, then the apprehension of similarity is impossible.
If you argue that the cognition of similarity occurs even when similarity itself does not exist, we say no.
This [objection] applies even to two cognitions, because it would entail that they have non-existent objects, just like the cognition of similarity.
If it is argued that all cognitions must simply have non-existent objects, we say no,
because that would entail that the cognition of a cognition would also have a non-existent object.
If it is argued that "let that also be so," we say no; for if all cognitions were false, a cognition of the unreal would be impossible.
Therefore, this claim that "the cognition of that [object] arises from similarity" is incorrect.
Therefore, the existence of the cause prior to the production of the effect is established;
and since the manifestation of the effect serves as its inferential mark,
the existence of the effect prior to its production is likewise established.
How is it that [the term] "having manifestation as its mark" means that manifestation is its mark? Manifestation is the attainment of becoming a direct objective support for cognition.

For instance, when an object such as a jar, which is covered by darkness and so forth in the world, attains the status of being an object of cognition through the removal of the covering by light and so forth, it does not deviate from its prior existence.
In the same way, we understand that this world also existed prior to its origination;

for a jar that does not exist is not perceived even when the sun has risen. If it is argued that it would indeed be perceived because there is no absence of existence [prior to its creation], [we reply: no.

If it is argued that, since your effect such as a jar is never non-existent, it would indeed be perceived when the sun has risen, provided the lump of clay is present and there is no obscuration such as darkness;
we say no, because obscuration is of two kinds.

For the obscuration of an effect such as a jar is twofold: first, darkness, walls, and so forth, which obscure what has already been separated from its material cause like clay; and second, the existence of the parts of clay and other materials in the form of another effect, such as a lump, prior to the manifestation of the jar.
Therefore, the non-perception of the effect, such as a jar, which exists even prior to its production, is due to its being concealed.
As for the distinction between the words and cognitions of "destroyed" and "produced," or of "existence" and "non-existence," this depends on the two-fold nature of manifestation and concealment.
If it is argued that this is untenable because the concealments [such as a lump of clay or potsherds] are different from each other?

If it is argued: "For darkness, walls, and the like are observed to be obstructions of jars and the like that occupy a location distinct from the jar; however, the lump and the potsherds are not observed in a location distinct from the jar.

Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the non-perception [of the jar] is due to its being obstructed while existing within the configuration of the lump and the potsherds, because the nature of an obstruction differs [from these cases]. [Response:
No, for in the case of milk and water and the like, it is observed that the milk and other substances occupy the same location as their own obstruction.

If it is argued that there is no obstruction because the parts, such as the potsherds and dust, are included within the effect such as the jar, we say no; for since separated parts constitute a different effect, their obstructive nature is logically established.
If it is further argued that one should simply exert effort toward the absence of obstruction itself, [we reply:]...

If it is argued that the effect, such as a jar, exists even during the states of the lump of clay and the potsherd, but is not perceived because it is concealed, then one who seeks the effect—the jar and so forth—should exert effort only toward destroying that concealment and not toward the production of the jar?
This is not the case;
therefore, if it is claimed that non-perception occurs simply because something already existing is concealed, that is incorrect.
No, because there is no necessity;
for the manifestation of a jar or the like is not invariably caused by an effort directed solely toward its destruction,
since we observe that effort is required when a lamp or similar object is produced for a jar or the like that has been covered.
If it is argued that even that [effort] is solely for the purpose of destroying darkness—[we reply:
the effort involved even in the production of a lamp and the like is for the sake of removing darkness; once that [darkness] has perished, the jar is perceived by itself.
If it is argued that nothing at all is being produced [in the jar]?
No, because the jar, being possessed of light, is perceived;
just as the jar is perceived as qualified by light, it is not so perceived prior to the lighting of the lamp.
Therefore, the lighting of the lamp is not solely for the purpose of removing darkness; what then?
Because it is perceived precisely as possessing luminosity;
even in some cases where there is the destruction of an obscuration, effort would still be required.
Just as in the case of the destruction of a wall or similar obstacles,

there is therefore no fixed rule that one who desires manifestation must exert effort solely toward the destruction of an obstruction; for [otherwise] there would be a restriction on the purposefulness of the effort.
We have stated that an effect existing within its cause acts as an obstruction to other effects.
In that case, if effort were directed solely toward the destruction of the previously manifested effect— whether it be the lump of clay or the unseparated potsherd—
then effects such as shards and powder would also come into being.
Since a jar covered by that [cloth] is likewise not perceived, it must again depend upon a further effort [of uncovering].
Therefore, for one who desires the manifestation of a jar or the like, the operation of causal factors is indeed purposeful.
Consequently, that very effect exists even prior to its production.
Furthermore, due to the distinction between cognitions of the past and the future:

it is not logical that the cognitions "the past jar" and "the future jar" should be devoid of objects, just as the cognition of a present jar is not; moreover, there is the activity of one who desires a future object.
For in the world, activity is never observed to occur in the absence of a desire for an object;
and since the knowledge of the past and future possessed by yogins is true,
if the future jar were non-existent, the yogin’s direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*) concerning that future jar would be false, yet such a perception is not treated as figurative.
We have already stated that there is inference regarding the existence of a jar;
furthermore, it is because of contradiction.

If it is determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while the potter and others are engaged in activity for the sake of a jar that "the jar will exist," and if it is said that at such a time the jar will be connected [with its future state], [then there is a contradiction].
At that very time, it is a contradiction to state that "the jar is non-existent," meaning that the jar which is yet to come into being is non-existent— that is, it will not exist.
It is just as one might say, "This jar does not exist. Now, if it were said that the jar was non-existent prior to its production,
then while the potter and others are engaged in activity for the sake of the jar, those very potters and others are, for the time being, present in the form of their exertion.
Likewise, if the meaning of the word "non-existent" is that "the jar does not exist," there is no contradiction.
Why? Because the jar exists by way of its future form; for the state of being present belongs neither to the lump of clay nor to the shards, but to the jar.
Nor does the jar possess that future state [of the potter].
Therefore, it is not contradictory to say that the jar is non-existent prior to its production while the activity of the potter and others is present.
This would be so if the jar's own future form as an effect were being negated.
To deny that would involve a contradiction;
yet you do not deny it.
Furthermore, it is not the case that all causal factors possessing activity have only one single state, whether present or future.

Furthermore, among the four kinds of absences, the mutual absence (itaretarābhāva) of a jar is seen to be distinct from the jar; for example, the absence of a jar is simply a cloth or the like, not the very nature of the jar itself.
Moreover, the existing cloth that constitutes the absence of the jar is not of the nature of an absence;
rather, it is indeed of the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa).
In this way, the prior non-existence, the non-existence after destruction, and the absolute non-existence of a jar would also have to be distinct from the jar itself,
because they are designated by means of the jar, just like the mutual non-existence of the jar.
The same applies to the positive nature of absences.
This being the case, if one says "the prior non-existence of the jar," it is not that the very nature of the jar does not exist prior to its production.

If, on the other hand, "the prior non-existence of the jar" were intended to mean that which is the very nature of the jar itself, then the designation "of the jar" would be untenable. If it were designated by such a conceptual construction, it would be like saying "the body of a stone statue."
Nevertheless, the designation "prior absence of the jar" refers only to an absence that is conceptually constructed, not to the very nature of the jar itself.
If it is argued that the absence of the jar is a distinct entity from the jar,
this has already been answered.

Furthermore, prior to its production, a jar—which is non-existent like the horn of a hare—cannot enter into a relation with the existence of its own cause, because a relation must reside in two things. If it is argued that this fault does not apply to inseparable entities (*ayutasiddha*), we say no; for it is impossible for existence and non-existence to be inseparable.

For conjunction (*yutasiddhatā*) or non-conjunction (*ayutasiddhatā*) may exist between two positive entities (*bhāva*), but not between a positive entity and a non-entity (*abhāva*), nor between two non-entities.
Therefore, it is established that the effect exists as a reality even prior to its production.
To the question, "By death of what characteristic is it veiled?", he says: "By hunger" (*aśanāyayā*). Hunger (*aśanāyā*) is the desire to eat; by that very [hunger]...?
The characteristic of death is indicated by that [desire] through which death is characterized.
How is it that hunger (*aśanāyā*) is death? It is said: for hunger indeed is death.
By the word "hi" (for), he indicates a well-known reason:
for whoever desires to eat, he kills living beings immediately after that hunger; therefore, Death is characterized by hunger, which is why he says, "For hunger."
Hunger is the characteristic of the intellect (buddhi) as its essence; thus, this Hiraṇyagarbha, existing in the state of the intellect, is called Death.
By that Death, this effect was covered, just as bells and other objects might be covered by clay while in the state of a lump. Such is the case here.
"He made that mind.
The word "that" (*tat*) is a reference to the mind.

That aforementioned Death, desiring to bring forth the effects to be described hereafter, created—that is, produced—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth, which is denoted by the term "mind" (*manas*) and is capable of contemplating those effects.
With what intention did he create the mind? It is said: "May I be *ātmanvī*, that is, possessed of a self (*ātmavān*).
The intention was: "By means of this self, the mind, may I be *manasvī*, possessed of a mind."

That Prajāpati, possessing a mind through his manifested intellect and being thus endowed with thought, moved about—meaning he performed his course of action—worshipping, causing others to worship, and honoring himself, thinking, "I have accomplished my purpose.
As that Prajāpati was worshipping and honoring, the waters, which consist of essence and serve as the constituent parts of worship, were born, i.e., they came into existence.
In this context, it should be stated that this occurred immediately after the production of the triad beginning with space.

Due to the force of other scriptural passages and because an option regarding the order of creation is impossible, Death thought, "For me who am being honored—that is, for me who am performing worship—water (ka) has come into being.

Because of that very reason, it is the cause of the "ark-ness" (arkatva)—meaning the state of being the *arka* fire utilized in the Aśvamedha sacrifice—of that very fire (*arka*). This is the meaning.
These are the etymologies of the name *arka* for Agni:

because of his being worthy of worship (*arcanāt*), because he performs worship as a cause of happiness, and because of his connection with water (*ap-sambandhāt*), this name *arka* is an epithet of Agni.

He who knows and understands the "ark-ness" of the sun (*arka*) as it has been described thus—namely, that it is water (*kam*) or happiness (*sukham*) due to the commonality of the name—[attains those].
The two particles *ha* and *vā* serve the purpose of introducing [the subject].
"It indeed comes to pass" means that it happens for one who knows thus, for the sake of one who knows thus. //1//
But what is this "Aka"? It is said: Water, indeed, is Aka.
That which was the foam of the waters solidified;
it became the earth.
Upon it, he exerted himself.
From him, thus exhausted and heated, the essence of his vital energy emerged as fire.
The waters which serve as a constituent part of the fuel are indeed *arka*, because they are the cause of the fire (*arka*);
for it is said that "fire is established within the waters.
However, they are not *arka* directly in themselves.
Because they do not form the subject matter [of that section], whereas fire does form the subject matter;
and it will be stated later: "This fire is the sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7).

In that process, what of the waters was like the cream of curd, or like the solid scum on top, became condensed and attained a state of massing together, being cooked internally and externally by heat.
Or, with a change of gender, it may be understood as "that which was the solid part of the waters became condensed.
That became the earth; that aggregate became this very earth.
The meaning is that from those waters an egg was produced.
When that earth had been brought forth, that Prajāpati Mṛtyu became weary;
he became afflicted with fatigue, for the entire world becomes weary after performing its work.
This creation of the earth was a great task for Prajāpati. What happened to him who had become weary?

It is said: from him who was weary, heated, and exhausted, his *tejorasa*—that is, his very essence of energy (*tejas*), his vital sap (*rasa*)—his *tejorasa-rasa*, his strength, issued forth; the meaning is that it emerged from the body of Prajāpati.
Who is it that went forth? Fire.

Within the egg, he was born as Virāj Prajāpati, the first-born, possessed of a collection of effects and instruments (body and senses), according to the traditional text: "He is indeed the first embodied being. //2//
He divided himself threefold: the sun as one third and the wind as one third. This very vital breath (prāṇa) is thus distributed threefold.
Of that [sacrificial horse], the eastern direction is the head, and those two [intermediate directions] are the two fore-feet;
then its western direction is the tail, and those two are the two thighs;
the southern and northern directions are the two flanks.
The sky is his back, the intermediate space his belly, and this earth his chest.
He is established in the waters;
wherever he goes, he is established there—so it is for one who knows thus.
And having been born, that Prajāpati himself divided—meaning he distributed—himself, his own aggregate of effects and instruments, into three ways.
In what way into three? He says: "He made the sun the third," which follows from the context as meaning he completed the triad in relation to fire and wind.
Likewise, fire is to be seen as the third in relation to wind and the sun;
similarly, fire is to be seen as the third in relation to wind and the sun.
This is because the capacity of all three is equal in fulfilling the number three.

This very Prāṇa is the Self of all beings; specifically, it is divided and distributed in three ways—by way of the forms of fire, wind, and the sun—not by the destruction of its own essential nature as Virāj.
Now, the vision of this first-born Agni, who is the Arka employed in the Aśvamedha and who consists of the piled altar (citi), is described as being like that of a horse.
For we have already stated that the entire previously mentioned account of his origin is for the purpose of praise, so that one may understand: "In this manner, his birth is pure."
The eastern direction is its head, due to the common quality of being preeminent.
That [northeast] and that [southeast] are the two shoulders (īrmāu), the arms;
for the root *īr* signifies the act of moving.
Now, the western direction of this fire-altar is its tail, that is, its hind part, because it is connected with the western direction for one facing east;
and those two, namely the northwestern (vāyavya) and southwestern (nairṛtya) corners, are its two thighs, due to their commonality as being the rear corners of the back.
The south and the north are the two sides, due to the commonality of their connection with both directions.
"The sky is the back and the atmosphere is the belly" is as explained before.
This [earth] is the chest, due to the commonality of being the lower part.
This very fire, which is of the nature of Prajāpati and consists of the worlds and so forth, is established in the waters, according to the Vedic revelation: "Thus these worlds are within the waters.

Wherever it goes—that is, to whatever place it moves—it becomes established right there; it finds its support. Who is this? It is one who knows, who understands, the aforementioned fact of the fire being established in the waters; such is the fruit of this quality. //3//
That which is death created, by means of the sequence beginning with water, the Virāj—endowed with a collection of effects and instruments—within the cosmic egg as its own self from itself;
and it has been stated that "it made itself threefold. What was its activity while creating? This is explained:
He desired: "Let a second self be born to me.
Through his mind, he entered into union with speech—[that is,] hunger, which is death.
That which was the seed became the year;
for prior to that, there was no year.
He bore him for as long as the duration of a year.
After that much time, he created him;
as soon as he was born, he opened his mouth wide,
and he uttered the sound "bhāṇ."
That very thing became speech.
That Death desired; what did he desire? "May a second self—a body—be born for me, by which I may become embodied. Thus he desired.

Having thus desired, he, through the mind that had previously arisen, entered into union with Speech as his characteristic—that is, he brought about a state of duality or pairing; he mentally contemplated the three Vedas.
The meaning is that he reflected in his mind upon the sequence of creation ordained by the three Vedas. Who is this? It is Death, characterized by hunger;
for it has been said that "hunger is death."
He refers back to that very same [seed] so that there may be no further digression elsewhere.
"That which was the seed"—that which was the seed in that couple; at the time of the birth of Prajāpati, the first embodied being, the seed was the cause, consisting of knowledge and action.
Upon reflecting on the three Vedas, he perceived that which had been performed in a previous birth.
Being permeated by the thought of that [past action], he created the waters and, having entered into those waters with that semen as his seed, became an embryo in the form of an egg;
he became the year, the Prajāpati who is the creator of the duration of a year.
Indeed, previously— before that,
prior to the creator Prajāpati who fashioned the year as time—
the year, known as time, did not exist.

He bore— that is, Death sustained— for as long as this well-known time exists here, for a duration consisting of so many years, that Creator of the time-period of a year who is the Prajāpati within the womb;
for as long as a year is well-known here.
What did he do after that?
After this much time—after a mere year—he brought him forth; that is to say, he broke open the egg. Thus, he created that newborn boy, Agni, the first embodied being.
Because he possessed hunger, Death opened his mouth wide to devour him;
and that boy, being afraid and endowed with innate ignorance, made the sound "bhāṇ. That very sound became speech.
Speech became sound. //4//
He reflected: "If I were to think of this [world] with my mind, I would create less food.
With that speech and by means of that self, he emitted all this—whatever exists here: the *ṛg* verses, the *yajus* formulas, the *sāman* chants, the meters, the sacrifices, progeny, and cattle.
Whatever he created, he resolved to eat;

because he eats everything, that is the essence of Aditi’s being Aditi. He who knows this essence of Aditi’s being Aditi becomes the eater of all, and everything becomes his food. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5)
"He looked": having seen the boy who was thus terrified and crying out, Death—the one possessed of hunger—looked (aikṣata) at him.
Even though he was hungry, he thought: "At some time or other, I shall even eat this boy"; for the verb *man* preceded by *abhi* has the sense of injury, meaning "I shall harm him.
He thought: "I shall make food scantier," that is, "I shall make the food very small."
Having perceived this, he desisted from eating it, [thinking]: "Indeed, much food must be produced by us for consumption over a long period;
if we eat that [earth], there would be less food, just as when seeds are eaten, there is an absence of crops.
Having thus reflected on the necessity of an abundance of food, with that very same threefold speech previously mentioned and with that same self—
Having repeatedly contemplated the act of sexual union with his mind, he created all this—whatever exists here, both the stationary and the moving.

What is that? It is the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and the meters, beginning with the seven such as the Gāyatrī, which consist of the threefold types of hymns and recitations that serve as the constituent parts of ritual action.

He created the mantras distinguished by meters such as the *gāyatrī*, the sacrifices accomplished by them, the progeny who perform those acts, and the domestic and wild animals that serve as the instruments for those rites.
Now, it was previously stated that he created [the world] through the three Vedas joined in union; how then is it said here that he created the *ṛc* verses and so forth?
This is not a fault;
for the mind, this union with the threefold [Veda] is unmanifest,
whereas for the external *Ṛg* and other Vedas, "creation" is the manifestation of those very [texts] already existing through their application (*viniyoga*) in ritual acts.
Having thus perceived the increase of food, that Prajāpati resolved—that is, fixed his mind—to eat whatever he created, whether it were a means for performing rituals or a fruit thereof.
Because he eats (*atti*) everything (*sarvam*) in its entirety (*kṛtsnam*), therefore the state of being Aditi belongs to Death, who is named Aditi.
And so says the mantra: “Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space, Aditi is the mother, she is the father,” and so forth (Yajurveda Saṃhitā 25.23).
He becomes the eater of this entire world that has become food, by means of his very self as the All; for otherwise there would be a contradiction.
Indeed, no single person is seen who is the eater of everything; therefore, the meaning is that he becomes the Self of all.
Everything becomes his food.
For this very reason, it is logical that everything becomes food for the eater who is the Self of all.
This is the fruit for one who thus knows, as has been described, the nature of Aditi—how she is called Aditi because she eats (adana) Death, Prajapati, and indeed everything. //5//
He desired: "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice. He exerted himself.
He performed austerity.
As he was weary from his exertion and heated by his penance, his glory and vigor departed.
Indeed, glory and vigor are the vital breaths.
When the vital breaths had departed, the body began to swell;
his mind remained within that very body.

Regarding the passage "He desired," this is stated for the purpose of defining the terms *aśva* and *aśvamedha*: "May I sacrifice again with a greater, more magnificent sacrifice. The word *bhūyaḥ* (again/greater) is used in reference to another birth. That Prajāpati sacrificed with the Aśvamedha in another birth.
Pervaded by that very state of being, he emerged at the beginning of the kalpa.
Having manifested as the essence of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha)—its ritual actions, its agents, and its fruits—he desired: "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice.
Having thus desired such a great undertaking, he became exhausted, just like people in the world.
He performed austerity.
As before, when he was weary and heated,
his fame and vigor departed.

He himself states the meaning of the terms: "The vital breaths" refers to the eyes and so forth; "glory" (*yaśas*) is so called because it is the cause of glory, for through them there arises an excellence of happiness;
likewise, "valor" (*vīrya*) is strength in this body. Thus, glory characterized by the vital breaths and valor have "departed," that is, they have gone forth.

Thus, when fame, vigor, and the vital breaths had departed—that is, when they had issued forth from the body—that body of Prajāpati remained fixed in a state of putrefaction, becoming swollen and impure. Even though he had emerged from that body, the mind of Prajāpati remained in that very body, just as the mind of someone remains fixed on a beloved object even when they have gone far away. //6//
With his mind fixed on that very body, what did he do? It is said: He desired, "May this [body] of mine be fit for sacrifice (medhya); may I be embodied through it."
From that, the horse came into being. Because it breathed (*aśvat*), it became fit for sacrifice (*medhya*); that is precisely why the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is called "horse-sacrifice.
Verily, he who knows it thus knows the horse-sacrifice.
He did not keep it confined,
but let it go; after a year had passed, he sacrificed it for himself and drove the other animals away to the deities.
Therefore, they immolate a victim consecrated for all the gods and dedicated to Prajāpati.
This one who shines yonder is indeed the Aśvamedha;
the year is his body.
This Agni is the Arka;
these worlds are its bodies.
These two are the Arka and the Aśvamedha.
Furthermore, that deity becomes one alone—namely, Death itself.
He conquers repeated death;
death does not overtake him.
Death becomes his very self;
he reaches a full lifespan;
he becomes one with these deities.

He desired: "How might this body of mine become *medhya*—fit for sacrifice, worthy of the sacrificial offering—and furthermore, how might I, possessing a self (*ātmanvān*), be embodied through this body? Thus he entered it.
Because that body, through separation from it, caused his movement, fame, and vigor to perish (*aśvat*), therefore he became a horse (*aśva*).
Thus, Prajāpati himself is praised as being directly named "Aśva.

Furthermore, because through its entry [into him], his impurity became pure due to his possession of movement, fame, and vigor, for that very reason the sacrifice named Aśvamedha obtained the name "Aśvamedha"—that is, the attainment of the designation Aśvamedha.
For sacrifice consists of action, its factors, and its fruit;
and it is Prajāpati himself who is thus praised.
The identity of the horse—the means for accomplishing the sacrifice—with Prajāpati has been stated in the passage beginning, "The Dawn, indeed, is the intelligence of the horse," and so forth.

The following section begins with the injunction that one should practice the meditation upon this very horse, which is fit for sacrifice and whose nature is that of Prajāpati and Agni as previously described, by way of identifying it with the essence of the fruit of the ritual (*kratu*).
Since no injunctive verb was heard in the preceding portion, and because a context requires a verb, this meaning is understood:
"He indeed knows the Aśvamedha sacrifice who knows him thus."
Whoever knows this horse— which is Agni and the Sun— as characterized by the aforementioned description and by the specific qualification that will be shown hereafter in brief,
he alone knows the Aśvamedha, and no other. Therefore, the meaning is that it should be known in this manner.
How so? First, he describes the view concerning the sacrificial animal (*paśu*):

In that regard, Prajāpati, having desired, "May I sacrifice further with a greater sacrifice," fashioned himself alone as the sacrificial animal; he considered—that is, reflected upon—that very animal as one released, having not penned it up, having not performed the penning-in of the animal, [and thus] with its tether unfastened.

At the end of the full year, he offered it up for himself—that is, for his own sake—with Prajāpati as its deity; he performed the act of offering. He then returned the other animals, both domestic and wild, to their respective deities according to their specific divinities.

And because Prajāpati thought in this way, therefore another person also, having prepared himself as a sacrificial animal—the horse—according to the stated rule, [should think]: "I belong to all the gods when being sprinkled with water; but when being offered, I am..."

One should know: "May I indeed belong to my own deity; other animals—both domestic and wild—are sacrificed to other deities according to their respective deities, but [I am sacrificed] to those who have become my very limbs.
For this very reason, even now, the ritualists sacrifice the consecrated animal dedicated to Prajāpati as belonging to all the deities.

"In this very way, indeed, the Ashvamedha is he who shines yonder"—that sacrifice which has the animal as its means is here pointed out directly as the result itself: "This, indeed, is the Ashvamedha.
Who is he? He who is the Sun (Savitṛ) shining there, illuminating the world with his splendor.
Of this [Sun], whose nature is the fruit of the sacrifice, the year is the specific period of time.
The self is the body, because the year is brought about by it;
and since that very [year] has the nature of a sacrifice (*kratu*) and the fruit is accomplished through fire, it is designated specifically by way of its form as a sacrifice.
This terrestrial fire is the sun, serving as the means of accomplishment.
And of that sun, when piled in the sacrifice, these three worlds are its own selves—that is, its bodily limbs.
This has been explained in the passage beginning with, "Its eastern quarter... and so forth.
These two, Agni and Āditya, as specifically characterized, constitute the Arka and Aśvamedha sacrifices, which are the fruits of ritual action.
That which is the earthly fire (Agni) is directly the form of the sacrifice, consisting of action;
because the sacrifice is accomplished by means of fire, it is designated by that very form.
And because the fruit is to be accomplished by means of the sacrifice, it is designated in the very form of the sacrifice, as in "The Sun is the Aśvamedha.
These two— Agni and Āditya— who constitute the sacrifice and its fruit as the goal and the means,
become once again, moreover, a single deity.
Who is she? She is death itself.
Even previously, she was one alone, differentiated for the sake of the distinction between action, means, and fruit.
And so it has been said: "He divided himself threefold" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.3).
Furthermore, after the completion of the ritual action, that very same deity becomes Death itself in the form of the fruit.
He who knows this Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha)—Death—the single deity in this way:

"I am indeed Death, the single deity Aśvamedha; I am of one form, to be accomplished through the means of the horse and the fire," he conquers repeated death; having died once, he is not born again for the sake of further dying.
This is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection that even though death has been defeated, it might nevertheless return to him, he says: "Death does not reach him.
Why? Because for one who knows thus, death itself becomes his very self.
Moreover, death itself, being the very form of the fruit, becomes one with those deities;
this is its fruit. //7//
Thus ends the second Agni-Brāhmaṇa in the first chapter.
What is the connection of this [section] beginning with "Two kinds" (*dvayā heti*) and so forth?
The supreme goal of actions accompanied by knowledge has been described through the statement regarding the goal of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), which is the state of being Death himself.
Now, the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa is commenced in order to illuminate that from which arise both action and knowledge, which serve as the means for attaining the state of being Death himself.
[Objection: But has it not been stated previously that the state of being death itself is the fruit of knowledge and action?

However, [in this section] he will state that the fruit of the knowledge and action concerning the *udgītha* is the transcendence of the state of being death itself. Therefore, since the fruits have different scopes, [this present passage] is not intended to reveal the manner in which the previous actions and knowledge arise.
[Reply: This is not a fault.
Because the fruit of the *udgītha* has fire (*agni*) and the sun (*āditya*) as its nature;
for even in the preceding section, this very same fruit was stated: "He becomes one of these deities.
But is it not a contradiction [to say] "he has transcended death," and so forth?
This is because the act of transcending has as its object an inherent attachment to evil.
What is this inherent attachment to evil? It is death.
And from what does its arising occur?
By what means or in what manner can there be its transgression?
To elucidate this matter, he begins a narrative.
How so?
There were two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring, the gods and the asuras; of these, the gods were fewer, while the asuras were more numerous.
They contended with one another for these worlds.
Those gods said, "Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha."
"Dvayā" means of two kinds.
The particle "ha" is an expletive used to indicate a past event;
by this word "ha," he brings to light what occurred in the previous birth of Vāmadeva.
The *prājāpatyas* are the offspring of Prajāpati while he was in the state of being born (*vṛttajanmāvastha*).
Who are they? They are the gods and the asuras. Furthermore, his vital breaths (*prāṇas*), such as speech and the others, are also [the *prājāpatyas*].
But how is it that they possess the nature of gods (*deva*) and asuras?
It is said: those who are cultivated by knowledge and action produced from the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*) become gods because they ascend to heaven (*dyodanāt*).
Those same beings, when cultivated by knowledge of action whose purpose is perceived through innate perception and inference, become asuras.
Because they delight in their own vital breaths (*asu*), or because they are other than the *surās* (the gods),
and because the *asuras* are characterized by knowledge and actions directed toward visible purposes, for that reason they are fewer in number.

*Kānīyāṃsaḥ* means *kānīyasāḥ*; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), resulting in the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*). Thus, *kanīyāṃsaḥ* simply means "few" or "small"; [here] the gods are indeed few.
The Asuras were superior to the Devas;

for the natural inclination toward action and knowledge is greater for living beings than the inclination toward action and knowledge produced by the scriptures, because the latter has a visible purpose.
For this very reason, the Devas were inferior, due to the smallness of their scripture-born inclination.
For that [creation] is to be accomplished through extreme effort.

Those gods and asuras, residing within the body of Prajāpati, contended—that is, they engaged in rivalry—within these worlds which serve as the instrumental causes and are to be accomplished through natural and non-natural karma and knowledge.
The rivalry between the gods and the asuras consists in the emergence and suppression of their respective modes of existence (*vṛtti*).
Sometimes there arises in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) a function consisting of the cultivation of knowledge of action produced by the scriptures;

and when that arises, the function of those very same vital breaths—which consists of the cultivation of knowledge of action produced by perception and inference and which has visible purposes—is overcome by the *āsura* [nature].
That is the victory of the gods and the defeat of the *asuras*.
Sometimes, by the reverse of that, the state of the gods is overcome and the state of the asuras arises;
that is the victory of the asuras and the defeat of the gods.
Likewise, when the gods are victorious, due to the abundance of dharma, there is an upward progression until the attainment of the status of Prajāpati.
When the Asuras were victorious, because of the predominance of unrighteousness, there was a decline [of life-span] until the attainment of the state of stationary beings.
When both sides were equal, there was the attainment of the human state.
Thus, being overwhelmed by the Asuras due to their inferiority, what did the gods do because of the numerical superiority of the Asuras?

Thus it is said: those gods, being overcome by the Asuras, reportedly said— how so?— "Come now, let us pass beyond [our distress] in this Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice by means of the Udgītha, by taking recourse to the nature of the performer of the ritual act of the Udgītha."

Having said to one another, "Let us overcome the Asuras and attain our own divine nature as revealed in the scriptures," they took recourse in the nature of the performer of the act and the meaning of the words of the *udgītha* through both knowledge and ritual action.
The ritual action to be performed—characterized by the silent recitation (*japa*) of mantras that is about to be described—is indicated by the injunction: "Therefore, one should recite these."
But this very knowledge is what is being defined here.

[Objection: Is it not the case that this [passage], consisting of a specific recitation (*japa*) performed during the ascent and being an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), does not have the definition of knowledge as its primary purpose?
[Response: No, because of the statement, "He who knows thus."
If it is argued that this refers to the injunction regarding the *udgītha* because of the hearing of a past account (*purākalpa*) at the beginning of the *prastāva*, we say no;
for it is not the relevant context (*aprakaraṇāt*), and the *udgītha* has already been enjoined elsewhere.
Furthermore, because this belongs to the category of *vidyā*,
and because the recitation for ascending (*abhyāroha-japa*) is not mandatory,
it may thus be separated [from its context].
And because consciousness is heard of as being eternal,
according to the Vedic text: "This, indeed, is the winner of the worlds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.28).
This is because of the statement regarding the purity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the impurity of speech and the other organs.
For it is not the case that the purity of the vital breath is taught as something to be meditated upon while the impurity of speech and the others—which are presented together with it—is not;
rather, the praise of the primary vital breath through the censure of speech and the rest is what is intended, and this is logically consistent.
And there is the statement regarding the fruit: "He shines, having transcended death," and so forth;
for the attainment of the nature of Prāṇa results in that state wherein speech and the other organs become fire and the other elements.
Let it be granted, then, that there is meditation upon Prāṇa.
But it does not possess qualities such as purity and so forth. [Objection:
But surely it must, because it is so stated in scripture.
[Reply: It would not.
[Objection: It may be argued that being an object of worship is justified as being for the purpose of praise.
[Reply: No; because the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) is possible through the comprehension of the non-erroneous meaning, as is seen in the world.
For in the world, he who comprehends the non-erroneous meaning attains what is desired and turns away from what is undesired.
It is not through the comprehension of a contrary meaning;
likewise here as well, in the comprehension of the meaning produced by the words heard in scripture, the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) is logical, and not in the opposite case.
Furthermore, there is no evidence that the object of the cognition arising from the words heard for the purpose of meditation is unreal.
Nor is any denial of that cognition heard;
therefore, because we observe the attainment of the highest good [from it], we conclude its correspondence with reality, and because we observe the attainment of misfortune in the opposite case.
For in the world, a person who perceives an object erroneously— such as taking a post for a man, or an enemy for a friend— is seen to meet with misfortune.
If even the grasping of the self, the Lord, the deities, and so forth from the Śruti were indeed unreal,
then the scripture would certainly result in the attainment of what is harmful, just as in the case of worldly [traditions];
and this is not desired.
Therefore, the scripture causes one to grasp the self, the Lord, the deities, and so forth exactly as they are, for the purpose of worship.
If it is argued that this is improper because we observe the practice of viewing names and the like as Brahman, [the reply is: the non-Brahman nature of names and the like is perfectly clear;
in those cases, the scripture is seen to cause one to grasp a contrary view—viewing them as Brahman—just as one might view a post as a person.

If it is argued that, therefore, it has been stated that spiritual welfare (*śreyaḥ*) arises from understanding [Brahman] exactly as it is according to the scripture, we say no; for the understanding [of Brahman] is based on a conceptualized distinction (*pratimāvat-bheda-pratipatti*).
The scripture causes one to grasp a contrary view—namely, the vision of Brahman in what is not Brahman, such as names and so forth—just as one might grasp the vision of a person in a post.

Thus, you have not spoken correctly. Why? Because the perception of Brahman is enjoined upon the name and other objects—which are understood as distinct from Brahman—just as the perception of Viṣṇu is enjoined upon an image and the like.
For the apprehension of the name and so forth serves as the objective support (*ālambana*), just as an image does.
But it is not that name and so forth alone are Brahman;
just as when a post is not correctly known, one does not think "this is a post," but instead apprehends it erroneously as "this is indeed a person."
But the perception of Brahman in names and so forth is not likewise a misconception;
for if it is argued that there is no such thing as the exclusive perception of Brahman,
then by this [argument] the perceptions of Viṣṇu and other gods, or of ancestors and so forth, in images, Brahmins, and the like, would be equal [to the perception of Brahman].
No, because we observe the viewing of the earth and so forth upon the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas.
For it is observed that there is a superimposition (*kṣepa*) of the very objects—the earth and so forth—which already exist, onto the domain of the *Ṛgveda* and others.
Therefore, by analogy with that, it is established that the views of Brahman and so forth upon names and the like have as their objects the existing Brahman and so forth.
By this, it is established that the cognitions of Viṣṇu and other deities, or of the ancestors and others, directed toward images, Brahmins, and so forth, have real entities as their objects;
for secondary (gauna) usage depends upon a primary (mukhya) one.

And just as in the case of the "five fires" and similar instances, where the nature of fire is secondary and thus implies the existence of a primary fire, so too, since the nature of Brahman in names and so forth is secondary, the existence of a primary Brahman is logically established.

And because there is no distinction [in their status] regarding those whose purpose is action, the same applies to those whose purpose is knowledge. Just as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rituals possess specific fruits, specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*), and are employed with specific sequences and subsidiaries— this being a non-worldly reality that is not an object of perception and other means of knowledge,
but is made known only by Vedic statements— so too is it with knowledge.

Likewise, the reality of the Supreme Self, the Lord, the Deity, and so forth, is made known by Vedic statements alone as being characterized by such attributes as "not gross" and being "beyond hunger and thirst";
therefore, because it is non-worldly, it must exist exactly in that way.
Furthermore, there is no difference in their capacity to produce cognition between sentences concerning ritual action and sentences concerning knowledge.
Furthermore, a cognition whose object is a reality such as the Supreme Self does not arise unless it is certain or free from error.

If it is argued that this is improper because there would be nothing to be performed, [we reply: by means of sentences whose purpose is action, even a non-worldly threefold *bhāvanā* is made known as something to be performed;
however, in the case of the knowledge of the Supreme Self, the Lord, and so forth, there is nothing whatsoever to be performed in that manner.

If it is argued that, for this reason, the claim of similarity with the objects of action is incorrect, we say no; for knowledge has as its object an entity as it actually is. Its "as-it-is-ness" does not arise from the fact of being something to be performed, but rather from the fact of being apprehended by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor does the cognition regarding that object possess such validity simply because its object is something to be performed;
rather, it possesses it precisely because it is produced by a Vedic statement.
When an entity understood through a Vedic statement is found to be so [as it appears], one performs it if it is qualified as something to be performed.
If it is argued that if one does not perform what is qualified by being something to be performed,
or if it is not something to be performed, then the status of the sentence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable—
[we reply: for indeed, in the absence of something to be performed, the co-occurrence (*sahati*) of words is not possible.

However, when there is something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), words are combined for the sake of that performance. In that case, a sentence (*vākya*) which culminates in what is to be performed becomes a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), in the form: "This should be done by this [means] in this manner. But a collection of even hundreds of words does not constitute a sentence if it lacks any one of the following five verbal suffixes: *kuryāt* (optative), *kriyeta* (passive optative), *kartavyam* (gerundive), *bhavet* (optative), or *syāt* (optative). Thus it is said: "There are five [suffixes]: *kuryāt*, *kriyeta*, *kartavyam*, *bhavet*, and *syāt*. In the absence of any one of these, there is no sentential unity.

If it is argued: "Therefore, the Supreme Self, the Lord, and so forth lack the status of being objects of verbal testimony; and if they were word-meanings, they would necessarily be objects of other means of valid cognition.
Consequently, this [position of yours] is untenable."
This is because we observe sentences such as "Mount Meru is endowed with four colors," which refer to things that cannot be performed;
nor does the hearing of a sentence like "Mount Meru is endowed with four colors" give rise to the notion that Mount Meru or the like is something to be performed.

Likewise, who can prevent the synthesis of the words in sentences that establish the Supreme Self, the Lord, and so forth, when they are accompanied by the word "is" (*asti*) and stand in the relationship of qualifier and qualified?
If it is argued that [the inquiry into Brahman] is improper because there is no purpose in the knowledge of the Supreme Self—just as there is none in the knowledge of Mount Meru and the like—we say:

no. For it is said: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; the knot of the heart is severed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
8) Because of the hearing of this result [in scripture],
because of the observation of the cessation of defects such as ignorance— the seed of saṃsāra—
and because that knowledge is not subordinate to anything else.
Just as in the case of the *juhū* ladle, the mention of a fruit [of action] cannot be taken as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, the connection between prohibited acts and undesirable results is known from the Veda itself;
yet, that [prohibited act] is not something to be performed.
Furthermore, for one who has engaged in an action regarding a prohibited object, there is nothing else to be performed other than its non-performance.
For, in the ultimate sense, the very culmination of prohibitive injunctions must consist in the knowledge that something is not to be done.

When someone afflicted by hunger, conditioned by the knowledge of the prohibition, encounters something unfit to be eaten or consumed—such as *kalaja* (mangoes in season) or food defiled by a criminal accusation—the cognition arises: "This is edible" or "This is fit to be consumed."
It is sublated by the memory of the cognition of negation directed toward that object,
just as the cognition of drinkable water in a mirage is sublated by the knowledge of the true nature of that object.
When that [cognition] is sublated, the activity of bathing or eating— which is inherently non-existent and harmful— no longer occurs.
There is simply the cessation of activity caused by erroneous cognition; no further effort need be exerted once that [activity] has ceased.
Therefore, the injunctions of prohibition have as their ultimate goal only the knowledge of the true nature of reality.
There is not even a scent of dependence upon human effort [in those cases].
Likewise here too, the injunctions for the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self and so forth would terminate in that alone;
and thus, for one whose cognition is refined by that [knowledge], the activities caused by cognitions of objects contrary to it would result in what is harmful.

Because it is something being known, when the innate cognition of its cause is sublated by the recollection of the knowledge of the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the Supreme Self and so forth, there would be an absence [of that innate cognition].

If it is argued: "But surely, just as the absence of activity toward harmful acts such as eating *kalañja* occurs when the innate erroneous cognition regarding the edibility of such things is removed by the recollection of the knowledge of the true nature of reality—that these acts lead to harm—it is not logical that there should be an absence of activity toward what is enjoined by scripture, since that does not fall within the scope of prohibition."
No, because they are equal in being caused by perverted cognition and in having the nature of being purposeless.
For instance, the engagement in such acts as eating *kalañja* is caused by false cognition,
and it is likewise purposeless.

The same applies to activities prescribed by the scriptures.
