Therefore, since even those activities prescribed by the scriptures are equal [to worldly actions] in that they are caused by false knowledge and result in what is harmful, their non-existence is indeed proper once false cognition has been sublated by the knowledge of the supreme Self.

If it is argued: "But in that case, [non-existence] is logical; however, since eternal things have solely the scripture as their cause and lack any purposeful utility, their non-existence is not logical."
It is not so, because [the obligatory rites] are prescribed for one who possesses defects such as ignorance, attachment, and aversion.

Just as the optional rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are prescribed for one who possesses defects such as the desire for heaven, so too are the obligatory rites prescribed for one who possesses the defect of ignorance—the seed of all misfortune—and the defects of attachment and aversion arising therefrom, which seek to obtain the desired and avoid the undesired; and for one who, impelled by those [defects], engages in non-specific activity and desires the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired.
It is not only the scriptural motives [that determine this].

Furthermore, there is no inherent distinction between the optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) nature of the rites of the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, Paśubandha, and Soma sacrifices.
For their status as being for the sake of desire arises from the defect of desiring heaven and so forth on the part of the agent.

Likewise, it is logical that for one who possesses defects such as ignorance, who seeks the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired as they arise by their own nature, the [Vedic] rites are eternal, because they are prescribed for him; however,
for one who possesses the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self, no rite whatsoever is found to be prescribed apart from the means of tranquility (śama).

For it is by means of the sublation of all cognitions regarding the instruments of action, such as deities and so forth, that the knowledge of the Self is enjoined; and for one whose cognitions of action, factors of action, and so forth have been sublated, engagement in ritual action is not possible,
since the commencement of action is preceded by the cognition of specific means of action and the like.
Indeed, for one who maintains the realization of Brahman—which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and is non-material and non-dual—there is no occasion for ritual action (*karma*).

If it is argued that there might be such an occasion, as in the case of engaging in activities like eating, we say no; for since activities such as eating are caused solely by defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*), their necessity is untenable [for one established in that realization].
But it is not the case that a permanent action (nitya-karman) could be established as something that is performed at some times and not performed at others;
for actions such as eating would be irregular solely because they are caused by defects (doṣa),
since the arising and subsiding of those defects are irregular, just as [the performance of] desirable acts is irregular with respect to the objects of desire.
Furthermore, because eternal duties depend upon scripture, specific times, and so forth, it is untenable for them to be indefinite.

Even though they are caused by defects [of the body], just as the optional *agnihotra*—being enjoined by scripture—depends on specific times such as evening and morning, so too would the engagement in eating and other such acts be subject to restrictive rules (*niyama*). If this is argued:

No, because the restriction is not an action, and since an action is not the motivator [of knowledge], it does not constitute a contradiction to knowledge. Therefore, even the injunction regarding the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self, by its very power, results in the purpose of an injunction prohibiting all ritual actions,
because the absence of engagement in action is the same as in the case of a prohibition.
Therefore, it is established that the treatise presents a real entity and has that as its primary purpose, just like a prohibition or a prescription. //1//
They said to Speech, "Chant the Udgītha for us.
"So be it," Speech replied, and she chanted the Udgītha for them.
Whatever enjoyment was in speech, that he sang forth for the gods;
whatever is auspicious that one speaks, that [he sang] for himself.
They understood: "Surely, with this Udgātṛ, they will surpass us."
They ran toward him and pierced him with evil.
That which is this evil is precisely that which one speaks here that is improper;
that itself is that evil.
Having thus reached a decision, those gods said to Vāk—the deity presiding over speech:
"Do thou sing for us; perform the office of the Udgātṛ."
They perceived the office of the Udgātṛ priest as being accomplished by the goddess of speech (Vāgdevatā),
and they designated that very deity in the mantra for recitation as "Lead me from non-existence to existence" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.28).
And here, it is Vāk and the other [senses] alone who are intended to be the agents of both meditation and ritual action.

Why? Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), every conventional transaction involving knowledge and its object has that [Brahman] as its agent and that very [Brahman] as its object.
For he will state in detail in the sixth chapter [of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*], “It meditates, as it were; it vibrates, as it were,” thus demonstrating the absence of the Self’s agency.

Furthermore, here too, at the end of the first chapter, he will conclude by summarizing the entire collection of actions, factors of action, and fruits, beginning with the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*).
“The threefold indeed consists of name, form, and action” (1.6.1);
this refers to the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*).

But that which is beyond the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), called the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is the domain of knowledge (*vidyā*), whose nature is not name, form, or action, as expressed by “not this, not this” (2.3.6).
6) Thus, by means of the rejection of other [theories], he will conclude separately:

"As for that transmigrating self which is conceptually constructed as having the aggregate of speech and so forth as its limiting adjunct, he will show that very self to be partial toward the aggregate of speech and so forth, in the words: ‘Arising from these elements, one perishes after them’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12)."
Therefore, it is logical that speech and the other [senses] alone are intended to be the agents of knowledge and action and the attainers of the fruit.

"So be it"—having been told this by the gods, Speech performed the *udgāna* for the sake of the gods who were seeking their own purpose. But what was this specific effect accomplished by Speech through the act of *udgāna* for the sake of the gods?

It is said as follows: when speech has become the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), that very benefit which is produced for the aggregate of speech and so forth through the activity of speaking and the like is [the result].

For this enjoyment (*bhoga*) produced by the speaking of speech is the fruit for all [the priests]. Having established that enjoyment in the first three *pavamāna* [stotras], she [Speech] performs the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) as prescribed by the text in the remaining nine *stotras*; the fruit is that which she speaks auspiciously and beautifully—that is, she brings about the articulation of phonemes (*varṇa*).
That [is] for myself alone;
for that—namely, the correct pronunciation of phonemes—is the unique function of the goddess of speech (vāgdevatā).
Therefore, it is specifically qualified as "that which speaks what is auspicious."
As for that function of speaking which consists in benefiting the entire assembly, that belongs exclusively to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Thereupon, having found an opening in the deity by way of attachment to the occasion of associating with the auspicious speech, those Asuras thought: "How?

By means of this Udgātṛ, having surpassed and transcended us—our innate knowledge—with a light consisting of ritual action and knowledge produced by the scriptures, in the form of the Udgātṛ-self, they will pass us by."
Having understood this, they rushed toward the Udgātṛ, approached him, and pierced him with their own evil characterized by attachment—that is to say, they struck him and joined it to him.
That very evil which had been cast upon the speech of Prajāpati while he was in his previous state of birth is now made manifest before our eyes.

What is it? It is that which one speaks in such a way as to be improper, unsuitable, and forbidden by the scriptures—by which, being impelled, one speaks even against one's will words that are indecent, loathsome, false, and so forth.
Being followed by this unseemly face as its effect, it exists within the speech among the creatures that constitute the work of Prajāpati.
That very thing, inferred by the unseemly face, is the evil situated in the speech of Prajāpati;
for the effect conforms to its cause. //2//
Then they said to the breath, "Sing the Udgītha for us.
"So be it," said the breath; and for them, the breath sang the Udgītha.
Whatever enjoyment there was in the vital breath (prāṇa), he secured for the gods by singing; whatever was auspicious that he smelled, he secured for himself.
They perceived: "Surely, with this as our Udgātṛ priest, they will surpass us."
They ran toward it and pierced it with evil.
That which is this evil is precisely that which one smells here as something disagreeable;
that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to the eye, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said the eye]. For them, the eye sang the Udgītha;
whatever enjoyment was in the eye, that it sang for the gods.
Whatever auspicious thing he saw, he directed toward himself;
they realized, "By this Udgātṛ priest, they will surpass us," and having rushed at him,
they pierced him with evil.
That which is this evil is indeed that which one sees here as unseemly;
that itself is that evil.
Then they said to the ear, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [it replied]. For them, the ear sang the Udgītha.
Whatever enjoyment was in the ear, that it sang for the gods.
Whatever auspicious thing he heard, he appropriated for himself. They realized, "By this Udgātṛ priest, they will surely surpass us. So, rushing toward him, they pierced him with evil.
That which is evil is this very thing that he hears here as discordant;
that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to the mind, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said] the mind; it sang the Udgītha for them.
Whatever enjoyment is in the mind, that it sang forth for the gods.
Whatever good intention he formed, they directed toward themselves; they knew, "By this Udgātṛ, they will surely surpass us," and having rushed upon him, they pierced him with evil.
That which is evil is this very thing: whatever one conceives that is improper;
that indeed is that evil.
In this very way, they indeed assailed these deities with evils;
in this very way, they pierced them with evil.

In the same manner, the deities of the sense of smell and the others, because they are the performers of the *udgītha* and are revealed by the mantra used for recitation, were examined in succession as objects of meditation.

It was determined by the gods that these deities—speech and the rest—when examined in order, were incapable of accomplishing the *udgītha* due to contact with the evil of the Asuras, caused by attachment to their own connection with specific beautiful objects;
therefore, they are not to be designated [by the mantra] "Lead me from the unreal to the real," nor are they to be meditated upon.
"Because they were impure and because they did not pervade the others.

Thus, although these deities of the skin and so forth were not explicitly mentioned, they are included by the very observation of their good and evil effects, just like the deities of speech and the rest.
As for what was said—"they pierced them with evil"—it means that they joined them with evils, that is, they brought about contact with evils. (3–6)

Even though they were worshipping the deities of speech and the other senses, the gods remained without refuge for transcending death; thus, in due order— Then they said to this breath in the mouth, "Do thou sing the Udgītha for us. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.7)
"So be it," [they said]; then this Prāṇa sang the Udgītha for them.
They realized, "With this as our Udgātṛ, they will surely surpass us.
They rushed at him, intending to pierce him with evil.
Just as a clod of earth would shatter upon striking a stone, even so they shattered and perished in all directions.
Thereupon the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated.
One prospers by oneself.
The one who knows this finds his hateful rival defeated. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.7.
Now, immediately after that, [the text says] "this one"—the word "this" is used for the purpose of indicating by gesture.
They said to the *prāṇa* located in the mouth (*āsanya*), which means situated within the cavity of the mouth: "You sing the *udgītha* for us.
To those who had thus approached him for refuge, saying "So be it," this very *prāṇa*, the principal one, sang the *udgītha*, and so forth, as described previously.

Desiring to pierce—that is, wishing to effect a penetration—of the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*), which was free from association with defects, those evils, having gained a foothold in speech and the other organs through their own inherent defect of attachment, were about to become defiled by following after that habit; they perished, were destroyed, and fell apart.
How so? An illustration is given: "Just as," meaning just as in the world, having struck—that is, having gone against and reached—a stone or rock...

Just as a clod of earth— a lump of dust— thrown against a stone for the purpose of grinding it would itself shatter, crumble, and be pulverized; even so, exactly like this illustration, they perished, having utterly shattered and fallen apart in various directions toward diverse destinies, because they were destroyed.

Then, from that destruction of the Asuras, through their separation from those inherent evils born of attachment which were obstacles to their divinity, the deities— the speech and the others under discussion— became [divine] by virtue of the power of the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), whose nature is non-attachment. What did they become?
Their own divine form consists of Agni and the others, which will be described later.

Previously, even while being of the very nature of Agni and the rest, their consciousness was obscured by an inherent evil (pāpman), and they possessed only the conceit of being mere physical bodies (piṇḍa).

The meaning is that, through separation from that evil, they abandoned the conceit of being mere bodies and came to possess the conceit of being Agni and the others—speech and so forth—as established by the scriptures.
Furthermore, the phrase "the Asuras, who were their adversaries, were defeated" follows [in the text]; "defeated" means they were destroyed.

Just as in the ancient account (*purākalpa*) described earlier, the former sacrificer of a bygone time, having observed this very sacred tradition (*śruti*) in the form of a narrative, examined the deities of speech and so forth in that same sequence.

Having set aside those [speech and the rest] because they possess the defect of being the locus of attachment and evil, and having approached the primary Prāṇa—which is free from such defects—as their Self, they abandon the identification with the Self that is limited merely to the physical body consisting of speech and so forth; instead, they attain the status of Prajāpati revealed by the scriptures, which consists of identifying with the cosmic body (vairāja-piṇḍa) as the essence of speech, fire, and the rest.
In the same way, this sacrificer becomes, through that very procedure, the Self in the form of Prajāpati.
Moreover, his supreme enemy—the evil that stands as an adversary to his status as Prajāpati—becomes a hating rival (*bhrātṛvya*).
For even one who is not a hater may be a rival, such as a Bharata or similar;
however, it is the evil born from attachment to the objects of the senses that is both a rival and a hater.
Because it is the cause for concealing the delight in the nature of the ultimate Self, he is defeated and shattered like a clod of earth from the embrace of the vital breaths.
To whom does this result belong?
He says: "He who knows thus."
The meaning is that, as it has been stated, one realizes the vital breath (prāṇa) as the Self, just like the previous sacrificer. //7//

Having thus concluded the result [of the discussion], the Śruti now resorts once again to the form of a narrative and says: "For what reason, moreover, should the principal breath alone be resorted to as the Self, setting aside speech and the others? In order to demonstrate the logical justification for this—namely, that this [breath] is the common Self of speech and the rest, as well as of the physical body and so forth—the Śruti speaks by means of a narrative: [The narrative follows: "Once upon a time, the vital breaths (prāṇās) were disputing among themselves as to who was the most excellent. They went to Brahmā and said: 'O Venerable Sir, who among us is the most excellent? He replied: 'He upon whose departure you all feel most distressed is the most excellent. Then speech departed; having stayed away for a year, it returned and asked: 'How did you manage to live without me? They replied: 'Just like the dumb, not speaking but breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and knowing with the mind. And so on. This shows that even when speech and the others are absent, the body continues to function through the breath. Therefore, the breath is the common Self of all. Thus the Śruti demonstrates this meaning through the narrative.
They said: "Where indeed was he who thus attached himself to us?
"He was here within the mouth."
He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga).
Those vital breaths (prāṇas) of Prajāpati, having been made to attain the nature of the deities by means of the principal breath (mukhya prāṇa), being in the state of fruition, spoke.
What did they say? He says: "Kva nu?"—the word "nu" expressing deliberation—where indeed, in what place, was that [breath] located?
Who is he? He is the one who has thus, in this manner, attached us—that is, joined us—to the state of being a deity, having led us to identify with that as our own self.
For in the world, those who have been benefited by someone remember the benefactor;
and remembering him just as people do in the world, they, upon inquiry, perceived him within the very self, which is the aggregate of the body and the senses.
How so? "This is within the mouth"; that is, this [Self] exists perceptibly within that space which is in the mouth. For everyone in the world reaches a conclusion after having investigated.

Likewise, the gods [perceived him]. Because this Āsyāya, existing in the intermediate space as the self of speech and the other senses, was perceived by the gods without relying on any specific distinction,
therefore he, together with the vital breath (prāṇa), being unattached due to his non-reliance on distinctions, set speech and the others in motion.
For this very reason, the Self (ātman) is the essence (aṅgirasa) of the effects and instruments. How so?
For it is well known that the Self is the essence—that is, the vital sap—of the limbs characterized as the effects and instruments.
How, then, does it possess the nature of the essence of the limbs (*aṅgarasa*)?
We shall explain that this is because, upon its departure, [the body] reaches a state of desiccation.
Furthermore, because it is the essence of the limbs and because it is not dependent on any particularity, it is the common self of the organs of action and the sense organs, and it is pure.
Therefore, the meaning of the passage is that one should set aside speech and the other [organs] and take recourse in *prāṇa* alone as the Self (*ātman*).

For the Self must be accepted as the Self through non-erroneous knowledge, since this leads to the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*); for in the opposite case, the attainment of what is undesirable is observed. //8//

It might be thought that the purity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is unestablished. But has this not already been refuted by the fact that, unlike speech and the other organs which possess attachment through their involvement in pleasant speaking and so forth, the vital breath lacks any locus for attachment? Certainly; however, because speech and the others are declared to be the Self by virtue of being "belonging to Aṅgiras" (*āṅgirasa*), there arises a suspicion of impurity—just as there is regarding the creation of the corpse and its contact—by means of speech and the rest. To this he says: "The vital breath is indeed pure."
Why so?
For this deity is indeed named "The Far."
Death is indeed far from him;
death becomes far from him who knows this. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.9)
This very deity is named Dūr (the Far).
Referring to that vital breath (prāṇa) which the Asuras reached and were shattered like a stone or a clod of earth, he calls it "She" (sā).
She is indeed this very one who resides within the body of the present sacrificer and was identified by the gods as "this one within the mouth."
And that [deity] would be the object of the act of worship,
because it is subordinate as the objective of the ritual action;
she whose name is *dūḥ*, known as "Dūḥ."
The word "name" (*nāman*) is a synonym for "making known.
Therefore, because its name is well-known as "purification," why is it called "distant"? [Because] it is far from the defilements.
Thus he says: "Dūraṃ" (far), because for this deity of breath (*prāṇa*), death—characterized by attachment—is indeed far away.
Since the nature of breath is non-attachment, even though death is situated nearby, it is distant from it; therefore, its renown is "dūra" (the Far).
In this way, the purity of the breath is made known.

The fruit for the wise one is stated: "Death indeed stays far away from him. From this knower—meaning from him who knows thus, that is, who meditates upon the vital breath (prāṇa) as described in the context, endowed with the quality of purity—the meaning is that death remains distant.

What is called *upāsana* (meditative worship) is the mental approach and sitting— that is, reflection— upon the nature of the deity or other object as it is made known by the sacred scripture (*śruti*) in its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such that there arises the manifestation of the conceit of identity with that very nature of the deity, uninterrupted by worldly cognitions, just like the worldly conceit of self-identity.

This is known from such scriptural passages as: “Having been a god, he goes to the gods” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2), and “Which deity do you have in this eastern quarter? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.20). //9//
This very deity is indeed far from him; thus it has been said that death becomes distant for such a person.
But how is it that death becomes distant for one who knows thus? It is said: because of the contradiction with the state of knowing thus.
For the evil born from attachment to the contact between the senses and their objects is indeed opposed to the conceit of the vital breath as the Self,
because that [evil] is caused by the conceit of the specific selves such as speech and so forth, and because it is caused by innate ignorance;
whereas the conceit of the vital breath as the Self is produced by the scripture.
Therefore, it is logical that evil remains far away from one who knows this, because of their opposition; this very point he demonstrates: START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.10.
This very deity, having struck away the evil—death—from these deities, sent it to where the end of these quarters is;
there he deposited their evils.
Therefore, one should not go among people, nor should one go to the ends [of the quarters], lest one fall into evil—into death.
"That indeed is this deity"—the meaning of this has already been explained.
Of these deities, speech and the others, "evil" is death; for everyone dies because of evil produced by attachment to contact with the objects of the senses, which is prompted by innate ignorance.
That is why it is called death.
It is said that "the vital breath (prāṇa) struck away [evil]" merely by means of the conceit that it is the self of the vital breath.
However, due to the very opposition [between the knower and evil], evil departs far from one who knows thus.
What, moreover, did he do after striking away the evil—death—from the deities?

Thus it is said: "In that place where there is the end—the limit—of these directions such as the east and so forth, he caused them to go; that is to say, he made them go. Now, one might ask: "Since there is no end to the directions, how did he cause them to reach an end?

It is replied: Because the directions are conceptually constructed based on the boundary-marking of people possessing Vedic knowledge, a region uninhabited by people who oppose that [Vedic knowledge] is indeed the end of the directions.
There is no fault here, just as it is said that "the edge of the country is the forest.
Having caused those evil things (pāpman) of these deities to go there— the word *pāpmanaḥ* being in the accusative plural—
The deity of breath (prāṇa) deposited it in various ways, having placed it in a state of subordination;
that is, by implication, among the lowest-born people who are devoid of the conceit of being the self of breath.
For since that [conceit] is born from contact with the sense organs, it is understood to have its locus in living beings.
Therefore, one should not lead that person to the end; one should not go [there], nor should one associate with them through conversation, sight, and so forth.
For by associating with them, one would become associated with evil, since he is the very locus of evil.
Furthermore, one should not lead him to the "end" of that people's dwelling—what is designated by the term *diganta* (the edge of the quarters)—even if it is devoid of people.

The intention is that even the people there are separated from that [place]. The particle *ned* is an indeclinable used in the sense of avoiding danger. [He thinks: "In this way, I might encounter evil, namely death, in the company of people."
"I shall go along," meaning "I shall follow"; thus frightened, he would not choose a crowd of people—this is the connection with what precedes. //10//
This very deity, having struck away the evil of death from these deities, then carried them beyond death.
This indeed is that deity;
this result of the knowledge and action regarding the Self as Prāṇa is now stated: that the speech and other organs have fire and the others as their essential nature.

Then Death carried her across; therefore, the evil that constitutes the limitation of the internal self was destroyed by the realization of the Self as Prāṇa. Consequently, he who possesses Prāṇa is the destroyer of evil, of Death.

Therefore, that very Prāṇa, having caused these deities—Speech and the others—to transcend the aforementioned evil, Death, led them to their own respective, undivided forms as the deities of Fire and so forth. 11.
She indeed carried speech across first.
When it was released from death, it became fire.
This very fire, having transcended death, shines beyond it.
He indeed carried speech across first.
"Speech" here refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) carrying speech itself as the foremost;
its preeminence (*prādhānya*) consists in its being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) with respect to the other instruments in the performance of the *udgītha* rite.
He carried her across—that is, he performed the act of conveying her.
Now, what was the form of that very speech which was married after having transcended death?
It is said: when that speech, at a certain time, was released from evil—death—that is, it was liberated by itself, having transcended [death].
Then it became fire.
That speech, although it was already fire even before, became fire once again upon separation from death;
however, this much is the distinction in the case of separation from death.
This fire has indeed transcended death; it shines beyond death, on the far side of death.
Prior to liberation, being bound by death, it was not as radiant as it is now through the self of the internal speech (*adhyātmavāgātman*);
but now, because it is free from death, it shines beyond death. //12//
Then it carried Prāṇa across.
When he was released from death, he became Vāyu.
Thus this wind blows, having transcended death on the far side.
Likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa) became the sense of smell—the wind;
it blows, having transcended death. Everything else has the meaning already explained. //13//
Then the eye carried it across.
When it was released from death, it became the sun.
That very sun shines, having transcended death on the far side.
Likewise, the eye became the sun, and it is that which shines. //14//
Then he carried the ear across.
When it was released from death, it became the quarters.
These directions, beyond which death has passed, are these.
Likewise, the ear became the quarters;
the quarters exist as divided into the east and so forth. //15//
Then he carried the mind across.
When it was released from death, it became the moon.
Thus that moon shines, having transcended death by means of the other;
even so, indeed, this deity carries across death him who knows this. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.16)
The mind is the moon; it shines.

Just as in the past this deity of breath (prāṇa) carried the former sacrificer beyond death by means of speech and the others becoming fire and the others, even so does she carry this present sacrificer beyond death by means of speech and the others becoming fire and the others.

Thus, whoever knows the vital breath (prāṇa) as distinguished by the pentad beginning with speech—according to the Vedic scripture: "In whatever way one meditates upon it, that very thing one becomes. //16//
Then he sang for himself the song for the sake of food.
For whatever food is eaten here, it is eaten by him alone.
Here it finds its firm foundation.

Just as the singing was performed by speech and the other organs for their own sake, so too the principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa), having performed the singing that has the fruit of Prajāpati as its common goal for all the vital breaths, [did so] in three stotras;
and thereafter, in the remaining nine stotras.
He sang for himself—for his own sake—the food and what is to be eaten, which together constitute "food" (annādya).
It has already been stated that the connection of the agent with a specific desire is based on scriptural declaration.
But how is it understood that this food was obtained by the breath for its own sake?
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Whatever" (*yatkiñca*) is intended as a reference to food in general;
"for" (*hi*) indicates the cause;
because in the world, whatever food is eaten or consumed by living beings, that is [transformed] by this very [process].
The word *ana* is well known as a name for the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The word *ana* ending in a nasal (*sānta*) denotes a cart;
however, that other form ending in a vowel (*svarānta*) is a synonym for the vital breath.
The meaning is that it is by the vital breath alone that it is eaten.
Furthermore, it is not only that the food is eaten by the vital breath;
rather, the vital breath establishes itself here upon that food which has been transformed into the form of the body.
Therefore, the food is brought in by the vital breath for the sake of its own support.

Furthermore, even that eating of food by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) is solely for the sake of support; thus, unlike in the case of speech and the other organs, there is no arising of attachment to the beautiful in the vital breath. //17//
Is it not the case that the restriction— that "it is by the vital breath alone that this is eaten"— is improper, since speech and the other organs are also seen to receive assistance caused by food?
This is not a fault.
Because the benefit [of speech and the other organs] is mediated through the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

To demonstrate how the benefit of speech and the others toward the production of food is mediated through the vital breath, he says: START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.18: "When one does not eat, speech departs from him; when he does not smell, the nose departs; when he does not taste, the tongue departs; when he does not hear, the ear departs; when he does not think, the mind departs; when he does not touch, the body departs; when he does not procreate, the generative organ departs; when he does not speak, speech departs; when he does not smell, the nose departs; when he does not taste, the tongue departs; when he does not hear, the ear departs; when he does not think, the mind departs; when he does not touch, the body departs; when he does not procreate, the generative organ departs. But as long as one eats, the vital breath does not depart from him. Therefore, it is through the vital breath that speech and the others are benefited in the production of food. Thus he spoke.
Those gods said:
"All this that exists is indeed as much as food; you have sung for yourself that very thing."
"Grant us a share in this food," they said. "Then enter into me," he replied. "So be it," they said, and they entered into him on all sides.
Therefore, whatever food he eats, by that these [dependents] are satisfied.
Thus indeed do his own people gather around him who knows this—he becomes the supporter of his own, the best, the leader, the eater of food, and the sovereign.
But whoever among his own people seeks to oppose one who knows this, he is not at all capable of supporting those dependent upon him.
Now, whoever experiences this, or whoever desires to support his dependents by means of this, he indeed becomes capable of supporting his dependents.

Those deities, namely speech and the others—being called "deities" (devas) because they illuminate their respective objects—said to the principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa): "This much [is all there is]; there is nothing beyond this."
The word "vā" is for the purpose of recollection.
All this is just this much; what is it?

Whatever food, which sustains the life of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is eaten in the world—all that you have sung for yourself, for the sake of the Self; the meaning is that you have made it your own by means of singing.
And we are not able to remain without food;
therefore, after that, include us in this food—include us in your own food for your sake.
The non-hearing of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is a Vedic archaism.
"And make us partakers of food.
The other replied: "If you indeed desire food, do not enter into me; do not settle around me, facing me from all sides."
When Prāṇa had spoken thus, they said, "So be it," which means they settled down surrounding that Prāṇa.
For those who have settled in this manner, by the permission of Prāṇa, food— which sustains Prāṇa— becomes a source of satisfaction for them through Prāṇa alone, and not independently.
Therefore, it is indeed logical to conclude that "by this alone is that eaten.

He states this very point: because the deities of speech and the other organs have entered into the body through the permission of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by being supported by it, therefore whatever food a person eats with this *prāṇa*, by that food these [deities] of speech and the rest are satisfied.

Furthermore, he who knows that the *prāṇa* is the support of speech and the others, and that the five [organs] beginning with speech are supported by the *prāṇa*—him, his own kinsmen likewise enter in this very same way, just as speech and the others enter the *prāṇa*.
The intention is that he becomes one who is to be resorted to by his kinsmen.
Furthermore, he becomes the sustainer of his own people who have settled [around him], just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the sustainer of its own [organs] such as speech (*vāk*).
Likewise, he becomes the foremost leader who goes ahead, just as the vital breath is the leader of speech and the other organs.
Likewise, "eater of food" means one who is free from disease.
And being the "lord," he is the presiding protector and independent master of speech and the other organs, just like the vital breath (prāṇa).
For one who knows the vital breath in this way, this aforementioned fruit comes to pass.
Furthermore, whoever among one's own kinsmen desires to become an adversary— that is, an opponent— toward such a knower of Prāṇa, he,
like the Asuras who were rivals of Prāṇa, is truly not capable (na haivālam), meaning he is not sufficient, to support those who are to be supported (bhāryebhyaḥ). This is the meaning.
Furthermore, he who among his kinsmen follows such a knower— just as speech and the other organs followed the vital breath—

and who, indeed, desiring to support his own dependents, seeks to maintain them by following after this knower, just as speech and the others desired to support themselves by following the vital breath; [for him, the kinsmen will not perish].
He alone is fully capable of supporting those who are to be supported and maintained by him; no other independent person is so able.
All this has been stated as the fruit of the knowledge of the qualities of the vital breath (prāṇa). //18//
In order to establish that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Self of the organs of action and perception, its status as Aṅgirasa was introduced in the passage, "He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa.
However, the reason why this [breath] is Āṅgirasa has not yet been stated;
therefore, the following section is commenced for the purpose of establishing that reason.

For the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the cause of the effects depends upon the establishment of that [nature]; and immediately thereafter, the dependence of speech and the other organs upon the vital breath was stated. How, then, is that to be demonstrated? To this he says:
START *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.3.19.
He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence of the limbs; breath indeed is the essence of the limbs,
for breath is truly the essence of the limbs.
Therefore, from whichever limb the vital breath (prāṇa) departs, that very limb withers;
for this, indeed, is the essence of the limbs.

The passage beginning with "He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa" and so forth is taken up exactly as it was introduced for the sake of what follows; the sentence ending with "Prāṇa indeed is the essence of the limbs" is recalled again precisely for the purpose of its explanation. How so? "Prāṇa indeed is the essence of the limbs."
Regarding the phrase "for breath" (*prāṇo hi*): the word *hi* indicates well-known fact—it is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs.
It is well known that this quality of being the essence of the limbs belongs to breath, and not to speech and the other organs.
Therefore, the reminder "breath indeed" (*prāṇo vā*) is appropriate.
But how is there established status [of the reason]? To this he says:
Therefore, the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is connected as being placed above for the purpose of a conclusion;
because from whichever member [of the syllogism], from whatever unspecified particularity.

From whichever limb—that is, from whatever unspecified part of the body—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs or withdraws, that very limb withers there, becomes sapless, and undergoes drying; therefore, "this indeed is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs"—such is the conclusion.
Hence, it is established that the vital breath is the self (*ātman*) of the organs and the body.
For if the self were to depart, the remainder would be death; therefore, by means of it, all living beings live.
Thus, having set aside speech and the other [senses], the vital breath alone is to be meditated upon—this is the collective meaning. //19//

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the self (*ātman*) only of the body and its organs—which are of the nature of form and action—but what then? It is the self of the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* mantras, which are of the nature of names. Thus, by praising the vital breath as the self of all, the text magnifies it for the sake of being an object of meditation.
He is indeed Bṛhaspati.
Vāc is the Bṛhatī;
he is her lord, and therefore he is Bṛhaspati.
This very one under discussion is the Āṅgirasa Bṛhaspati.
How is he Bṛhaspati? It is said: Speech indeed is the Bṛhatī; the Bṛhatī is a meter consisting of thirty-six syllables.
And speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
How so? Because of the Vedic revelation: "Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*" (Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad 1.1).
And that speech, as the *anuṣṭubh*, is included within the *bṛhatī* meter.
Therefore, it is appropriate to state, as a well-known fact, that "Speech is indeed the Bṛhatī.

And all Ṛgvedic verses are contained within the Bṛhatī because of its identification with the vital breath (prāṇa), according to another scriptural passage: "One should know that the Bṛhatī is the vital breath and the Ṛks are the vital breath."
Because speech is of the nature of the self, its inclusion within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows. How so? To this he says: "This vital breath is the lord of that speech, of the *bṛhatī* verse;
for it is the bringer-about of that [speech]."
For the *ṛc* is produced by the wind impelled by the digestive fire within the belly;
or else, he is the Lord of Speech because of his protection of speech,
for speech is indeed protected by the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Because one who is without breath lacks the capacity for the utterance of sound, the meaning is that Bṛhaspati is the breath and the self of the Ṛgvedic verses. //20//
Likewise with the Yajus formulas. How so? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.21)
He indeed is Brahmaṇaspati.
Speech is indeed Brahman;
he is its lord, therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati.
He indeed is also Brahmaṇaspati.
Speech is indeed Brahman;
Brahman is the Yajus.
And that is indeed a specific form of speech;
he is the lord (*pati*) of that speech, of the *yajus*, and of the *brahman*, and for that reason he is *Brahmaṇaspati*, as explained previously.
But how is it understood that the *bṛhatī* meter and the *brahman* possess the nature of *ṛc* and *yajus* respectively, rather than having some other meaning?
This is stated because, at the end of the passage, there is a designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with speech (*vāk*), as in: "Speech indeed is the *sāman*" (1.3.22).

And likewise, since it is said "Speech indeed is the *bṛhatī*" and "Speech indeed is Brahman," it is logical that the status of being *ṛc* and *yajus* belongs to those two which are coreferential with speech.
Furthermore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), when the *sāman* has been mentioned, only the *ṛc* and *yajus* remain.
And because of the distinction of speech— since the *Ṛk* and *Yajus* are indeed specific forms of speech,
it is therefore appropriate that they stand in grammatical apposition with "speech.
Furthermore, because otherwise there would be the consequence of non-distinction— the terms "Sāman" and "Udgītha" clearly denote specific distinctions.

Likewise, it is appropriate that the words *bṛhatī* and *brahman* also denote specific [entities], because otherwise there would result the futility of two terms whose specific referents remain undetermined; and because if denoting specific entities were a mere matter of verbal expression, there would be redundancy in both cases. Furthermore, this is because such a sequence is observed in the Śrutis for the words *ṛc*, *yajus*, *sāman*, and *udgītha*. //21//
This very one is indeed the *sāman*.
Speech is indeed *sā*, and this [Self] is *ama*; because it is both *sā* and *ama*, that is the essence of the name *sāman*.
Moreover, because it is equal to a flea, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe, it is therefore called *sāman*.
He who knows this *sāman* thus attains union with and residence in the same world as the *sāman*. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.22)
"This very [breath] is indeed *sāman*.
How so? He says: Speech (*vāk*) is *sā*; whatever is denotable by feminine words, that is speech.
The word *amaḥ* refers to the object denoted by all masculine words."
"By what do you obtain my masculine names?
"By the vital breath (prāṇa)," he should say. "By what my feminine names? "By speech (vāc).
From this other scriptural passage (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.7), it follows that this word *sāman* denotes speech and vital breath.
Likewise, the word *sāman* denotes merely the collection of vowels and so forth brought about by the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
therefore, there is no such thing as a *sāman* apart from the vital breath and speech, because vowels, syllables, and the rest are produced by the vital breath and are dependent upon it.
This very breath is indeed the *sāman*.

Because it is both *sā* (speech) and *ama* (breath), it is called *sāman*; therefore, the nature of the *sāman* belongs to that collection of notes beginning with the musical scale (*svara*), which consists of speech and breath, and is sung upon the earth.
The phrase "yad u eva samastulyaḥ" means that which is equal (*sama*) and uniform (*tulya*) in every respect according to the manner about to be described;
this connects with the statement "therefore it is called *sāman*.
The word "vā" (or) is to be understood through the force of indicating another mode [of derivation] as the cause for obtaining the term "*sāman*."
In what manner, then, is the breath equal? It is said: it is equal to a flea, that is, equal to the body of a flea; equal to a mosquito, that is, equal to the body of a mosquito;
equal to a serpent, that is, equal to the body of an elephant.
The equality of the vital breath (prāṇa) consists in its being equal to these three worlds by means of its body as the Lord of Creatures (Prājāpatya),
and equal to this world-form of Hiraṇyagarbha;
it is equal because it is fully present in its entirety within bodies such as those of a gnat, just as "cowness" (gotva) is present in individual cows.
Furthermore, it is not merely of the same dimension as the body,
because it is formless and all-pervading;
nor is its equality with the body limited to that size through contraction and expansion, like a lamp in a jar or a palace.

"‘All these are indeed equal, all are infinite’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.13)—so says the Śruti. For that which is omnipresent, the acquisition of a functional state corresponding to the size of the body is not contradictory. Thus, for one who knows the Prāṇa called Sāman—which is equal and whose greatness is revealed by the Śruti—this is the fruit: he attains, or pervades, union with the Prāṇa as Sāman; that is, the state of being joined with it (sāyug-bhāva), characterized by having a common body, senses, and sense of self-identity."
Through a particular excellence of meditative cultivation, one attains either *sālokya* (residence in the same world) or *samānalokatā* (residence in the same realm).

This refers to one who knows this *sāman* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the manner described—that is, one who worships it until the manifestation of the conceit of identity with the self of the vital breath. //22//
This, indeed, is the Udgītha.
Breath is "ut," for by breath all this is upheld.
Speech indeed is the *gīthā*;
because it is both "high" (*ud*) and "song" (*gīthā*),
it is the *udgītha*.
This, indeed, is the Udgītha.
By "Udgītha" is meant a specific part of the Sāman, namely a particular division (bhakti), and not the act of singing, because the context concerns the Sāman.

How is the *udgītha* the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? The vital breath is indeed "ut" (*ut-prāṇa*). For it is by means of the vital breath that this entire world is "uttabdha"—that is, held up, supported from above, and sustained; such is the meaning.
This syllable "ut" illuminates the sense of being held up and denotes a quality of the vital breath.
Therefore, it is *utprāṇa*.
Speech alone is the *udgītha*, because the term *udgītha* is a specific form of sound;
since the root *gai* signifies "sound," that [udgītha] is indeed speech.
For no form of the *udgītha* portion is conceived apart from sound;

therefore, the restriction "speech alone is the *gīthā*" is appropriate. Since the breath is high (*uccaiḥ*) and speech is dependent upon the breath, both are denoted by the single word *udgītha*. //23//
Regarding this, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while consuming the King [Soma], said:
"May this King strike off his head, if Āyāsya Āṅgirasa sang the Udgītha by means of anything other than this!"
For he sang the udgītha both with speech and with breath. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.24)
Moreover, regarding this very matter— that is, for the sake of confirming the meaning already stated— there is also a traditional narrative (ākhyāyikā) heard by Śruti.
Brahmadatta by name, the son of Cikitāna (thus Caikitāneya), being a youth,
spoke while consuming the Soma at a sacrifice during a royal ceremony.
What? May this King, while remaining in the cup and not being drunk by me, cause—

the word *vipātayatāt* being the imperative (loṭ) in the sense of a benediction with the substitution of *tāt* for *hi*— clearly strike off, that is, fell away, the head, the skull, of each and every such person as I who speak untruth.
The meaning is: "If I were to be a speaker of untruth.
But how, then, does the possibility of speaking untruth arise?
It is said: "If [speech] were separate from this aforementioned breath conjoined with speech..."

Ayāsya is designated by the term *ayāsyāṅgirasa*, which denotes the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). During the sacrificial session (*satra*) of the ancient seers, the creators of the universe, the Udgātṛ priests were about to chant the *udgītha* with another deity distinct from speech and breath;
[the text says], "In that case, I would become a speaker of untruth;
may the head of me, who as a deity have fallen into such a misconception, fall off."
"Thus he made this oath"—this shows that one must establish firm conviction through such means of knowledge.

The Śruti concludes with its own words this very meaning determined by the narrative: "With speech, which has breath as its chief, and with breath, which is his own self, that Ayāsya Āṅgirasa sang the Udgītha"; this is the meaning determined by the oath. 24.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.25:
He who knows the property of this Sāman—verily, he comes to possess property;
for its property is indeed the tone (svara).
Therefore, one who is about to perform the office of a priest should desire excellence of tone in his speech;
with that speech, endowed with excellence of tone, he should perform the priestly office. For this reason, people truly desire to see one who possesses excellence of tone at a sacrifice.
Moreover, he who possesses property—
he indeed possesses property, who thus knows this property of the Sāman.

The word "of that" (tasya) refers back to the vital breath under discussion; by the phrase "of this very one" (haitasya), he points specifically to the principal breath through a demonstrative gesture.
He who knows the "wealth" (sva) of the Sāman—that is, the wealth belonging to the vital breath which is denoted by the word "Sāman"—[attains it].

"What indeed would belong to him? "He certainly possesses his own property. Having enticed him with this fruit and turned him toward [the teaching], he said to the one desiring to hear: "Of that Sāman, the tone (*svara*) alone is the property (*svam*)."
"Svara" refers to the sweetness residing in the throat; that indeed is his own ornament.
For by it, the chanting (*udgāna*) appears as adorned with prosperity.

Since this is so, therefore one who is about to perform the office of the *ṛtvij*—the work of the *udgātṛ*, namely the chanting—should desire "svara" (melodic tone) in the domain of speech, that is, dependent upon speech. Desiring to effect the wealth of the *sāman* through tone, the *udgātṛ* should so desire.
This, however, is stated as a relevant digression:

when the quality of having a beautiful voice (*sausvarya*) is required for the cognition of the correct accentuation of the *sāman*, since such beauty of voice does not arise by mere wish alone, one must perform acts such as cleaning the teeth and drinking oil through their efficacy; this is the meaning.
In that very way, one should perform the priestly office (*ārlijya*) with speech that is refined and endowed with the proper accent.

Therefore, since *svara* (the musical accent) is inherent to the *sāman*, the *sāman* is adorned by that which belongs to it; hence, in the sacrifice, people desire indeed to see the *udgātṛ* priest who possesses *svara*, just as in the world it is well known that people desire to see a wealthy man whose own wealth exists. Thus, the connection between the knowledge of this quality and its fruit is concluded: "He indeed comes to possess his own wealth."
Thus one knows this as the own nature of the Sāman. //25//
Now, another quality characterized by "goldenness" (*suvarṇavatā*) is prescribed; this too is simply melodiousness (*sauṣvarya*).
This much is the distinction: whereas the former was the sweetness residing in the throat, this is the technical [quality] denoted by the word *suvarṇa*.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.26:
Of this very Sāman, he who knows its *suvarṇa* (golden) [aspect] indeed obtains *suvarṇa*.
Its *suvarṇa*, verily, is its tone (*svara*).
He who knows this gold of the Sāman becomes possessed of gold. Bṛhad Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.26.
Regarding this very Sāman, he who knows its *suvarṇa* (gold) indeed acquires gold for himself.
Because of the commonality of the word *suvarṇa*, the result of this knowledge of the quality is ordinary gold;
the meaning is that his own voice (*svara*) is indeed its gold.
"He who thus knows this 'gold' of the Sāman becomes possessed of gold"—all of this is as explained previously. //26//
Likewise, desiring to explain the quality of its foundation, [the text] says:
"He who knows the foundation of this very Sāman, indeed stands firm."
His support is indeed speech;
for this breath is sung as being supported in speech. Some, however, say it is supported in food. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.27.

Regarding this very *sāman*, he who knows its foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*)—it is called "foundation" because one stands firm upon it—that foundation is speech. He who knows that foundation as an attribute of the *sāman* indeed becomes firmly established.
For it is logical that it possesses those attributes, according to the scriptural statement: "In whatever way they meditate upon it."

To one who desires to hear, as before, what constitutes the enticement and what the support are for that which has been enticed by its fruit, he says: "Of that *sāman*, speech indeed is the [enticement];
'speech' is the designation for the places of articulation such as the root of the tongue, and that itself is the support."

Regarding this, he says: Since this Prāṇa, being established in speech—specifically in the *jihvāmūlīya* and other such [consonants]—sings this song, that is, attains the state of being sung (*gītibhāva*), therefore speech is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the Sāman.
Some others say, "It is sung as being established in food. However, it is more appropriate to say, "It is established here [in speech]."
Since the view of certain authorities is not censured, one may optionally perform the recognition of the quality of stability, thinking, "Speech is stability" or "Food is stability. //27//
Thus, the act of recitation is intended for one who possesses knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa).
That knowledge, by virtue of which one has the qualification for the act of recitation,
has been explained.
Now, therefore, follows the ascending of the *pavamāna* chants. The *prastotṛ* indeed chants the *sāman*;
when he is about to chant it, he should mutter these [formulas].
Lead me from unbeing to being; lead me from darkness to light; lead me from death to immortality.

When he says, "Lead me from non-existence to existence," death is indeed non-existence and immortality is existence; thus he says, "Lead me from death to immortality, make me immortal. When he says, "Lead me from darkness to light," [he means the same].
"Death is indeed darkness; light is immortality. 'Lead me from death to immortality; make me immortal'—this is what he says.
'Lead me from death to immortality':
there is nothing here that is obscure."
Now, regarding those other hymns, he should sing for himself the acquisition of food during them;
therefore, he should choose a boon during them—
whatever desire he may wish for.
This very Udgātṛ priest, knowing thus, sings for himself or for the sacrificer whatever desire he may desire;
and this, indeed, is the conquest of the worlds.
For one who knows this Sāman thus, there is no hope of not attaining the worlds.
Now, immediately following this, since the act of recitation (*japa*) performed by one who knows thus has as its fruit the ascent to the state of a deity, it is therefore enjoined here.

Because of its connection with the *udgītha*, it would apply everywhere; however, since the rule "of the *pavamānas*" restricts it to the three *pavamāna* chants, and thus its performance in all three would otherwise follow, he again limits the time: "He..."
Indeed, the Prastotṛ priest chants the Sāman.
At whatever time—that is, at whichever moment—the Prastotṛ should chant or begin the Sāman, at that time he should mutter these [formulas].
And the designation for this act of muttering is "Ascent" (abhyāroha).
"Abhyāroha" (the ascent) means that by this very act of recitation (*japakarman*), one ascends directly toward such a divine state as one's own self.
Because of the plural number in the word "etāni" (these), there are three *yajus* formulas.

Due to their being indicated in the accusative case and because they originate from the Brāhmaṇa, the accentuation should be employed exactly as it is recited in the text, and not according to the standard mantra accent.
The ritual of recitation (*japakarma*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
These are those *yajus* formulas: "Lead me from non-existence to existence," "Lead me from darkness to light," and "Lead me from death to immortality.
Since the meaning of a mantra is often concealed, the Brāhmaṇa itself explains the meaning of the mantra: "What did that mantra say? What was it that he said? What is that meaning?"

Thus it is said: "Lead me from non-being to being. Death is indeed non-being; natural action and innate cognition are called death because they cause one to fall into the lowest state. Being is immortality; scriptural action and spiritual knowledge are called immortality because they are the causes of not perishing.

Therefore, from the unreal, from the action of the unreal, and from ignorance, lead me not—do not cause me to go—to the real, which consists of the knowledge and action prescribed by the sacred scriptures; that is to say, bring about my self-nature as the means for attaining the state of divinity. Regarding this, he states the meaning of the sentence: "He says this very thing when he says, 'Lead me from death to immortality. Likewise, "Lead me from darkness to light" means "lead me from death."
Death is indeed darkness; for all ignorance, being of the nature of obscuration, is darkness, and that very thing is death because it is the cause of dying.
Light is immortality; it is the divine essential nature, which is the opposite of what was previously described.
Because its nature is luminosity, knowledge is light.
That very [state] is immortality because its nature is indestructible.
Therefore, "Lead me from darkness to light" means, as before, "Lead me from death to immortality," and so forth.
He says this very thing: "Make me immortal"—the meaning is, "Bring me to the state of being the fruit belonging to the divine and to Prajāpati."
"May the first mantra bring about the state of being a means (*sādhana*) from that which is not of the nature of a means;
may the second, however, bring about the state of being the goal (*sādhya*) from that which is a means yet consists of ignorance.
"Lead me from death to immortality"—this is simply the well-known meaning expressed by the third mantra as the combined sense of the two preceding mantras.
In this third mantra, there is no hidden or obscured meaning of the object as there was in the two preceding mantras;
the meaning is exactly as it is heard.
Having performed the *udgāna* for the patron (*yājamāna*) during the three *pavamāna* chants, [the text continues:]

Immediately thereafter, regarding those other remaining hymns, the Udgātṛ who knows the vital breath (prāṇa)— being himself of the nature of breath— should sing for his own sake the attainment of food, just like the vital breath. Since that very Udgātṛ knows the vital breath as it has been described,
he is therefore capable of accomplishing that desire just like the vital breath itself.
Therefore, while those chants (stotras) are being performed, the sacrificer should choose a boon;
whatever desire he may wish for, that desire he should choose as a boon—that is, he should pray for it.
Because of the word "sa eṣa" ("this very one"), [the phrase] "one who knows thus" (evaṃvid) is to be connected with [the subject] even before that word.
Whatever desire the Udgātṛ priest desires for himself or for the sacrificer—whatever he wishes—he attains it through singing; he accomplishes it by means of his song.
Thus, it has been stated that through knowledge and ritual action one attains the nature of the vital breath (prāṇātman);
in this regard, there is no possibility of doubt.
Therefore, one might raise the doubt: "Does the loss of life occur upon the exhaustion of karma, or not?
To dispel that doubt, he says: "For this [breath] is indeed the winner of the world."
Therefore, this vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), even when it is isolated and devoid of ritual action,

is indeed "world-conquering" (*lokajit*), meaning it is the very means for attaining the world. Indeed, there is no hope, expectation, or prayer whatsoever for the state of being "non-worldly" (*alokyatā*), that is, for unworthiness to attain the world.
For one who has already developed the conceit of "I" with respect to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the self, it is not possible to desire its attainment;

indeed, a person living in a village does not pray, like someone in the forest, "When shall I reach the village? For such a desire pertains only to an object that is not present and is not yet the self.

That [destruction] is not possible in its own self; therefore, there is no occasion when one would not attain the state of being the vital breath (prāṇa). For whom is this true? It is for one who knows this Sāman as the vital breath, whose greatness has been determined as described: "I am the vital breath, invincible by the demonic evils consisting of attachment to the senses and their objects, and I am pure."

The pentad beginning with speech, because it has me as its support, is of the nature of fire and the other elements; it is free from the defect of the demonic evil born from attachment to the objects of the senses arising from natural ignorance; and through my support, it is bound to the consumption of food within all beings.

Furthermore, I am the Self of all beings because I am the essence of the Aṅgirases, and I am the Self of speech—which consists of the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Udgītha—because I pervade it and because I bring it about.
"As my *sāman* attains the state of being sung, external wealth and ornaments are its beauty; even more internal than that is the beauty consisting of the excellence of voice (*sauṣvarya*).
For me, as I attain the state of being sung, the locations such as the throat are the foundation.

Thus endowed with these qualities, I am fully and completely present within the bodies of gnats and other creatures, because of my formlessness and omnipresence"—the meaning is that one should meditate upon [the *sāman*] until such self-identification is manifested. //28//
Thus ends the third Udgītha Brāhmaṇa in the first chapter.

The attainment of the state of Prajāpati through the combination of knowledge and action has been explained; and the attainment through the vision of the vital breath alone has been explained by the passage beginning with, "This, indeed, is the winner of the worlds.

Now, this section is commenced for the purpose of describing the excellence of the fruit of Vedic knowledge and action by means of a description of the majesty of Prajāpati—the very fruit of those two—consisting in his sovereignty over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
By doing so, there will also be, by implication, a glorification of the knowledge and action prescribed in the Karma-kāṇḍa.

What is intended here, however, is this: all of this—the fruit of knowledge and action—is indeed transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) alone, because it is heard to be joined with fear, dissatisfaction, and so forth;
because it is characterized by the body and the instruments [of perception]; and because its objects are gross, manifest, and non-eternal.
And it is for the sake of the subsequent point that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), which is about to be described as a solitary [means], is the cause of liberation.

For one who is not dispassionate toward the sphere of transmigratory existence— which is characterized by the distinction between the goal and the means— there is no qualification for the subject matter of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, just as there is none for one who is not thirsty regarding the act of drinking.

Therefore, the description of the excellence of the fruits of knowledge and action is for the sake of what follows; and so he will say: "This is the path leading to that" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), and "This is dearer than a son" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8), and so forth.
In the beginning, this universe was the Self alone, in the form of a person.
He looked around and saw nothing other than Himself.
He first uttered, "I am he" (so 'ham asmi);
from that, the name "Aham" arose.
Therefore even now, when addressed, one first says, "It is I," and then pronounces whatever other name one may have.
Because he burnt away all evils before all this [universe], therefore he is called Puruṣa.
He who knows this burns away anyone who seeks to be before him. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1)
"Ātman alone is the Ātman"—thus Prajāpati, the first embodied being born from the egg, is designated.
Is he indeed the very fruit of the knowledge and ritual action prescribed by the Vedas?
This entire collection of diverse bodies is non-different from that body of Prajāpati.
In the beginning, before the production of another body, there was only the Self;
and He was of the form of a person, that is, of the nature of a person characterized by a head, vital breaths, and so forth—namely, Virāj.
Having first come into being, He performed an investigation, that is, a thorough contemplation.
"Who am I, or what are my characteristics?"—
he did not see, nor did he perceive, any other distinct entity apart from himself, consisting of the vital breaths, the physical body, and the instruments of action.
He perceived only himself as the Self of all;
likewise, refined by the Vedic knowledge of his previous birth, he first uttered, "I am Prajāpati, I am the Self of all."
Therefore, because he first designated himself as "I" (*aham*) based on that prior latent impression of knowledge (*pūrvajñāna-saṃskāra*), he came to have the name "Ahaṃ" (I).
[The text] will later state his secret name (*upaniṣad*), which is precisely the name indicated by the Śruti.
For this reason—that such occurred in Prajāpati—therefore...

Among the living beings who have come into being as effects of that [cause], even at this present time, when addressed and asked "Who are you?", he first says "I am this one," identifying himself by means of the designation of the causal self (*kāraṇātman*); thereafter, for one who desires to know his specific name, he subsequently declares and tells the designation of the particular body, such as "Devadatta" or "Yajñadatta," which is the name of this specific body.
He explains that it is brought about by his parents;
and he, Prajāpati, in a previous birth, through the practice of the cultivation of correct knowledge of karma during the stage of a practitioner,
was the first and foremost among those desiring to attain the state of Prajāpati by means of such practices of the cultivation of knowledge of karma.

From this entire assembly desiring to attain the state of Prajāpati, he first burnt away all evils— characterized by attachment and ignorance— which serve as obstacles to the attainment of the state of Prajāpati. Because it was so, therefore [he is called] Puruṣa.
"He burns away" (*auṣat*) means "he becomes a person" (*puruṣaḥ*).

Just as this Prajāpati, having burned away all obstructing evils, became the Person Prajāpati, so too another person—by means of the fire of the practice of the cultivation of knowledge and action—burns away, indeed, by the power of knowledge alone; whom? That [evil].

The meaning is: "him who, prior to this wise one, desires to become—the first Prajāpati. He indicates him by saying, "he who knows thus," which implies by the force of the context that he possesses the excellence of the cultivation of knowledge.
But surely, the desire to attain the state of Prajāpati would lead to misfortune if one who knows thus were to be consumed [by fire];
this is not a fault.
Because there is no excellence in the cultivation of knowledge, the burning consists merely in the initial failure to attain the status of Prajāpati; thus,
it is said that "he burns him" in the sense that one who possesses superior means attains the status of Prajāpati first, whereas one with inferior means does not.
Furthermore, one person is not literally burned by another through a superior means of accomplishment;
rather, it is just as in the world among those who run a race, where he who first reaches the finish line renders the others as if burned, stripped of their capacity—so it is here. //1//

Desiring to show this point—that the fruit of knowledge and action prescribed in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), characterized by the state of Prajāpati, did not at all transcend the sphere of saṃsāra—he said:
"He was afraid; therefore, one who is alone is afraid. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2)
He then reflected:
"Since there is nothing other than myself, of what am I afraid? Thereupon, his fear departed from him.
Why would he have been afraid? For it is from a second that fear arises. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2)

He was afraid—this Prajāpati who has been explained as the first embodied being, having the form of a person. He was afraid; he was frightened just like ourselves and others. He says this because, since this one had the form of a person and possessed a body, he was afraid due to having a perception contrary to the truth regarding the destruction of the self.
Therefore, by virtue of that similarity, even today one who is alone feels fear.

Furthermore, just as in the case of ourselves and others, the cause for removing the perception of what is contrary to the cause of fear is the vision of the Self as it truly is (*yathābhūtātmadarśana*).
This very Prajāpati performed—that is, he made—an act of seeing (*īkṣā*).
How so? He says: "Since there is no other entity distinct from me as an adversary, in the absence of such a cause for the destruction of the self, why indeed should I fear?
From that very perception of the self as it truly is, Prajāpati’s fear departed—that is, it clearly vanished.
He states that whatever fear belonged to that Prajāpati was caused solely by ignorance (*avidyā*) and is untenable in the light of the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):
"For from what would he have been afraid?"—the intention being that upon an investigation into ultimate reality, fear is simply untenable.
This is because fear arises only from a second thing, another entity.
And the second thing is merely presented by ignorance;
for a non-perceived second thing cannot be the cause of the arising of fear, as stated in the Vedic mantra: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).
And it is logical that he dispelled his fear by means of the vision of oneness.

Why? Because fear arises from a second thing, from another entity; since, through the vision of oneness, the vision of duality has been removed, there is therefore no [second thing] from which fear could arise.
Regarding this, they raise the following objection: From where did Prajāpati’s vision of oneness arise?
Who instructed him? Or did it manifest spontaneously, without any instruction at all?
Otherwise, the same consequence would apply even to people such as ourselves.
If, on the other hand, it were caused by impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed in previous lives,
then the practice of viewing [the self] as a single entity would be rendered purposeless.
Just as Prajāpati, even though he possessed the vision of oneness beyond the state of birth, did not thereby remove the cause of bondage consisting of ignorance—
since he was born joined with ignorance and feared—
so too it follows that the vision of oneness would be useless for everyone.

If it is argued that only the final [cognition] is the remover [of error], we say no; for, as in the previous case, this would lead to an over-extension (anaikāntya) due to the recurrence of the same problem.
Therefore, the realization of oneness is indeed purposeless.
This is not a fault,
because it arises from superior causes, as is seen in the world.
Just as when one is born endowed with distinct faculties and organs produced by meritorious karma, wisdom, intelligence, memory, and confidence are observed.

Likewise, because Prajāpati’s birth arose from the burning away of all sins—which are the causes contrary to dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—his birth was superior and his instruments (the senses) were purified; thus, even without being taught, the realization of oneness was appropriate for Prajāpati. And so says the Smṛti: “The knowledge of the Lord of the World is unsurpassed, as is his dispassion.”
And the fourfold sovereignty of Dharma is indeed co-emergent with it.
“If it is argued that fear is untenable because [the self] exists simultaneously with its accomplishment, we reply:
no; for darkness does not arise together with the sun.”
No, because the sentence [of the Upanishads] establishes its meaning independently of anything else.

If it be thought that faith, intentness, prostration, and so forth are not the causes [of knowledge], one might argue: "The man of faith gains knowledge, being intent upon it and with senses restrained" (Gītā 4.39);
"Know that by prostration... (Gītā 4.34).

If it is argued that these aforementioned causes of knowledge prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti—such as Prajāpati—are not actually causes, because knowledge has its cause in the dharma performed in previous births, we say:
no; for it is possible to establish distinctions based on whether they are instrumental causes (nimitta), or whether they are combined or not, and whether they possess excellence or lack it.
For in the world, the distinction among the signs of various effects produced by prognosticators is conceptualized in many ways;
likewise, there is a combination of signs.
Furthermore, regarding those signs that have been either conceptualized or combined, there occurs a further distinction based on whether they possess excellence or lack it.

For example, regarding the cognition of form (*rūpa-jñāna*) itself in its various causal effects: for nocturnal creatures, the contact between the eye and form in the absence of light is the cause for the cognition of form;
for yogis, the mind alone is the cause for the cognition of form.
For us, however, the specific causes are those that are combined with both contact and light, as well as the various distinct types of light such as those of the sun and the moon.
Likewise, there may be distinctions based on whether one possesses the special quality of light or lacks it;
in the very same way, even regarding the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, in some cases karma performed in another birth serves as the cause, as was the case with Prajāpati.
In some cases, austerity is the means, according to the Vedic scripture: "Seek to know through austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.4);
in other cases, it is the teacher, according to the scripture: "The man who has a teacher knows" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
2) “The one possessed of faith attains knowledge” (Gītā 4.39);
“Know that through prostration” (Gītā 4.34);
“Only from the teacher indeed” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.9.3).

3) From such scriptural and traditional texts as "He is to be seen, He is to be heard" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), faith and the other [virtues] are the cause for attaining exclusive knowledge, because they serve as the means for dissociating from causes such as unrighteousness (*adharma*);
furthermore, hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption upon the Vedānta have the knowable reality itself as their direct object.

And because the self and the mind possess an inherent nature that causes knowledge of things as they truly are once obstacles such as evil have been destroyed, faith, prostration, and so forth are never the cause of knowledge. //2//
Furthermore, the state of Prajāpati pertains only to the realm of saṃsāra, because:
"He indeed did not find delight. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.3)
Therefore, he did not delight in being alone;
he desired a second.
He became as large as a man and a woman in close embrace.
He split this very self into two parts;
from that, there came to be a husband and a wife.
Therefore, Yājñavalkya used to say, "For this reason, this [body] is, as it were, half of oneself."
Therefore, this space was indeed filled by her;
he united with her,
and from that, human beings were born.
That Prajāpati indeed did not find delight; he did not experience pleasure—
the meaning is that he was possessed by discontent— from this first deity.
Even now, because he possesses qualities such as being alone, he does not delight in solitude; that is, he does not experience pleasure.

Pleasure (*rati*) is defined as play arising from union with desired objects; conversely, for one addicted to that [pleasure], the state of mental agitation resulting from separation from the desired is called "non-delight" (*arati*).
In order to dispel that dissatisfaction, he desired—and became greedy for—a second object of womanhood capable of destroying that dissatisfaction.
As he was thus greedily longing for the sphere of women, his state of being became as if he were actually embraced by a woman.
Because of his desire for truth, he became exactly this much, of this very measure.
"What was its size?
