To this he says: "Just as in the world a woman and a man might embrace each other for the removal of their desire, so too did He become of that same size.
Thus, He divided Himself into two parts—that is, He caused Himself to fall into two modes. The restrictive particle *eva* ("just") is used to distinguish Him from the primordial cause, Virāj.
It was not that Virāj became this much by the total destruction of himself, as when milk attains the state of curd through the complete dissolution of its own nature;

rather, while Virāj remained established in his own self, because of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), there came into being another body distinct from himself, consisting of a man and woman in close embrace.
And it is that very same Virāj, having become thus, who is referred to in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the phrase "he became this much."
Therefore, because they both fell from that descent, they became husband and wife; this is the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the worldly couple.
For this very reason, since this woman is a half of the Self that has become separate, [she is called *ardhāṅgī*].

Therefore, this body is an "ardhabṛgalam": half of a *bṛgala*, and that *bṛgala* is a split (*vidala*); thus, "ardhabṛgalam" means half of a split. To the question, "Whose half-split [is it] prior to the taking of a wife? it is said: "one's own," meaning one's self.
Thus he spoke; it is said that Yājñavalkya spoke. "Yajña-valka" means the speaker (valka) of sacrifice (yajña); his descendant is Yājñavalkya, meaning Daivarāti—or else [the son] of Brahmā.

Since this half of a person is the void of space, being empty of the female half, it is filled by that female half through remarriage, just as one half of a split shell is filled by joining it back together.
Prajāpati, known as Manu, united with her—known as Śatarūpā—who had been designated as his own daughter for the purpose of becoming his wife; he approached her in sexual union.
Then, from that approaching of her, human beings were born, i.e., produced. //3//
Then he reflected: "How indeed can it be that, having produced [me] from himself alone, he comes into being?
Well, let me become invisible."
She became a cow, and the other became a bull;
he united with her,
and from that cows were born.
One became a mare, the other a stallion; one became a she-ass, the other a donkey. He united with her.
From that, the single-hoofed animal was born;
one became a goat, the other a he-goat;
one became a ewe, the other a ram.
He united with her;
from that, goats and sheep were born.
In this very same way, he created everything whatsoever that exists in pairs, down to the ants.

She was Śatarūpā; indeed, she was this very [woman]. Recalling the Smṛti prohibition against approaching one's own daughter, she reflected: "How is it that he, having produced me from his own self, approaches me—that which is an improper act?
Even though he is pitiless, well then, I shall now hide myself by becoming another species."
Having perceived thus, he became a bull.
Again and again, as she was impelled by the karma of living beings yet to be born, that same thought occurred to Śatarūpā and Manu;
and from that, the other became a bull.
"He united with her," and so forth, as before.
From that, cows were born;
likewise, one became a mare and the other a stallion.
Likewise, the female donkey was one [partner] and the male donkey was the other;
from their union with mares, stallions, and so forth, there were born three types of single-hoofed, one-humped animals known as horses, mules, and donkeys.
Similarly, the female goat was one [partner] and the male goat was the other.
Likewise, the ewe was one and the ram was the other;
he united with her—
“with her” being used repeatedly to indicate distribution.
The meaning is that she became "ajā" (the unborn) and "avi" (the sheep); from her were born goats and horses— goats and horses—
and likewise whatever exists here, whatever pair there is characterized by female and male, every such couple.
Down to the ants—along with the ants—he created all that by this very same principle; he brought forth the entire world. //4//
He knew: "I indeed am the creation, for I have created all this.
From that, he became the creation (Sṛṣṭi).
He who knows this becomes a creator in this creation. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.5.
Having created this entire world, that Prajāpati understood:
"How so? I alone am the creation.
By the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi), the created world is meant—that which is being created, or that which has been created. Thus he thought: "I alone am the creation."
That which was created by me is non-different from me; therefore, it is I alone, and it does not exist apart from me.
Why is this so? Because I indeed created all this world—I am its creator—this is the meaning.
Since Prajāpati designated his very self by the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi), [it follows that the world is himself].
From him, therefore, creation came into being; he was named Sṛṣṭi. In this creation, in this world, of this Prajāpati—within this very world.
He becomes a creator like Prajāpati of the world that is non-different from his own self; who is he?

He who knows, as Prajāpati does, "I am this world"—the world consisting of the internal self (ādhyātmika), the elements (bhūta), and the divine (adhidaivika), which is non-different from his own self, exactly as described. //5//
Then,
saying "So be it," he rubbed.
From his mouth and from his hands, he created fire as its source.
Therefore, both of these are hairless within;
for the womb is hairless within.
Thus, when they say, "Sacrifice to that one, sacrifice to that one," sacrificing to each individual deity is actually an emanation of this very [womb].
For he indeed is all the gods.
Now, whatever here is moist, that he created from semen;
and that is Soma.
All this, indeed, is just this much: both food and the eater of food.
Soma is the food; Agni is the eater of food.
This is the further creation of Brahman.

Because he created the gods who are superior, and because, being mortal himself, he created the immortals, this is called the "Exceeding Creation" (atisṛṣṭi). He who knows this comes to participate in this Exceeding Creation of his. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6.
Thus, having created this world consisting of pairs, Prajāpati, desiring to create first the deities who are the regulators of the social classes beginning with the Brahmins, [said] "aya"—
the two words "aya" are for the purpose of demonstrating a gesture; in this manner, having placed his hands on his mouth, he rubbed it by way of friction.

Having churned with his mouth and hands— from his mouth and from his hands, that is, from his two sources— he created fire, the benefactor of the Brāhmaṇa caste. Since both of these, the hands and the mouth, were the source (*yoni*) of the burning fire, therefore both of them are hairless, being devoid of body hair.
Is it everything? No; rather, from within, that is, from the interior;
for there is a commonality between both of these by way of their origin.
Why? Because the womb of women is hairless within;
likewise, the Brāhmaṇa was also born from the very mouth of Prajāpati.
Therefore, due to their common origin, the Brāhmaṇa is favored by Agni, just as a younger brother is favored by an elder.
Therefore, it is established by Śruti and Smṛti that the Brāhmaṇa has Agni as his deity and possesses the power of the mouth;
likewise, from the two arms, which are the locus of strength, arose the Kṣatriya caste—the restrainer—along with Indra and others who shatter the forces of opposition.
Therefore, it is understood from both Śruti and Smṛti that the Kṣatriya belongs to Indra and possesses the power of the arms.

Likewise, from his thighs he created effort and exertion; because they depend upon those [limbs], he created the Vaiśya, characterized by wealth (*vasu*) and so forth, as the ruler of the people (*viś*) and the people themselves.
Therefore, the Vaiśya is devoted to agriculture and the like, and has the deities of wealth (*vasu*) and so forth as his presiding deities.
Similarly, it is well-known from the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* that from his feet he created Pūṣan, whose deity is the earth, and the Śūdra, who is capable of service.

In this context, he concludes the creation of the deities beginning with the Kṣatriyas— which was not explicitly mentioned here but will be discussed later— just as he did for what was already stated, in order to proclaim the entirety of the creation. Just as this Śruti is established, the certain meaning is that Prajāpati alone is all the gods,
because those who are created are non-different from the creator.
However, because the gods were indeed created by Prajāpati,
once the meaning of the context has been thus established, there is the presentation of a critique of other opinions held by the ignorant, intended as praise for them;
for the censure of one thing serves as the praise of another.

In that context, regarding the section on ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), the mere ritualists (*kevalayājñikāḥ*) say at the time of sacrifice: "Sacrifice to this Agni; sacrifice to this Indra," and so forth.

The intention is that they speak thus because they consider the deity—Agni and the others—to be indeed distinct and one, based on the differentiation of names, *śastra*-hymns, *stotra*-chants, rituals, and so on.
One should not understand it in that way.
Because this entire differentiation of gods is indeed the creation of this very Prajāpati; for he alone is Prajāpati, and all the gods are indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
Regarding this, they disagree: some say it is the supreme Hiraṇyagarbha, while others say it is the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī).
But [the Self] is indeed the Supreme, according to the wording of the mantra:
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni," as stated in the Śruti;
and "He is Brahman, He is Indra, He is Prajāpati, He is all these gods" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 5).
3) Thus it is from Śruti;
and from Smṛti as well: “Some call him Agni, others Manu, and others Prajāpati” (Manu 12.123); and:
“He who is beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal...”
“Consisting of all beings, inconceivable, he himself shone forth” (Manu 1.7).
Thus, he might indeed be a transmigrating being.
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "He approaches all evils" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1).
For there is no possibility of the burning away of evils for one who is not subject to saṃsāra;
this is because [the scriptures] speak of his connection with fear and aversion.
And from the Vedic mantra: "Then, being mortal, he created the immortals" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6), and from the mantra: "He beholds Hiraṇyagarbha being born" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.12).

And from the *Smṛti*, in the context of the process of the ripening of karma: “Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—these the wise call the supreme Sāttvika goal” (Manu 12.50).
Now, if it is argued that because such contradictory meanings are untenable, there is a contradiction of authority (*prāmāṇya-vyāghāta*)?
No, for there is no contradiction, as another conceptualization arises;
through connection with a particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), another specific conceptualization becomes possible:
"Seated, he goes far; lying down, he goes everywhere."
"O God, who other than I could know that Lord, who is difficult to grasp and beyond both pride and intoxication? (KaU 1.2.21).

From such scriptural passages as these, it follows that the state of being a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritva*) is due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and not in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*);
by its own nature, it is indeed non-transmigrating.
In this way, there is both unity and diversity regarding Hiraṇyagarbha,
and likewise regarding all living beings,
according to the Vedic revelation: "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.16).

However, the declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti proceed on the basis that Hiraṇyagarbha is generally the Supreme Lord himself, with respect to the excellence of his purity of limiting adjunct (upādhi);
they show his state of transmigratoriness only in certain instances.
Because of the abundance of impurity residing in the limiting adjuncts of individual souls (jīvas), their state of transmigratoriness alone is generally predicated.
However, with respect to the exclusion of all differentiated limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), everything is designated as "the Supreme" (*para*) by the declarations of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

But by the logicians (*tārkika*), who have abandoned the authority of scripture, the meaning of the scriptures has been thrown into confusion by many contradictory arguments such as "it exists," "it does not exist," "it is a creator," "it is not a creator," and so forth; therefore, the ascertainment of the true meaning is difficult to attain.
But for those who follow the scripture alone and whose pride has been stilled, the meaning of the scripture regarding deities and so forth is as certain as an object of direct perception.
In that regard, since a distinction characterized by "eating" and "being eaten" was intended for the single deity Prajāpati, Agni was there described as the eater;
now Soma, the food, is being described: "Now, whatever moist thing of a liquid nature exists here in this world, he created that from his own self, from the seed."
According to the Vedic scripture, "From semen [comes] water" (AiU 1.4),
and Soma is of a liquid nature;
therefore, whatever was emitted as semen by Prajāpati when it was moist, that indeed was Soma alone.
This much indeed, this alone, and nothing more than this, is all this.
What is that? Food and Soma; for Soma, being liquid in nature, is nourishing, while Agni, the eater of food, is so because of his heat and dryness.
It is restricted to that very point:
the meaning is that Soma alone is food; whatever is eaten, that indeed is Soma.
He who is the eater is Agni himself; this restriction follows from the force of the context.
Even fire, when being offered into, is essentially of the nature of Soma; and even Soma, when being worshipped as the object of sacrifice, is indeed fire because it is the consumer.
Thus, one who perceives the world as consisting of the essence of Agni and Soma as one's own self is not tainted by any fault whatsoever.
And he becomes Prajāpati.
This is the "over-creation" (*atisṛṣṭi*) of Brahmā Prajāpati, which exceeds even himself.
If one asks what that is, he says: because he created the gods—who are superior and more praiseworthy—out of himself, therefore the creation of the gods is called an over-creation.

But how is there the creation of an excellence for oneself? To this he says: Now, because being mortal—that is, subject to death—one has created the immortals, those not subject to death, namely the gods, having burnt away all one's own evils by means of the fire of ritual action and knowledge;

therefore, he who knows this "excessive creation" (atisṛṣṭi) belonging to Prajāpati as his own self becomes like Prajāpati in this excessive creation; that is, he becomes a creator just like Prajāpati. //6//

All Vedic means of accomplishment, characterized by knowledge and action, depend upon various factors such as the agent; they culminate in the fruit of lordship over all creatures (*prajāpatitva*), and they are entirely limited to this much: namely, this manifested world, which is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

Now, in order to point out that seed-state of this very manifested world—characterized by means and ends—which existed prior to its manifestation, just as the state of a tree is inferred from its effects such as sprouts, [the text says:
"this tree of transmigration, having karma for its seed and ignorance for its soil, must be uprooted along with its roots."
For in its eradication lies the complete fulfillment of the human goal.
Thus it is said in the *Kaṭhaka*: “Rooted above, with branches below”;
and in the *Gītā*: “Rooted above, with branches below.”
And in the Purāṇa it is said: "The eternal tree of Brahman.
At that time, this [universe] was indeed undifferentiated.
That [Self] was differentiated by name and form alone, as "He is such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a form.
Even now, this very [Self] is differentiated by name and form alone, as "He is such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a form.
He has entered here even to the tips of the fingernails, just as a razor might be placed in a razor-case, or as fire might be present in its hearth.
They do not perceive Him, for He is incomplete: when breathing, He is called "breath" (prāṇa);
when speaking, "speech" (vāk); when seeing, "the eye" (cakṣus); when hearing, "the ear" (śrotra); and when thinking, "the mind" (manas).
These are indeed just his names according to his actions.
He who worships any one of them individually does not know him,
for he is incomplete when considered through any one of these alone.
"One should venerate it as the Self alone;
for herein all these become one.
This Self is the goal to be reached by all this."
For by this one knows all this.
Just as one might find [something lost] by means of a footprint, so does he who knows this find fame and praise. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7.
"Then this was that"— this refers to the world in its state as a seed prior to creation, at that time.
It is denoted by the pronoun "that" (*tat*) because it is not directly perceived,
and because the world, existing in an unmanifest state, is connected with past time.
The particle *ha* is used for the sake of easy comprehension as a traditional narrative device (*aitihya*).
When it is said, "Thus indeed it was then," one easily understands that even that remote seed-state of the world;
just as when it is said, "Yudhiṣṭhira, it is said, was indeed the king."
The word "this" (*idam*) refers to that which has been described as consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), characterized by the relationship between the goal and the means.

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words "that" (*tat*) and "this" (*idam*), which denote the world in its unmanifest and manifest states respectively, the oneness of the world in its unmanifest and manifest states is understood: "That indeed was this; and this indeed was that unmanifest."
This being so, it is established that there is no arising of the non-existent, nor the destruction of the existent, with respect to the effect.
Thus, this world, being unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), was manifested precisely through name and form—that is, by name and by form alone.
From the use of the reflexive passive construction "it was manifested," it follows that it was manifested by itself; that is, its very self manifested itself.

It was unfolded; it attained a state of manifestation clearly defined by the determination of specific names and forms, implying—by the force of the context—the causes of action consisting of a controller, an agent, instruments, and activity.
By the use of the pronoun "this one" (*asaú*), he designates it merely as a name through a general designation that does not specify [the particular name].

"His name is Devadatta" or "Yajñadatta"—thus he is "one who has such a name. Likewise, regarding white, black, and so forth without distinction: "This is his form"—white or black—thus he is "one who has this form."

This very indeterminate reality, even at this present time, is manifested through name and form alone—as "this one has such a name" and "this one has such a form"—for which purpose the undertaking of all scriptures exists. It is that in which, by means of innate ignorance, the superimposition of agent, action, and fruit is made;
it is the cause of the entire world, within whose nature name and form are manifested from the undifferentiated, just as foam arises from clear water or impurity from it.
And that which is distinct from those two, name and form— by its very nature eternal, pure, enlightened, and free— is this very Self which,

while making manifest the undifferentiated name and form that were its own being, has entered into bodies beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass, here in this world which is the locus of the fruits of karma and characterized by hunger and other such states.
But was it not stated that the undifferentiated itself undergoes differentiation?
How can it now be said that "it is the Supreme Self alone who, explaining the unexplained, has entered here"?
This is not a fault.
This is because even for another [opponent], the Self is intended to be the unmanifest nature of the world;
for we have stated that the unmanifest world is manifested as the cause consisting of the implied controller, agent, and action,
and because the word "unmanifest" stands in grammatical apposition with the word "this."
Just as this manifest world is characterized by various distinctions such as a controller, multiple agents, causes, and so forth,
so too is that unmanifest state characterized by not having abandoned any one of those same distinctions;
the only difference lies in its being merely manifest or unmanifest.
Moreover, it is observed in the world that the use of words depends upon the speaker's intention (vivakṣā), as in the expressions "the village has arrived" and "the village is empty.
Sometimes, when there is an intention to express merely the dwelling place by the word "village," the expression "the village is empty" occurs;
sometimes, when there is an intention to express the inhabitants of the dwelling, the expression "the village has arrived" occurs.
Sometimes the word "village" (grāma) is used even when both [the village and its inhabitants] are intended to be expressed,

as in the expression, "one should not enter the village. Likewise here, in the desire to express non-difference between the manifest and the unmanifest, there occurs the designation of this world as both "self" (ātman) and "non-self" (anātman).
Likewise, the mere designation "the world" refers to this world whose nature consists of origination and destruction.
Similarly: "The Great, Unborn Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22);
"Neither gross nor subtle; He is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
26) And so forth; this is the designation of the isolated Self (*kevalātman*).
Now, since the world has been explained by the supreme expounder as being all-pervading and existing at all times, how can he be conceived here as having entered [into it]?
For a region that has not already been entered can be entered by one who is limited in size, such as a person entering a village or the like;
but space cannot be so entered, because it is eternally entered by everything.
If it is argued that [the Self entered] by means of another property, like a stone-serpent or the like—suppose it were thus:
the supreme Self did not enter in its own essential form; what then?
Remaining in that very state, it arises through another property;
therefore, it is figuratively described as having "entered" it,
just as a serpent is naturally inherent within a stone, or water within a coconut.
No, because of the scriptural text: "Having created that, He entered into it.
For it is heard in scripture that the Creator, without having undergone any change into another state of being, created the effect and subsequently entered it.

Just as in the expression "having eaten, he goes," there is a distinction between the earlier and later times of the two actions of eating and going, yet the agent remains the same; so it would be here as well.
But this [process] is not possible for one who already resides in that very place through the production of another state of being.
Furthermore, entry characterized by separation from one location and conjunction with another location is never observed in the case of that which is partless and undivided.
If it is argued that this is because entry is heard of only in the case of things possessing parts, we say no.
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "For the divine Person is formless" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2),
and "Partless and actionless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19), as well as from those scriptures which negate all specific attributes that could serve as designations.
If it is argued that it is like the entry of a reflection, no; for spatial separation by another entity is impossible.
If it is argued that it is like the entry of a quality into a substance, no; [for that too is untenable].
No, because it is non-dependent.
It is only for a quality (*guṇa*) that is dependent and eternally reliant on another that "entry" into a substance (*dravya*) is figuratively attributed;
however, such entry is not possible for Brahman, because its independence is heard [in scripture].

If it is argued that [the world] is like a seed in a fruit, we say no; for this would entail the consequence that Brahman possesses qualities such as having parts (*sāvayavatva*), growth, decay, origination, and destruction.
Moreover, Brahman cannot possess such qualities, because it contradicts both scripture and logic, as evidenced by texts such as "He is unborn and undecaying" (*ajo 'jaraḥ*).
If it is argued that, therefore, there must be another transmigrating being, limited and distinct, who has entered here—[we reply]:
No; for starting from the passage, "That divinity thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), it continues, "Let me manifest name and form" (6.3.2).
3) Thus, because it is heard that she alone is the agent of both entering and bestowing prophecy;
likewise: "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), and "He, having split open this very suture, entered through this door" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 3...).
12) "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and assigned names, sits calling them forth: 'You are a boy, or perhaps a girl; you are an old man tottering with a staff' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.3);
'He made bodies with two feet' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.18);
'Form after form' (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.9)."
9) Thus, from these words of the mantra, there is no entry of another [self] into the Supreme.
If it is argued that because those who have entered are mutually distinct, there must be a multiplicity of Supremes, we say no.

For [the scriptures declare]: "The one God is seated in many ways" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11); "Being one, he moved about in many ways" (Ṛgveda 10.114.5); "You are one, having entered into many" (Atharvaveda 10.8.43); and "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
[This is] from such scriptural passages as these.
Let us set aside for now the question of whether entry is possible or not possible.

If it is argued that because those who have entered [the body] are subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva), and because [the Supreme Self] is non-different from them, the Supreme Self itself must be subject to transmigratory existence—[we reply: no.
No, because of the scriptural statement regarding the transcendence of hunger and other such needs.
If it is argued that this is not so because we observe states such as happiness and suffering [in the self], we say no;
for there is the scriptural text: "He is external and is not tainted by the suffering of the world" (KaU 2.2.11).

If it is argued that this is untenable because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, we say no; for perception and the rest have as their objects specific distinctions produced by dependence upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
As it is said: "One cannot see the seer of seeing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2).

2) From such scriptural passages as, “By what, O Maitreyi, should one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.19), and “The knower is itself unknown” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11), it follows that knowledge does not have the Self as its object.

What then? The perceptual cognition such as "I am happy" or "I am suffering" has as its object merely the reflection of the Self (ātman) within limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi).
This is due to the figurative application of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the subject and the object in the expression "this is I. [As it is said:
"There is no other seer but this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
11) Furthermore, because of the negation of another self, and because pleasure and pain are predicated of specific parts of the body, they are attributes of the object [the body]. [As it is said:
"But selves are for the sake of desire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4).
5) If it is argued that the purpose of the self (*ātmartha*) is untenable because [the self] is not heard of [as an object], we say no;

for in the passage, “Where there is, as it were, another” (*yatra vā anyadiva syāt*), the purpose of the self is admitted as being within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, [it is stated]: “By what means could one see whom? (*tat kena kaṃ paśyet*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), and “There is not the slightest diversity here” (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).

19) Furthermore, because [ignorance] is negated in the domain of knowledge by such passages as, "What delusion, what sorrow, can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7), it cannot be an inherent attribute of the Self.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because it contradicts the tenets of the logicians (tārkika), we say no.
Furthermore, the suffering of the self is untenable even through reasoning.
For the self cannot be qualified by suffering, which is an object of perception, because the self is not an object of perception.
If it is argued that the self's state of suffering is like space’s possession of the quality of sound, we say no.
Because it is logically impossible for [the self] to be the object of a single cognition.

For it is not possible that the self, which is eternally inferable, be made an object by a cognition that is perceptible and grasps pleasure; and if it were so made an object, since the self is unitary, it would follow that there is no subject [of cognition], as one and the same thing would be both the object and the subject, like a lamp. If you argue that this is indeed the case?
This is because simultaneous occurrence is impossible, and because it is untenable for the self to possess parts;
by this, the status of consciousness as both the grasped and the grasper is refuted.
Furthermore, there is no inference regarding the relationship of quality and qualified between suffering and the self, which are both objects of perception and inference;
for suffering is always an object of perception, and it stands in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality with color and other such qualities.
Even if suffering were produced by contact with the mind, it would follow that the self possesses parts, is subject to modification, and is non-eternal;
for nowhere is it observed that a substance which does not undergo modification can ever have a quality that arrives or departs through conjunction.
Nor is anything seen anywhere that is partless yet undergoes modification, or that is eternal while being the substratum of non-eternal qualities.
Furthermore, space is not accepted as eternal by those who follow the scriptures,
nor is there any other example [of such a thing].
If it is argued that even though it undergoes transformation, it is indeed eternal because its causal conditions do not cease?
No, because modification is impossible for a substance apart from a change in the state of its parts.
If it is argued that there is permanence despite having parts, we say no;
for that which has parts, being preceded by the conjunction of its parts, necessarily allows for their disjunction.
If it is argued that [the soul is not eternal] because it is not perceived in the case of diamonds and the like, we say no;
for its being preceded by conjunction is inferable.
Therefore, it is not possible for the self to be the substratum of impermanent qualities such as suffering and so forth.
If it is argued that, since there is no one else who is suffering and no other who is a sufferer, the undertaking of this treatise for the sake of pacifying suffering would be purposeless—
this is not so; for its purpose is to remove the delusion of being a sufferer superimposed by ignorance,
just as one removes the delusion of being the "thirteenth" person in a group.
And because of the acceptance of a self that is imagined to be subject to suffering;
and because the entry of the Self is like a reflection, since it is perceived within the manifested effect just as a reflection [is seen] in water or in the sun;
the Self, which was unperceived prior to creation, is subsequently perceived within the intellect once the effect has been produced and manifested.

Just as the reflection of the sun and other luminaries appears to have entered into water and the like after producing its effect therein, so too is He pointed out as being perceived as if having entered: "He has entered here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7);
and "Having created those [worlds], He entered into them; having split open this very aperture, He entered through that door" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 3).
12) This [is shown] by such passages as: "That Deity thought: 'Well, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman)' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
However, for that which is all-pervading and partless, an entry characterized by moving away from one direction, place, or time and reaching another is never logically possible.

And we have already stated this on the basis of such scriptural passages as, "There is no seer other than this Self; there is no other seer than this; there is no hearer other than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
Furthermore, the statements concerning creation, entry, maintenance, and dissolution exist for the purpose of [facilitating] perception.
Because it is heard that apprehension is for the sake of the person:
"He knew only himself" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10);
"Therefore, he became all this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
10) "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
"He who indeed knows that Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9);
"The person who has a teacher knows [it]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
2) From such scriptural passages as "For him, the delay is only so long" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2),
and "Then, having known Me in truth, he enters [Me] immediately thereafter" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.55).
Furthermore, this is supported by such Smṛti passages as: "For that is the foremost of all sciences, for through it immortality is attained.
Moreover, because the perception of difference is sublated, it is logical that statements concerning creation and so forth have as their ultimate purpose the realization of the oneness of the Self.
Therefore, the term "entrance" is used figuratively to mean simply the perceptibility of [the Self] while residing within its effects.
Consciousness is perceived in oneself from the tips of the nails up to the limits of the nails. How, then, has it entered therein?
To this he says: just as in the world, in a "razor-receptacle" (*kṣuradhāna*)—so called because a razor (*kṣura*) is placed (*dhīyate*) within it—in that receptacle for the barber's implements.
The razor is perceived as being within;
it may be placed there or inserted, just like the fire called Viśvambhara—
the "bearer of all"— which is the fire in the *kulāya*, that is, in the nest, so called because it sustains (*bharaṇa*) everything.
The phrase "it should be placed in wood and so forth" is understood to follow here;
for it is perceived there when being rubbed.
Just as a razor is situated in one part of a razor-case, and just as fire is situated pervading all parts of wood and so forth, [so too is the soul].
Thus, the Self exists pervading the body both generally and specifically;
for therein it is perceived as possessing activities such as breathing and as possessing activities such as seeing.
Therefore, they do not see, nor do they perceive, that Self which has thus entered [the body] and is characterized by activities such as breathing.
But is this not a prohibition of something unestablished, namely "they do not see him," since seeing has not been the subject under discussion?
This is not a fault.

Since the passages concerning creation and so forth have as their ultimate purpose the realization of the oneness of the Self, that very vision is the one under discussion; for it is stated in a Vedic mantra:
"He became the counterpart of every form; that is his form, for the sake of being seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).

Regarding that, he states the reason why [the Self] characterized by the activity of breathing and so forth is not perceived: "For it is incomplete," meaning it is not the whole, because it is characterized by the activity of breathing and so forth. But why is it incomplete? It is said: when performing only the activity of breathing, it is called "Prāṇa"—that is, designated as "Prāṇa" and named "Prāṇa.
For it is called "Prāṇa" because it performs the activity of breathing; it is not called Prāṇa while performing any other activity.

Just as in the case of "the cooker" (*lāvaka*) or "the cook" (*pācaka*), because it does not include [the agent] as qualified by another action, that [agent] is incomplete. Likewise, one who speaks, performing the act of speaking, is called "speech" (*vāk*).
The eye is the seer because it sees;
the ear is the hearer because it hears;
the breath is the breather because it breathes; and speech is the speaker because it speaks—by these two, the emergence of the power of action is demonstrated.
By the two phrases "seeing with the eye" and "hearing with the ear," the emergence of the power of consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti*) is demonstrated,
because the power of consciousness has name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its object;
the ear and the eye are the instruments of consciousness.
Consciousness, however, is the means for the establishment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
for there is no object of cognition apart from name-and-form,
and the eyes and ears are the instruments for the perception of those two.
Action, which is accomplished by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and inherent in the vital breaths (prāṇa), has speech as its manifesting instrument; likewise,
it has those called the hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
Speech is for the purpose of indicating all things; for it is this very [speech] that explains everything. Indeed, these three are name, form, and action (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6).
1) For it will be said thus:
"The mind (manas), thinking, thinks. The mind is the common instrument for the expansions of the power of cognition; it is called "mind" because one thinks by means of it.
But the Puruṣa, being the agent and thinking with the mind, is called "mind. These [entities] beginning with prāṇa are the action-names of this Self;
they are names born of action, which are indeed simply "action-names" (karmanāmāni).
But they do not have the mere thing-in-itself as their object;
therefore, they do not illuminate the entire reality of the Self.

For in this way, that Self, while being differentiated and illuminated by the various names and forms—such as "prāṇa" (breath) and so forth—produced by those respective activities like breathing and the rest, [is nevertheless not fully revealed].

He who, from this collection of activities such as breathing and so forth, meditates upon—contemplates with his mind—the Self as being any one specific organ, such as the eye, while not withdrawing the other specific activities that constitute it, does not know, he does not understand Brahman.
Why? Because this Self is incomplete (*akṛtsna*), for it is not fully realized apart from this collection of breathing and the rest.
Therefore, being distinguished by each individual attribute, it becomes qualified [as such] because of the non-inclusion of other distinct attributes.
As long as one knows, sees, hears, or touches—knowing it as qualified by its own inherent activity—one does not truly know the Self in its entirety.
But how can one know while seeing?
Thus he says: "It is the Self (ātman) indeed.
That which attains those specific attributes previously mentioned—such as "breath" and so forth—is called the "Self.
It does not, however, become "the Whole" by withdrawing all particular attributes.
For, in its form as pure existence alone, it pervades the specific qualifications produced by the particular activities of limiting adjuncts such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
And so the text will say: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
Therefore, one should worship it as the Self (*ātman*) alone.

Thus, this entire [Self] is indeed grasped in its own essential form as a real entity. Anticipating the question, "Why is it 'entire'? he says: because in this Self, in its primordial state, there are no distinctions, just like the reflections of the sun in water when free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The distinctions produced by limiting adjuncts such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and designated by names arising from the functions of the vital breath and so forth— though thus described— indeed become one and attain non-difference.
Therefore, the injunction "one should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" is not an original injunction (apūrvavidhi).

Since [the knowledge of the Self] is already established as a prerequisite, the knowledge concerning the Self has been produced by such scriptural passages dedicated to the exposition of the Self as "That Brahman which is immediate and direct" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1) and "Which is the Self?— This one who consists of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).

In that case, by the very knowledge of the true nature of the Self, ignorance—which consists of the superimposition of the notions of agency and so forth, as well as the results of action, upon the objects of that [Self] through the false conceit of "I" regarding the non-Self—is dispelled.
When that ignorance has been dispelled, since defects such as desire cannot arise, the contemplation of the non-Self is no longer possible.
Therefore, in this view, meditation upon that [non-Self] need not be enjoined.
Because it has already been attained.
Let us set aside for a moment the question of whether the attainment of the meditation on the Self is occasional or obligatory;
[in either case], it would constitute an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction).
Since knowledge (*jñāna*) and meditation (*upāsanā*) are one and the same, [meditation] is not something that needs to be newly acquired.

This is understood from the fact that, having introduced the subject with the words "He does not know," the text states, "One should meditate [on him] as the Self alone" (*ātmety evopāsīta*); thus, the two terms "knows" (*veda*) and "meditates" (*upāsana*) are seen to have the same meaning.
For by this, it is said: "All this he knows; he knew himself alone" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.10).
10) From such scriptural passages as these, it follows that *vijñāna* is worship (*upāsana*).
And because this [worship] has not been previously established, it is fit to be the object of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, human engagement is not possible in the mere description of an existing nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, this is indeed an original injunction (apūrvavidhi),
because it shares the general character of an injunction for action;
just as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) and "one should offer oblations" (juhuyāt) and so forth are injunctions for action.

From such injunctions for the meditation on the Self as "One should meditate upon Him as the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7) and "The Self, my dear, is indeed to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), a specific distinction is understood.

Furthermore, because consciousness is a mental activity, a mental action is enjoined in such passages as: "When the oblation has been taken for whichever deity, one should meditate upon that deity mentally while about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call," and likewise:
"One should venerate [the Self] as the Self alone" (1.4.7);
"It is to be reflected upon; it is to be meditated upon" (2.4.5).
5) Thus, it is action itself, consisting of knowledge, that is enjoined;
as we have stated, the words *veda* (to know) and *upāsana* (meditation) have the same meaning.

Furthermore, because the three factors of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) are established—just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), within this efficient force, the three factors are understood as the means of removing the expectancy regarding what is to be produced (*bhāvya*) and so forth, namely: by what means, and in what manner.

Likewise, when this meditation (*upāsīta*) is enjoined, in response to the expectancy—"What should one meditate upon? and "By what means should one meditate?"—the three requirements are established by the scripture itself, stating: "One should meditate upon the Self with the mind, conjoined with the necessary duties (*itikartavyatā*) such as renunciation, celibacy, tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), cessation (*uparama*), and endurance (*titikṣā*). Thus, the triad [of object, means, and procedure] is supported.
Just as the entire section concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is utilized for the purpose of enjoining the performance of those sacrifices,

so too the Upaniṣadic section concerning the meditation on the Self is utilized solely for the purpose of enjoining the meditation on the Self— [as in passages such as] "Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6) and "Neither coarse... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8).

8) Regarding such passages as "One alone, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and "Beyond hunger and so forth," their utility lies in imparting the specific nature of the Self that is to be meditated upon; and the fruit is liberation, or the cessation of ignorance.
Others describe it thus: through meditation, one should cultivate a distinct, superior realization concerning the Self.
Therefore, it is that [knowledge] which knows the Self and which alone removes ignorance,
not the discriminative cognition (*vijñāna*) produced by Vedic statements concerning the Self.
Regarding this matter, there are also scriptural statements such as: "Having known [this], one should practice wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21);
"It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5);
and "That is to be sought after, that is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
No, because there is no other meaning [to be conveyed].
Nor is "one should meditate on [the Self] as the Self alone" an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Why?
Because, apart from the cognition produced by the statements that describe the nature of the Self and negate the non-Self, there exists neither a mental nor an external [object of meditation].
For an injunction is effective only where human activity is understood to occur apart from the mere cognition produced by hearing the injunctive sentence;
as, for example, in such cases as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices].
Indeed, the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is not identical to the cognition itself produced by the injunctive sentence regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
And that [result] is experienced in dependence upon qualifications and so forth;
however, unlike the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, no human activity is possible apart from the knowledge produced by such statements establishing the Self as "not this, not this" (neti neti).
This is because the cognition produced by those words is the cause for the cessation of all activity;

for a neutral cognition does not generate engagement, and because it brings about the cessation of the cognition of Brahman as non-self, [as stated in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2]: "One alone, without a second."
1) [This applies] to statements such as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8–16).
Furthermore, once that [ignorance] has ceased, activity is not possible, because of the contradiction.
If it is argued that the cessation of the cognition of non-Brahman and non-Self does not occur through the mere cognition produced by the statement [of scripture], we say no;
for [the scriptures declare] "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7–16) and "Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
6) "This is the Self alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2); "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1);
"This immortal Brahman alone" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).

11) Because [the Upaniṣads] teach that very same [truth] through such statements as, "There is no seer other than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11) and "Know that very thing to be Brahman" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.4).

If it is argued that these [sentences] serve to present the object for the injunction to see (*draṣṭavya-vidhi*), we say no; for this has already been answered by the fact that there is no other meaning [possible].

Since the vision of that [Self] is already accomplished at the very time of hearing through those very sentences—such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*)—which present the essential nature of the reality of the Self, there is no further performance of the injunction to see to be undertaken; thus, this objection has already been answered.

If it is argued that one does not engage in the knowledge of the Self without an injunction, merely through the verbal description of the Self’s true nature, we say no; for the knowledge of the Self is already produced by hearing the words of one who teaches the Self—what, pray, is there left to be done?
If it is further argued that even upon hearing that, one still does not engage [in practice], we say no.
Because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Just as one does not engage in action upon hearing the meaning of a sentence from a proponent of the Self (*ātmavādin*) without an injunction (*vidhi*), so too one would not engage upon hearing the meaning of an injunctive sentence without an injunction; thus, there would be a requirement for another injunction, and for the hearing of its meaning as well, leading to an infinite regress.

If it is argued that the continuous stream of recollection of self-knowledge produced by sentences is something distinct from the mere cognition arising from hearing [the scriptures], we say no, because it is already implied by the meaning [of those sentences].
For as soon as the cognition having the Self as its object arises from hearing the sentences that establish the Self, [the result follows].
At that very moment, as that arising song arises, the cognition regarding its object arises;
at that very moment, as that arising song arises, it does so precisely by subverting the false cognition regarding its object.

And when the false cognition regarding the Self is subverted, the natural recollections—which have as their objects the various distinctions of non-Self entities—no longer occur, for they are produced from that [false cognition].
And because of the realization that [everything else] is not the ultimate goal:

for when the Self is realized, everything else is understood to be non-beneficial, since it possesses many defects such as impermanence, suffering, and impurity, whereas the reality of the Self is of a nature entirely different from that.
Therefore, for those whose cognitions and memories are devoid of the Self, there results the non-existence of the realization of the Self.
By the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), since the continuity of the cognition and memory of the oneness of the Self exists by implication alone, it cannot be something to be enjoined;
furthermore, because that memory serves to eliminate defects such as the suffering of grief, delusion, fear, and exertion.
For defects such as sorrow and delusion arise from erroneous knowledge;
thus it is said: "What delusion can there be in that? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7), and "The wise man fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).
1) "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4);
"The knot of the heart is severed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8)—
such are the scriptural passages.
If it is argued that cessation (*nirodha*) is therefore a different entity:

even so, since the cessation of mental fluctuations is a distinct entity from the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-vijñāna*) produced by Vedic statements, and because it is understood as something to be performed (*kartavya*) in other systems (*tantra*), it must be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). If this is your position?
Because it is not understood as a means to liberation;
for in the Vedāntas, nothing other than the knowledge of Brahman as the Self is understood as a means to the supreme goal of man, as in:
"One should know the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
10) “Therefore all this became that” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6);
“The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
“He who knows that supreme Brahman indeed becomes Brahman itself” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).
9) “A man who has a teacher knows” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2);
“For him, the delay is only so long” (6.14.2);
“Verily, he who knows thus becomes the fearless Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
25) This is because of hundreds of such scriptural passages (*śruti*),
and because cessation (*nirodha*) has no other means of accomplishment.
For there is no means for the cessation of mental fluctuations apart from the knowledge of the Self and the continuous stream of its remembrance.
This has been stated by way of concession; however, no means for liberation other than the knowledge of Brahman is perceived.
Furthermore, due to the absence of any further expectancy, there is an absence of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).

As it has been stated that in injunctions such as "one should sacrifice," the expectations of the *bhāvanā*—namely, "what [is to be accomplished]," "by what means," and "how"—are satisfied by the result (*phala*), the instrument (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) respectively; so too, it is argued, this applies here to the injunction for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavijñāna*). That is incorrect, because [the Upanishads teach] "One alone, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
1) “That thou art” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8–16); “Not this, not this” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6); “Without interior, without exterior” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5).

19) Because all desires cease at the very moment of realizing the meaning of such statements as “This Self is Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), one does not engage in the realization of the meaning of the sentence impelled by an injunction; furthermore, we have already stated that if it were impelled by another injunction, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, no injunction is understood in such statements as "Brahman is one only, without a second," because they terminate solely in the description of the nature of the Self.
If it is argued that these statements lack authority because they consist merely in the description of the nature of an existing reality, [we reply:]...

Now, it might be argued that just as in passages such as "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra," there is a lack of authority because they are merely descriptive accounts of the nature of things, so too it must be for the sentences concerning the self (*ātman*). To this we say: no, because there is a distinction.
It is not whether a sentence describes a thing or describes an action that is the cause of its authority or lack thereof; what then?
It is the capacity to produce a cognition that possesses a determined result.
That sentence in which this capacity exists is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); that in which it does not exist is not a valid means of knowledge.
Furthermore, sir, we ask you: in sentences devoted to explaining the true nature of the Self, does a certain and fruitful knowledge arise, or not?
If it does arise, how can there be a lack of authority [in them]?
Or do you not see that the fruit of such knowledge is the cessation of the defects that are the seeds of saṃsāra—namely, ignorance, grief, delusion, fear, and so forth?

Do you not hear hundreds of such Upanishadic passages as: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7), and "I am indeed a knower of the mantras, but not a knower of the Self; therefore, O Venerable One, I grieve. May the Venerable One carry me across to the further shore of this grief" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3)?
Thus, in cases such as "Why did he weep? and so forth, there exists a cognition that is both certain and fruitful.
If such [cognition] does not exist, let there be invalidity [of those passages].
But when that [other passage] is invalid, why would there be invalidity for that which produces a certain and fruitful cognition?
If that [scripture] lacks authority, what confidence can there be in the sentences concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices?
But surely, the sentences concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others possess authority because they produce in a person the cognition for engaging in action;
whereas in the sentences concerning the knowledge of the Self, that is not the case.
True, this is so;
yet there is no fault here,
because the causes for its being a valid means of knowledge are present.
And the cause of validity is exactly as previously stated, and nothing else.
Furthermore, this is an ornament [of our position]:
that the production of a cognition which contradicts the seeds of all worldly activity is not a cause for the invalidity of those statements that establish the self.

As for the claim that statements such as "Having known, one should practice wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21) have the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*) distinct from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence,
this is true.
However, it does not have the sense of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); rather, it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) for that which is already established in some cases.
But how, then, is meditation established as being established in some cases?
To the extent that it has been stated— by way of elimination— that the continuum of self-consciousness and memory is indeed eternal, that is certainly so; nevertheless,
[this must be qualified] because the initiation of a body results from the determinate fruitfulness of a particular karma.
Even upon the attainment of right knowledge, the activity of speech, mind, and body necessarily persists,
because an action that has already acquired its momentum is more powerful [to continue], like the initial flight of a released arrow;
therefore, in this view, the weakness of knowledge in initiating activity is established.
Therefore, by relying on the strength of means such as renunciation and detachment, the continuous flow of mindfulness regarding the realization of the Self must be regulated;
it is not something that needs to be newly produced,
for we have considered that it has already been attained.

Therefore, having understood that sentences such as "one should cultivate wisdom" are intended to prescribe the rule for the necessity of maintaining a continuous stream of memory regarding attained consciousness—since no other meaning is possible—one should act accordingly.
Now, one might object: "But this is merely the meditation on the non-self (anātma-upāsanā)."

Because of the use of the word "iti"; just as in such passages as "one should meditate on this as 'the dear'" and so forth, it is not the qualities like "dear" themselves that are to be meditated upon, but rather the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth which possess those qualities like "dear."

Similarly here as well, from the use of the words "other" (*para*) and "self" (*ātman*), it is understood that the non-self entity (*anātmavastu*) is the object of meditation, just like the qualities of the self.
Furthermore, because this sentence differs from those concerning the self as the object of meditation, the author will later state: "One should meditate on the self alone as the world" (1.4.15).
And in that sentence, the self alone is intended as the object of meditation, as indicated by the use of the accusative case in the phrase "the self alone" (*ātmānam eva*).
But here, a second [accusative] case is not heard;
for the word "ātman" followed by "iti" is used as "ātmenaivopāsīta" (one should meditate by means of the Self alone).
Therefore, it is understood that the Self is not the object of meditation, nor is there any other quality of the Self [to be meditated upon].
No; for it is understood from the remainder of the passage that the Self is the object of meditation.
In the remainder of this very passage, the Self alone is understood as the object of meditation: "That which is the Self of all this is what one must seek to reach" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7);
"That which is the Self is more internal than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8).
8) "He knew himself alone" (1/4/10).
If it is argued that because the vision [of the Self] is prohibited for one who has entered, it cannot be an object of worship—[we reply:
the vision of that very Self whose entry was mentioned is what is being precluded; "they do not see Him" (4/3/14).
23) Since this is the subject under discussion,
[if it is argued that] therefore the self is simply not to be meditated upon,
we say: no, because of the fault of its being incomplete.

The prohibition regarding "seeing" is intended on account of the defect of incompleteness (*akṛtsnatva*), not for the purpose of prohibiting the Self as an object of meditation (*upāsya*). This is because [the text] qualifies [the Self] by means of its distinction with activities such as breathing and so forth. If the status of the Self as an object of meditation were not intended, then the statement that the Self—qualified by each single activity such as breathing—is incomplete would be meaningless; for it says: "For this one is incomplete through each [single function] alone. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1)
7) Therefore, it is established that the Self, being distinguished by many [attributes] and yet being one, is indeed to be meditated upon because of its totality (*kṛtsnatva*).

As for the usage of the word "Self" followed by "iti," it is for the purpose of knowing that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), neither the word "Self" nor the cognition thereof has the reality of the Self as its object.
Otherwise, [the scripture] would have said, "One should worship the Self.
In that case, by implication, both word and cognition would be admitted with respect to the Self;
and that is undesirable, as it is stated: "Not this, not this" (2.3.6).
6) "By what means could one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14);
"The knower is unknown" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.12);
"From whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.

As for the statement, "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15), that is not a separate injunction, since its purpose is merely to preclude the practice of meditating on what is not the Self.
Because they share the common characteristic of being unknown, both the Self and the non-Self are to be known.
In that regard, why is effort directed toward the meditation on the Self alone—as in "one should meditate [on it] as the Self"—and not toward the knowledge of the other?
To this it is said: this very thing is what is under discussion, what is to be reached, and what is to be attained, and nothing else.
The genitive case in "of this all" (*asya sarvasya*) has the sense of specification;
its meaning is "in this all.
"That which is this self" (*yadayam ātmā*) refers to that very reality of the self (*ātmatattva*).
Is it that nothing else is to be known at all?
No; what then?
Even though other things are to be known, they do not require a separate, subsequent cognition apart from the knowledge of the Self.
Why? Because when this Self is known, one knows all this—that which is other than what is born of the non-Self; that is, one knows it in its entirety. [Objection:
But surely, by the knowledge of one thing, another thing is not known.
We shall provide the answer to this with the passage beginning with "the drum" (*dundubhi*).

How, then, is this term to be understood? It is explained as follows: just as in the world, a place marked by the hoof-prints of cows and other animals is called a "track" (pada), and by means of that track, one searching for a lost animal that one wishes to find would find it—that is, obtain it.

The meaning is that when the Self is thus attained, everything is attained. Now, since knowledge is the subject under discussion— in the sense that "when the Self is known, everything else is known"— how can "attainment," which is not the subject at hand, be mentioned?
This is because it is intended that knowledge and attainment have the same meaning;
for the non-attainment of the Self is indeed ignorance,
and therefore knowledge itself is the attainment of the Self.

Self-acquisition is not characterized by the attainment of what was previously unattained, like the acquisition of various other things, because there is no distinction between the acquirer and that which is to be acquired;
for in such a case, the non-self would be the acquirer of the self.
That which is to be attained is the selfless (anātman).

Being unattained and separated by such activities as production, it must be attained by performing a specific action through the employment of specific causal factors (kāraka). However, that which is characterized by the attainment of what was previously unattained is impermanent.
Because it arises from the activity of desire produced by false knowledge, like the attainment of a son and so forth in a dream;
however, this Self is the opposite of that.
Precisely because it is the Self, it is not separated by actions such as being produced;
even though its own nature is eternally attained, ignorance alone constitutes the separation.
Just as, even when mother-of-pearl is being perceived, its non-perception due to the appearance of silver through error is merely a separation caused by contrary cognition.
Likewise, apprehension is merely knowledge itself,
since the purpose of knowledge is to remove the intervention of erroneous cognition;
in the same way, here too, the non-attainment of the Self is merely the intervention of ignorance.
Therefore, the gain resulting from knowledge is merely the removal of that [ignorance], and no other gain is ever possible.
Consequently, we shall explain that once the Self is attained, any means for accomplishing something other than that knowledge is useless.
Thus, wishing to state without any doubt that knowledge and attainment have the same object, he speaks concerning knowledge: [He says: "Knowledge..."
"One should find" (*anuvindeta*):

because the root *vid* has the sense of "obtaining," this is stated as the fruit of the knowledge of the qualities—namely, that this Self, having entered into name and form, became known as the "Self" and so forth, and thus attained the state of being the aggregate of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest, as well as the verse (*śloka*). Thus...
He who knows this attains—along with his beloved ones—fame (*kīrti*), renown (*khyāti*), and glory (*śloka*), that is, a collective assembly;

or rather, he who knows the subject matter as described obtains the primary fruit itself: the knowledge of oneness denoted by the word "fame" which is desired by those seeking liberation, and the liberation denoted by the word "glory. //7//
And for what reason does he say that the reality of the Self alone is to be known, setting aside everything else?—*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.8:
"This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else; it is more internal."
If someone were to say to another who speaks of something other than the Self as dear, "He will lose what is dear to him," it would likely come true.
One should worship the Self alone as dear.
For one who worships the Self alone as dear, his dear ones do not perish. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8)
This very reality of the Self is dearer than a son;

for while a son is well known in the world as dear, it shows that this [Self] is dearer even than him, thereby demonstrating its state of being unsurpassably dear. Likewise, it is dearer than wealth, such as gold, jewels, and so forth.
Likewise, "than all else" means than whatever else is renowned in the world as being dear.
Why is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) alone more dear than the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth?

It is said: because it is "more internal" (*antaratara*) than external things such as son or wealth; for the aggregate of the vital breaths and the physical body is internal—that is, more inward and closer—to the Self.
Therefore, that which is more internal than the internal is this Self, this very reality of the Self.
For whatever is most dear in the world must be obtained with every effort;
likewise, this Self is dearer than all things dear in the world.

Therefore, the meaning is that one should apply great effort toward attaining that [the welfare of others], even setting aside the effort required for attaining other things that are dear to oneself. But why, when the choice arises between abandoning the pleasure of one and adopting the pleasure of the other— between the self and the non-self— is the abandonment of the latter performed precisely by adopting the pleasure of the self, rather than the reverse?

Thus it is said: Suppose someone were to say to another person who speaks of anything other than the Self—such as a son or the like—as being dearer than the Self, including even the ether: "O you who speak of what is dear to yourself! That which you hold dear, characterized by a son and so forth, shall obstruct you; it shall come to a state of confinement, a suppression of the vital breaths; it shall perish."
Why does he speak thus?

Because the Lord is capable and competent to speak in this way; therefore, what he has said—that one will attain the restraint of the vital breaths—must be exactly so, for he is a speaker of things as they truly are.
Therefore, that [term] can be said to mean "Lord" (īśvara).
Some maintain that the word *īśvara* signifies "swiftness," provided that such a conventional usage were established.
Therefore, having abandoned other things that are dear, one should worship the Self alone as dear.

He who worships the Self alone as dear realizes that the Self alone is dear and nothing else exists; having determined that even other worldly objects of affection are indeed not dear, he worships—that is, he contemplates—this.
For one who knows thus, that which is dear does not become subject to death— that is, prone to perish.
This is merely a restatement,
because for the knower of the Self, there exists nothing else that is either dear or not dear.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of praising the grasping of what is dear to oneself, or for the purpose of prescribing the fruit of beloved qualities, because the suffix denoting habitual action (*tācchīlya*) is employed for those who perceive the self as dull-witted. //8//
The science of Brahman has been set forth in the aphorism, "One should meditate upon the Self alone," which is the purpose for which the Upaniṣad was composed.
Desiring to explain this very aphorism, and wishing to state its purpose, the author now introduces the inquiry.

Regarding this they say: "What indeed was that Brahman which, when known, became all this—whereby men think that through the knowledge of Brahman they shall become everything? Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.9.
Regarding the word "tat" (that), they say it refers to the reality to be elucidated in the immediately following sentence.

Those Brahmins desiring to know Brahman—having approached a Guru as their boat for crossing the shoreless great ocean whose waters consist of the suffering and exhaustion caused by revolving on the wheel of the continuous succession of birth, old age, and death; and being disenchanted with the nature of means and ends characterized by merit and demerit as well as their respective fruits—desire to reach the further shore.
To those who desire to attain that eternal and unsurpassed supreme good which is distinct from that [worldly existence],
he says what they declare: "That by means of which, through the knowledge of Brahman— that is, through the knowledge of Brahman as the Supreme Self—
everything without exception shall come to be, we shall become such," so do men think.
The mention of "human beings" is for the purpose of making known their specific qualification;
the intention is that human beings alone are specifically qualified for the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Just as they consider the attainment of results from actions in the sphere of ritual activity to be certain, [so too is the attainment of the goal through knowledge].

Likewise, they consider the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman—the state of being the Self of all—to be certain, since the authority of the Veda is the same in both cases. In this regard, a contradictory matter is perceived; therefore, we ask: what is that Brahman, through the knowledge of which men think they shall become everything?
In that case, by what cognition did that Brahman become everything?
For it is heard in scripture that "Brahman is everything.
If it became everything without cognizing anything at all, then let it be so for others as well.
What is the use of the knowledge of Brahman?

For if one becomes everything after having realized it, then, because it is accomplished through realization, the result of the knowledge of Brahman would be equivalent to the fruit of ritual action; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence that the attainment of the state of being everything is impermanent.
If it is argued that there is the fault of infinite regress— namely, that "having cognized this other thing, it became everything, and prior to that, having cognized yet another"—
it is not the case that it became everything without cognizing [anything],
for that would entail the fault of contradicting the meaning of the scripture.
If it is argued that there is then the fault of the impermanence of the result, we reply: not even a single fault exists, because a specific distinction in meaning is established. //9//

If it was only after knowing something that that Brahman became all this, we ask: what did that Brahman know, by virtue of which it became all this? When thus questioned, he offers a reply untainted by any defects:
In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone.
It knew only itself.
"I am Brahman.
Therefore, it became all that.
Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became that.
So it is with the seers;
so it is with human beings. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: "I was Manu, and I was the Sun."
So even now, whoever knows thus— "I am Brahman"— he becomes this all. Indeed, not even the gods are masters over his failure to become [Brahman],
for he becomes their very Self.
Now, he who worships another deity, thinking "He is one and I am another," does not know.
He is like an animal to the gods.
Just as many animals serve a man, so does each individual person serve the gods.
When even a single animal is taken away, it becomes unpleasant; how much more so when many are?
Therefore, that which humans know is not dear to them. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)
The Brahman referred to here is the lower Brahman,
because it is logically possible for it to attain all states of being;
for the attainment of all states of being by the higher Brahman cannot be accomplished through knowledge.
And the attainment of all states of being is accomplished by consciousness; indeed, the attainment of all states of being is accomplished by consciousness.
And he speaks of this attainment of all states of being accomplished by consciousness when he says, "Therefore, it became all that.
Therefore, in the passage "In the beginning, this was Brahman," it must be the lower Brahman (apara-brahman) that is intended here.
Or rather, because the qualification belongs to human beings, one who is destined to become such [a Brahman] would be a Brahmin.

For it has been stated that human beings are the subject under discussion in the passage, "All men think they shall become everything," and that they possess a specific qualification for the means of attaining worldly prosperity and the supreme good.
He is neither the higher Brahman nor the lower Prajāpati;
rather, through the knowledge of the lower Brahman—which consists of both duality and unity—accompanied by ritual action, he attains the state of the lower Brahman.

Having turned away from the realm of objects of enjoyment, having severed the bonds of desire and karma through the attainment of all things, and being destined for the state of the higher Brahman, he is designated as "Brahman" on account of the cause that is the knowledge of Brahman.

Furthermore, the use of words based on a future state is observed in the world, as in "he cooks rice," and in the scriptures, as in "the wandering mendicant [gives] the gift of fearlessness to all beings," and so forth;
likewise, some explain it thus: "Brahma" refers to the person who is becoming Brahma, i.e., a Brāhmaṇa.
That is not so, because it would entail the attainment of all states of existence and thus incur the fault of impermanence.
For there is nothing in the world that, by virtue of a cause, attains another state of being and yet remains eternal.
Likewise, if the attainment of all states of existence were produced by the knowledge of Brahman as its cause, [it would likewise be impermanent].
To say it is eternal is a contradiction; and if it were non-eternal, the fault already mentioned—that it would be equivalent to the fruit of karma—would apply.
Furthermore, if you consider the attainment of omniscience to be the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, consisting in the cessation of the non-omniscience produced by ignorance, [then...]
The conceptualization of a person who is to become Brahman would be futile;
for even prior to the realization of Brahman, every living being is eternally possessed of all states by virtue of being Brahman from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha).
However, through ignorance (avidyā), non-Brahmanhood and non-universality are superimposed, just as silver is superimposed upon mother-of-pearl.
Or, just as the sky possesses such qualities as having a surface or impurity,
if you think that here in Brahman the non-Brahmanhood and non-omnipresence superimposed by ignorance are removed by the knowledge of Brahman,
then it is logical that [Brahman] was in reality the Supreme Brahman.

This is said in order to state that the primary meaning of the word "Brahman" is expressed in the sentence, "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," because the Veda speaks of things as they truly are.
However, this [other] interpretation is not tenable.
