It is not tenable to claim that the person who is to become Brahman (brahmabhāvī) is called "Brahman" because he is the opposite of the meaning of the word "Brahman," for that would involve the abandonment of what is heard in scripture (śrutahāni) and the assumption of what is not heard (aśrutakalpanā), especially in the absence of any other more significant purpose.
If it is argued that non-Brahmanhood and non-omnipresence actually exist as distinct from [the self] due to ignorance (avidyā), we say no;
for it is impossible for those to be removed by the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).
For nowhere is it observed that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) directly removes or produces any property of a real entity;
rather, it is seen everywhere as the remover of ignorance (avidyā).
Likewise here, let non-Brahmanhood and non-universality—which are produced solely by ignorance—be removed by the knowledge of Brahman.

But the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is not capable of creating or destroying an ultimately real entity (pāramārthika-vastu). Therefore, the abandonment of what is heard [in scripture] and the postulation of what is not heard are indeed futile.
If it is argued that ignorance (avidyā) is impossible with respect to Brahman?
No, because knowledge is enjoined regarding Brahman.

For when mother-of-pearl has not been superposed as silver, its true nature as mother-of-pearl is not made known once it has come within the range of the eye—[namely,] "This is mother-of-pearl, not silver.

Likewise, when there is no superposition of ignorance upon Brahman, the realization of oneness regarding Brahman—such as "All this is Being alone," "All this is Brahman alone," "All this is the Self alone," and "This duality does not exist, for there is no non-Brahman"—need not be enjoined.

We do not say that there is no superimposition of non-brahman attributes upon Brahman— as there is, for example, upon mother-of-pearl; rather, we say that Brahman is not the cause of the superimposition of non-brahman attributes upon itself, nor is it the agent of ignorance.
Let it be so that Brahman is neither the agent of ignorance nor deluded;
however, no other conscious, deluded agent of ignorance distinct from Brahman is admitted, for [the scripture states]:
"There is no other knower than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
23) “There is no knower other than this” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11); “That thou art” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7);
“I am Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
10) From such scriptural passages as, “He who thinks ‘that one is one thing and I am another’ does not know” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10),
and from the Smṛtis— such as, “The same in all beings” (Gītā 13.27)— it is established that [the Self is one].
27) [This is known] from such passages as: “I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa” (Gītā 10.20), “Even in a dog and even in an outcaste” (Gītā 5.18), and “He who [sees all] beings... (Gītā 6.29).
And from the wording of the mantra: "In whom all beings... (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).
[Objection: But if this is so, would it not follow that the instruction of the scripture is purposeless?
Certainly, if this is understood, there is indeed futility;
if you say it is the futility of the act of understanding,
we say no, because the cessation of non-understanding is observed [to occur].
If it is argued that even the cessation of that [ignorance] is untenable because of oneness, we say no, because it contradicts what is observed;
for it is indeed observed that the cessation of non-understanding occurs precisely through the cognition of oneness.
To say that what is being perceived is untenable would constitute a contradiction with what is observed;
moreover, no one accepts a contradiction with what is observed.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as the "untenability" of what is actually perceived.
Because it is indeed seen.
If it is argued that "seeing is impossible," the same reasoning applies there as well:
"One becomes virtuous through virtuous action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).

13) From such scriptural passages as “Knowledge and action follow him,” from the *smṛtis*, and from logical reasoning, a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*) is understood to be distinct and different from the Supreme.
And the Supreme is distinct from that [transmigrating being], as stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (3.9.26): “This one is ‘not this, not this’ (*neti neti*).”

23) [The Self] "transcends hunger and so forth," as stated in such scriptural passages as: "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, and deathless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), and "By the command of this Imperishable One... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9).
Furthermore, in the systems of logic such as those of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda, God is established through reasoning as being distinct from the transmigrating world.
Since we observe that people engage in activity out of a desire to remove the suffering of worldly existence, it is clearly understood that the transmigrating soul is different from God.
As it is said: "He who is beyond speech and beyond respect" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
2) From such scriptural passages as, "I have no [need for] possessions, O Pārtha" (Gītā 3.22),
and "He is to be sought after, He is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
1) "Having known that, one is not tainted" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23);
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
"This is to be seen as one alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.20).
20) “O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10);
“The wise man, having realized that very [Self]” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21);
“The *praṇava* is the bow, the Self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4).

4) Furthermore, because of the designation of the object and the agent in such [passages] as "he goes," and because of the instruction regarding the specific location on the path of travel for one desiring liberation—
if there were no distinction [between the two], whose going would there be, and from where?
Furthermore, in the absence of that [distinction], the distinction between the southern and northern paths would be untenable, as would the destination to be reached; however,
all of this is logically consistent if the self were distinct from the Supreme Self.

And because of the instruction regarding action and knowledge as means: if the transmigrating soul were different from Brahman, it would be appropriate to instruct that soul in action and knowledge, which are the means to prosperity and the supreme good, but not the Lord, since His desires are already fulfilled. Therefore, if it is argued that it is logical to say "Brahman" refers to the person who is to become Brahman— [The response to this objection follows: No, because of the teaching concerning the identity of the two. If they were different, the teaching would have been "Become Brahman," just as one says "Become a king. But the teaching is "Thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*), which indicates identity, like "This is that Devadatta. Furthermore, if they were different, the transmigrating soul would be subject to birth and death, while Brahman would be eternal; thus, the teaching of their identity would be false, just as saying "the rope is a snake. Moreover, if the transmigrating soul were different from Brahman, liberation would be impossible, for no one has ever seen a transmigrator becoming something other than itself. And if the transmigrator were different from Brahman, it would follow that Brahman is subject to transmigration, or else that the transmigrator is eternal. Therefore, it is established that the transmigrating soul is not different from Brahman. As for the argument regarding the instruction on action and knowledge, that is merely a statement of conventional usage, just as one might say, "Bring the firewood," when one actually intends to bring the fuel. Thus, the conclusion remains that the transmigrating soul is not different from Brahman.
No, for it would follow that the instruction regarding Brahman is purposeless.

If [the one who knows] were a transmigrating being (saṃsārī)— that is, one who, though not yet Brahman, realizes "I am indeed Brahman" and thereby becomes everything— then since the fruit of becoming the Self of all would already be accomplished through that very cognition of the transmigrating self, the instruction regarding the Supreme Brahman would certainly become useless.

If it is argued that because that cognition is not employed for the accomplishment of any human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the instruction "I am Brahman" is intended merely to bring about the state of being Brahman for one who is still a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*);
[we reply: for if the true nature of Brahman is not known, what could one possibly accomplish by thinking "I am Brahman"?
Indeed, such an identification can only be effected when Brahman’s defining characteristics have been fully ascertained.
No; for [the scriptures state]: "This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), "Brahman is that which is immediate and direct" (3.4.1), and "That which is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7).

1) Having introduced [the subject] with "That is the Truth, that is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), [it continues]: "From this very Self... (2.1).

1) Thus, from the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "Brahman" and "Self" occurring thousands of times, it is understood that they have precisely the same referent; for identification (*sampad*) is performed when one thing is different from another, not when they are identical.
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).
6) And thus it demonstrates the oneness of the very Self under discussion, which is the object to be seen.
Therefore, the realization of the Self as being Brahman through meditative identification (*sampad*) is not tenable;
nor is any other purpose for the instruction regarding Brahman perceived.
"One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).
"O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
"For Brahman is indeed fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
25) And because it is heard that there is such an occurrence [of attainment];
for if there were perfection, there would be no such occurrence,
since the non-existence of one thing in another is not logically possible.
If it is argued that from the statement [of identity] there would also follow the actual attainment of that state, we say no; for attainment is merely a mental conception.
Furthermore, we have already stated that consciousness has no other function than the removal of false knowledge.
Furthermore, a statement does not produce the capacity of a thing;
for it is an established principle that a scripture is informative (*jñāpaka*), not productive (*kāraka*).
This very [scripture] has entered here (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.7).
7) And in such statements as these, it is established that it is the Supreme [Self] alone who enters.
Therefore, the hypothesis of a person who will later become Brahman is not tenable; furthermore, it contradicts the intended meaning.
The intended meaning to be established throughout this entire Upaniṣad is the realization that Brahman is without interior or exterior, like a lump of salt, and is of a single essence.

This is understood from the definitive conclusion at the end of both sections: "This much alone, my dear, is immortality; this is the instruction. Likewise, the certain meaning in all the Upaniṣads of every branch of the Veda is the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman.

In that context, if one were to assume that the transmigrating soul is something other than Brahman, [as in the interpretation of the text]: "He knew himself alone," [it would contradict the aforementioned conclusions].
There would be no attainment of the desired object;
furthermore, the scripture would be rendered inconsistent by the contradiction between its opening and its conclusion,
and because the designation [of the Self as the enjoyer] would be untenable.
Moreover, if it were imagined that the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) knew only itself,

the designation "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) would not be appropriate; for in the statement "he knew only himself," it would logically follow that the transmigrating soul alone is the object of knowledge.
If it is argued that "Self" is said to be something other than the knower, we say no;
for there is the specific qualification, "I am Brahman.
If the object of knowledge were something else, it would be qualified as "this is that," but not as "I am."
From the qualification "I am" and from the restriction "he knew only the Self," it is understood with certainty that the Self alone is Brahman;
for if this were so, the designation "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) would be appropriate, but not otherwise,
as otherwise it would merely be the knowledge of a transmigrating being (saṃsārī).
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), both being Brahman and not being Brahman cannot logically belong to a single entity,
because they are as contradictory as darkness and light in relation to the sun.
Nor is it appropriate to apply the definitive designation "knowledge of Brahman" based on both causes when there is a desire to express the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
For the listener would likewise have doubt;
yet it is held that certain knowledge is the means for accomplishing the goal of human life, as stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "He who has this [knowledge] and no doubt...
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4), and in the Bhagavad Gītā: "The man of a doubting nature perishes" (Gītā 4.40).
40) Thus, according to the Śruti and Smṛti, one who seeks the welfare of others must not state a doubtful meaning of a sentence.

If it is argued that the conception of Brahman as an agent of accomplishment is as inappropriate as it would be for those like us—as in the passage, "The Self alone knew Itself; therefore, It became all"—then [the reply follows].
No, because it is a criticism of the treatise;
for this is not our own conceptualization,
but rather one made by the author of the treatise.
Therefore, this is a criticism of the scripture;
and one who desires to accomplish what is intended by Brahman should not engage in an interpretation contrary to the meaning of the scripture or abandon its own purpose.
Nor is it appropriate for you to be so intolerant regarding this much alone.

For all diversity is merely imagined in Brahman, as stated in: "It should be viewed as one alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.20), "There is not even the slightest diversity here" (4.4.19), and "For where there is duality, as it were... (2.4.14).
14) From hundreds of scriptural passages such as "one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1),
all worldly transactional activity is indeed imagined within Brahman alone; it does not exist in an ultimate sense.
This which is said—"this very conception is improper"—is far too little.
Therefore, that Brahman which entered as the creator is indeed that Brahman;
the word "vai" (indeed) serves the purpose of emphasis.
This which is perceived as residing within the body was, even prior to awakening, nothing other than Brahman itself; indeed, all this is Brahman.

However, due to a lack of awakening, through the superimposition upon the Self that "I am not Brahman" and "I am not the All," one superimposes [upon it]: "I am an agent, I am active, I am an enjoyer of fruits, I am happy, I am miserable, I am a transmigrator.
But in reality, one is indeed Brahman, which is distinct from that [transmigration], and the All is likewise.
When one has been somehow awakened by a compassionate teacher [with the words] "You are not a transmigrator," one should know one's own natural Self.
The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is that [the Self] is devoid of distinctions superimposed by ignorance.
Tell me, what is this innate Self which Brahmā had known?
But do you not remember yourself?
For he has been shown to you as the one who, having entered here, breathes out, breathes in, breathes pervasively, breathes upward, and breathes evenly.
"But surely you designate him as 'this is a cow,' 'this is a horse,' and so forth; you do not show the Self directly to yourself.
[The opponent replies: "In that case, he who is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower—that is the Self."
But surely here too, you do not show that the essential nature of the agent of actions such as seeing is perceptible;
for movement (*gati*) is not the essential nature of the mover, nor is cutting (*chidi*) the essential nature of the cutter.
If that is so, then [the Self is] the seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing, the thinker of thinking, and the knower of knowing—that is the Self.
Now, what distinction is there here regarding the seer? Whether he is the seer of the seer, or the seer of the jar,
in every case, it is simply the seer.
But you must indeed admit that the seer is to be seen; for by saying "the seer of seeing," whether he is the seer of seeing or the seer of a jar, the seer remains simply the seer.
No, because a distinction is established.
There is this distinction here: the seer of seeing is the seeing itself;
there is never a time when the seeing is not seen by the seer.
In that case, the seer's vision must be eternal;
for if the seer's vision were impermanent,
then that vision which is the object of seeing might at some time not be seen at all.
Just as an object such as a jar is perceived by a vision that is impermanent,
so too the seer of that vision never fails to see the vision.
Are there two visions for the seer— one eternal and invisible, and [the other visible]?
Is it not observed that other [views] are impermanent?
Certainly; for it is well known that view is impermanent, since one observes the state of being sighted in those who were previously blind.
If it were eternal, everyone would necessarily be non-blind;
for the vision of the seer is eternal, according to the Śruti: "Indeed, there is no loss of the vision of the seer.
This is also known from inference: even in a dream, the vision of a blind person is observed to have as its object the appearance of jars and other such things.
In that case, when other forms of vision perish, she does not see;
she is the vision of the seer.

By means of that unimpaired, eternal vision, which constitutes its own essential nature and is designated as self-luminous, it constantly perceives this impermanent vision—which, in the states of dreaming and waking, takes the form of impressions and mental objects—as the seer of vision.
This being so, vision itself is its very nature, like the heat of fire;
there is no conscious seer distinct from vision, as the followers of Kaṇāda maintain.

That Brahman knew itself alone as the eternally perceiving form, devoid of the superimposed notions of impermanent perception and so forth. But is this not a contradiction? For the Śruti states, “One cannot know the knower through knowing” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2), which implies that there is no cognition of the cognizer.
No; there is no contradiction with this understanding.

In this way, it is indeed understood that "the seer is the vision. Furthermore, because it does not depend on another cognition—once it is understood that the vision of the seer is eternal—the seer does not desire any other vision as an object for itself.
For the desire for the vision of an object by the seer ceases precisely because that [object] is impossible;
indeed, no one’s desire arises for an object that does not exist.
Furthermore, the visible vision is not capable of making the seer its own object.
Since one would desire that [knowledge],
and since there can be no desire for its own nature as an object,
therefore, the cessation of the superimposition of ignorance is precisely what is meant by the statement, "One should know the Self alone."
There is no making of the Self an object [of cognition]. How is that known?

To this he says: "I am the Seer of seeing; I am the Self, I am Brahman"—that is, Brahman which is immediate and direct, the innermost Self, beyond hunger and so forth, "not this, not this," neither gross nor subtle, and so on.
"I am that very one,
not another transmigrating being,
just as you have said."
Therefore, from that very consciousness, that Brahman became everything.
For this reason, it is indeed appropriate that men think, "By the knowledge of Brahman, we shall become everything.
This addresses what was asked: "What is that Brahman which, having known it, became all this?"
That has been determined: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself as 'I am Brahman,' therefore it became all.
In that regard, whoever among the gods awakened—that is, having realized the Self as the aforementioned Brahman—he became that Brahman.
Likewise among the sages, and likewise among human beings.

The passage beginning with "Of the gods" (*devānām*) and so forth is stated from the perspective of worldly perception and is not spoken with the intention that [the individual] possesses the nature of Brahman.
By the statement, "A Person entered into the cities," it is expressed that Brahman alone has entered everywhere.

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), in each respective case, Brahman alone existed from the beginning; prior to awakening, it was merely conceptualized otherwise within the bodies of gods and others.
Then he knew himself alone, and thus he became everything.
To strengthen this point—that the fruit of this knowledge of Brahman is the attainment of the state of being all—the Scripture cites these mantras.
How so? That Brahman, perceiving himself alone as "I am this," Vāmadeva—so named—attained, indeed, through that very vision of Brahman, the state of being the Seer (Ṛṣi). He truly attained it.
He saw these mantras in this [text]: "I was Manu and I was the Sun," and so forth.
By the phrase "perceiving this Brahman," the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is referred to.
Through the mantra beginning with "I was Manu and I was the Sun," he refers to the attainment of all states of being as the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman.

From this application— “seeing [Brahman], he attained the fruit which is the state of being the Self of all”— it is shown that liberation is to be accomplished by means of the aids to the knowledge of Brahman,
just as one says, “eating, he is satisfied.
This attainment of the state of being everything through the knowledge of Brahman occurred due to the extraordinary power of the great ones, such as the gods.

Someone might think that this is not possible for people of this age, especially for humans, because of their meager vigor; to dispel that notion, he says: "This very Brahman under discussion is that which has entered into all beings, having sight, action, and so forth as its indicative marks."

Even now, at this present time, whoever has turned away from external longing and knows himself thus— "I am Brahman"— having set aside the distinctions superimposed by the erroneous cognition born of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and being untouched by the attributes of transmigratory existence, [realizing] "I am indeed only Brahman, without interior and without exterior"— he, through the knowledge of Brahman which brings about the cessation of non-universality created by ignorance, becomes this entire universe.
Indeed, there is no distinction in Brahman or in the knowledge of Brahman between those of great power, such as Vāmadeva and others, and those of inferior power among present-day humans.

However, since it might be doubted that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is uncertain for people in the present age, he says: "For him who knows Brahman, according to the aforementioned method, even the gods of great power do not become [anything other than what they are], nor does Brahman—the Self of all—become non-existent."
They do not have the power [to prevent], nor are they sufficient; how much less so others?
What doubt could there be that the gods and others have the power to create obstacles to the attainment of the fruit of Brahman-knowledge?
To this it is replied: because mortals are, in relation to the gods and others, like those who owe a debt.
For the Śruti shows that a person is born already possessing debts: "By the life of a student (brahmacarya) to the sages, by sacrifice to the gods, and by progeny to the ancestors.
Furthermore, because of the illustration of cattle [in the passage] "Now this one indeed...

(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.16) and other such scriptural texts regarding the worlds, it is logical that the gods—being like creditors—would create obstacles for men who are dependent on them, with the desire to protect the fulfillment of their own functions, regarding the attainment of immortality. Thus, this [view] is indeed reasonable.
Doubt: The gods protect their own subjects as if they were their own bodies.
For he will show that the gods and others possess a more exalted mode of existence dependent on ritual action, based on the notion that each individual human being is equivalent to many cattle.
For it will indeed say: "Therefore, that which humans know as these sciences is not dear to them" (1.4.10);
and also: "Just as one would desire safety for one's own world, even so do all beings desire safety for one who knows thus" (1.4.16).

The intention—that even Brahmā and the Viśvedevas, because they lack the state of being for the sake of another (pārārthya), do not possess their own worlds and are subject to the state of being bound (paśutva)—is understood from the two statements regarding what is unpleasant and misfortune.
Therefore, the gods would certainly create obstacles for one who has attained the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman;
for they are indeed possessed of great power.
If this were so, then even in other instances of attaining the fruits of one's actions, the gods' creation of obstacles would be equivalent to drinking what should not be drunk.

Alas! In that case, there would be no confidence in the performance of the means for attaining worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Likewise, because the Lord possesses inconceivable power, he has the capacity to create obstacles.
Likewise, this applies to time, karma, mantras, herbs, and asceticism;
for it is well known both in the treatises and in the world that these are the causes of the attainment or failure of results.
Therefore, there is likewise no confidence in the performance of the meaning of the treatises.
This is because all things arise from specific causes and materials,
and because we observe the diversity of the world;
furthermore, under the view of inherent nature (*svabhāva*), both of these [facts] would be untenable.

When this position— that action is the cause of results such as pleasure and pain— is established, being accepted by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, logic, and the world, then God, the Lord, and Time certainly cannot be the agents who cause the reversal of the fruits of actions,
because actions are the producers of what is desired.
For the auspicious and inauspicious karma of persons does not attain its own nature without depending on causal factors such as God, Time, or Īśvara;
and even when it has attained its own nature, it is incapable of yielding its fruit,
because action by its very nature requires the employment of various instrumental causes such as the agent and so forth.
Therefore, since the lords of the gods and others are indeed subject to the influence of action, there is no lack of confidence regarding the attainment of results from ritual acts;
for even these [deities] are sometimes under the control of actions,
because their own power cannot be set aside.

The relative predominance or subordination among action, time, destiny, material substances, and so forth, as well as their intrinsic natures, is indefinite and difficult to discern; thus, people are deluded by this, some thinking that "action alone is the agent in the attainment of results and nothing else," while others say it is "destiny" alone,
and still others say it is "time."
Some maintain that [the self] has the nature of substance (*dravya*) and so forth;
others hold that all these [factors] are merely an aggregate.
Regarding this, the declarations of the Vedas and Smṛtis—such as "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13)—accept the primacy of karma.
Even though, within their own respective domains, the emergence of predominance in one may cause a temporary suppression of the power of predominance in the others,
nevertheless, there is no uncertainty regarding the attainment of the fruit of action,
because the predominance of action has been definitively established by both scripture and logic.

No; because the fruit of attaining Brahman consists merely in the removal of ignorance. As for what was said—that the gods might create obstacles to the fruit of attaining Brahman—in that regard, the gods lack the power to create obstacles. Why?
Because the fruit of attaining Brahman is not separated from the time of knowledge by any interval.
How so? Just as in the world, at whatever time there is a conjunction of the eye of the seer with light, at that very same time there is the manifestation of form;
in the same way, at whatever time there is consciousness having the self as its object—
At that very moment, there would be the disappearance of the cognition of those objects; therefore,
since the effects of ignorance are impossible when the knowledge of Brahman exists— just as the effects of darkness are impossible when a lamp is present—
who could obstruct whom, and for whose sake, by the gods, in a case where the gods themselves are the very Self of the knower of Brahman?
This is what he says: the Self is one's own nature, which is the object of meditation; that is Brahman, to be known through all the scriptures, for it is this [Brahman] that belongs to these gods.
One becomes a knower of Brahman;

for we have stated that at the very moment of the knowledge of Brahman, the obstruction consisting of mere ignorance departs—just as the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is seen to be the shell itself.
Therefore, it is not possible for the gods to exert effort against the Self, since it would be contrary to their own nature.

For in a case where the fruit is not one's own self and is separated by differences of place, time, and cause, effort directed toward that non-self object may be fruitful for the gods to employ as an obstacle;
but this is not so here, where [the fruit] is coeval with knowledge, is one's own self, and is not separated by place, time, or cause.
Because there is no opportunity [for such a sequence].

If that is so, then since there is an absence of a continuous stream of cognitions based on knowledge (*vidyā*), and because erroneous cognition and its effects are observed, it would follow that only the final cognition of the self (*ātmapratyaya*) is the remover of ignorance (*avidyā*), and not the preceding ones.
This is not so; for [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the first [cognition].
For if the first cognition regarding the self does not remove ignorance, then the final one likewise will not, because they have the same object.
If that were so, then ignorance would be removed by a continuous [series] and not by a discontinuous one.
This is not the case, because when life and so forth exist, a continuous series is impossible.
For when conditions such as life are present, a continuous series of conditions for knowledge cannot arise, due to their mutual contradiction.
If it is argued that the continuity of knowledge (*vidyā-santati*) lasts until death precisely by setting aside the notions of "living" and so forth, we say no;
for there would be the fault of not determining the meaning of the scripture, since the exact number of such notions cannot be ascertained.
Because one could not ascertain that "the continuity of this many notions is what removes ignorance," the meaning of the scripture would remain undetermined.
And that is undesirable.
If it is argued that [the agent] is determined to be merely a continuum,
we say no, because there is no distinction between the beginning and the end.

The first [position]— that the continuum of conditions for consciousness ends at the time of death— is untenable because there would be no distinction [between it and the other], and the two previously mentioned faults would apply to the first and last moments of consciousness.
If it is argued that, in this case, [the continuum] simply does not cease?
No, because of the Vedic revelation: "Therefore, all that became this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10);
and [because of the texts]: "The knot of the heart is severed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8) and "What delusion can there be in that? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).
And from such scriptural passages as these.
If it is argued that these are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), we say no; for they are the Upaniṣads of all the Vedic branches.
If it is argued that [the Self] indeed exists because it is an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no; for the refutation has already been stated.
It has been stated that the refutation consists in the fact that the cessation of defects such as ignorance, grief, delusion, and fear is itself perceptible.
Therefore, it is not to be questioned whether [the cognition] is initial, final, continuous, or non-continuous;

for since the purpose of the injunction culminates in the fruit of the cessation of defects such as ignorance, we accept that whatever cognition effects the fruit of the cessation of defects such as ignorance—whether initial, final, continuous, or non-continuous—that alone is "knowledge" (vidyā). Thus, there is not even a scent of an objection here.

As for what was said—that [the existence of the body] is due to the observation of contrary cognitions and their effects—it is not so; because that [karma] is the cause for the continued existence of its remainder.

Since the body has been commenced by a certain karma, that very karma, being characterized by such contrary cognitions and defects, possesses the capacity to yield its fruit only when conjoined with those contrary cognitions and defects.

As long as the body lasts, knowledge does not remove that [residual] misconception or defects such as passion, because it merely projects just enough of them to serve as the means for experiencing the fruits [of past actions] until the fall of the body;
this is because the karma caused by those [defects] has already begun to bear fruit, like an arrow that has been released.
Therefore, knowledge does not cause its cessation, as there is no contradiction between them.
Rather, it is precisely from its own substrate that [the knowledge] obstructs that effect of ignorance which is contrary to its own nature and is about to arise, because that [effect] is yet to come;
for the other [effect] is already past.
Furthermore, a distorted cognition does not arise in one who possesses knowledge,
because it lacks an objective basis.
For a distorted cognition arises only by relying upon a mere generality whose specific nature as an object has not been determined.
Just as in the case of [the cognition] "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl,

that [cognition] cannot occur as before once it has been sublated by one who possesses the ascertainment of the specific nature of the object and who relies upon the removal of all contrary cognitions;
for it is observed that when a correct cognition arises regarding mother-of-pearl and the like, [the erroneous cognition] does not recur.

In some cases, however, from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by contrary cognitions that arose previously, memories arise in which contrary cognitions appear; these suddenly produce the delusion of contrary cognitions even for one who possesses true knowledge.
This is just as, for example, a person who has already correctly understood the directions may suddenly experience the confusion of a reversal of directions.
Even for one who possesses right knowledge, if a contrary cognition arises as before, [the delusion occurs].

Furthermore, due to a lack of confidence even in right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), activity toward the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures and so forth would be improper, and all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would become invalid (*apramāṇa*), because no distinction between what is a valid cognition and what is not could be established.
By this, the objection— "Why is it that the body does not fall away immediately after right knowledge?"— is refuted.

The destruction of those [karmas] accumulated prior to the arising of knowledge, as well as after it, and during that very time, or in other births, is established precisely by the scriptural texts that negate obstacles to the attainment of the fruit:
“And his karmas are exhausted” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8) and “For him, there is delay only so long” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
2) “All evils flee away” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3);
“Having known Him, one is not smeared by evil action” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23);
“Verily, these two do not cross over this” (4.4.22).
22) “Neither what has been done nor what has not been done torments him” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22);
“Verily, this does not torment him” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9.1);
“He fears nothing from anywhere” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).
This is also established by such scriptural passages as these,
and by such traditional texts (smṛti) as: "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.37).
As for the claim that [liberation] is obstructed by debts,
that is not so,
because that refers to the domain of those possessed of ignorance.
For one who possesses ignorance is a debtor, since for such a person agency and the like are possible; as it is said:
"But where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31)

31) For it will say this: where there exists that non-different real entity called the Self, which appears as if it were something else while ignorance (avidyā) is present— just like a second moon produced by a visual disorder (timira)—
there [the scripture] demonstrates the action of seeing and so forth, which depends upon various factors (kāraka) created by ignorance, as well as the fruit produced thereby.
By the passage beginning with, "There, one might see another," and so forth;
whereas when true knowledge exists, there is the abandonment of the delusion of manifoldness produced by ignorance, [it is said]:
"Then, by what means would one see whom? (BU 4.5.15).
15) Thus he demonstrates the impossibility of karma.
Therefore, the state of being a debtor exists only in the realm of one possessed of ignorance, because karma is possible there; it does not exist elsewhere.
We shall demonstrate this in detail through the very passages that we intend to explain further on.

For instance, right here: "Now, whoever—being ignorant of Brahman—worships some deity other than the Self, thinking, 'That one is another, distinct from me,' and approaches it with praise, salutation, sacrifice, offerings, oblations, meditation, and so forth... [he worships] that which is other than himself, not the Self.
"I am another, I am the one authorized; I must repay this man like a debt"—one who possesses such a notion knows the truth according to the Veda.
He is not merely an ignorant person characterized by the defect of nescience (avidyā); what then? [He is one who understands his duty.]
Just as an animal, such as a cow, is utilized through various services like being yoked for transport or milked,
so too is he to be enjoyed by each of the gods and others through numerous services such as sacrifices;
therefore, the meaning is that he is authorized for all ritual actions, just like an animal.

For this ignorant person—who possesses distinctions such as caste and stage of life (*āśrama*), is qualified for action, and performs the duties prescribed by the scriptures either in conjunction with knowledge or independently—the result is an upward progression from the human state up to the level of Brahmā.
Conversely, the result of that which is contrary to scriptural injunctions and is merely natural is a downward degradation from the human state down to the level of stationary objects (*sthāvara*).
And how this is so is stated [in the scripture]: "Now, there are indeed three worlds... (1.5).
We shall explain this and more with the remainder of the entire chapter.
Furthermore, the effect of knowledge (*vidyā*)—namely, the attainment of the state of being the Self of all—has been shown in brief.
Indeed, this entire Upaniṣad is exhausted by the very demonstration of the distinction between knowledge and ignorance (*avidyā*).
We shall demonstrate how this meaning applies to the entire treatise.
Since this is so,
it shows that with respect to a person possessed of ignorance, the gods are indeed capable of both creating obstacles and bestowing grace.

Just as in the world many animals, such as cattle and horses, serve and protect their master— their own controller— so too each ignorant person, standing in the place of many animals, serves and protects the gods; the word "gods" is used here as an elliptical expression to include the ancestors and others.

The underlying intention here is this: "These others, Indra and the rest, are my masters, and I am their servant; by performing propitiation toward them through praise, salutation, sacrifice, and so forth, I shall attain prosperity and the highest good—the fruit bestowed by them.

In that regard, just as in the world a person possessing many cattle experiences great displeasure when even a single one among them is taken away or seized by a tiger or similar predator, so too does displeasure arise when a single person—who stands in the place of many cattle—rises above the state of being a mere beast.
What is surprising about this, other than the way a householder [is distressed] when his many cattle are stolen by the gods?
Therefore, that is not dear to these gods: what is it?

It is that humans might somehow know—that is, understand—the reality of Brahman as the Self. And thus is the recollection of the blessed Vyāsa in the *Anugītā*: "For by those who perform ritual acts, O son of Kuntī, the world of the gods..."
It is thus encompassed;
nor is it desired by the gods that mortals should exist above them.

Therefore, the gods desire to create obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman for people, as if [protecting] cattle from tigers and other predators, thinking, "Let them not rise up [from bondage], for they are to be enjoyed by us. However, those whom they wish to liberate, they will endow with faith and other virtues, while those who are the opposite, they will endow with lack of faith and the like.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should be intent on propitiating the gods, devoted to faith and devotion, humble, and vigilant; this is shown by the gods' seemingly paradoxical statement:
"Brahman indeed was this in the beginning, one alone. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.11)
Being one, it did not flourish.
It emitted from itself that superior form, the *kṣatra*—those which are the *kṣatras* among the gods: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna.
Therefore, there is nothing higher than the *kṣatra*.
Therefore, in the *rājasūya* sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya;
he thereby places that glory in the *kṣatra* alone.
This Brahman is the womb of the Kshatriya;
therefore, even when a king reaches the highest state, he finally resorts to the Brahman as his own womb.
But he who harms him goes to his own womb [in ruin].
He becomes evil, just as one who has harmed a superior.
The meaning of the scripture has been summarized in the aphorism: “One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone.

And for that [Self], which is intended to be explained, the connection and the purpose have been stated by means of an explanatory passage (arthavāda), beginning with: “Regarding this they say: ‘By the knowledge of Brahman...
Furthermore, the fact that ignorance is the cause for one’s involvement in saṃsāra has been declared by the passage beginning: “Now, he who worships another deity... and so forth.
In this regard, it has been stated that the ignorant person is a debtor and is dependent upon others due to the necessity of performing duties toward the gods and so forth, like a beast.
But what is the cause for the necessity of performing such duties toward the gods and so forth?
It is the social classes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*).
In this regard, what are the castes (*varṇa*)?
For this reason, the following is commenced:
that transmigrating being who, in relation to actions connected with their respective causes, is himself subject to dependence and is thus authorized [to perform them].
To demonstrate this very point, the creation of Indra and the others was not mentioned immediately after the creation of Agni;
rather, the creation of Agni was shown for the purpose of completing Prajāpati’s act of creation.
This creation of Indra and the others, however, is to be understood from that same context, as it is supplementary to it.

But here, that very same [Brahman] is designated as such in order to demonstrate the cause for the ignorant person's entitlement to ritual action: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman"—that is, Brahman which, having created Agni, assumed the form of Agni;
because of the conceit of belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste, it is called "Brahman.
Indeed (*vai*), this entire collection of castes, beginning with the Kṣatriya, was non-different from Brahman alone, being one only.
There was no distinction such as the Kṣatriya and so forth.

That Brahman alone—devoid of protectors such as the Kṣatriyas and others—did not become manifest (*sadam na vyabhavat*); that is to say, it did not expand, meaning it was not capable of performing its function.

Then that Brahman, desiring to perform action motivated by the caste of the Brāhmaṇa—thinking, "I am a Brāhmaṇa; thus must I act"—emitted, that is, created in an extraordinary manner, a form of excellence, a praiseworthy form, for the sake of manifesting the glory of the self as the agent of action. What, then, was that which was emitted?

*Kṣatra* refers to the Kṣatriya caste; he demonstrates it through its individual manifestations by saying: "those which are well-known in the world as *kṣatras* among the gods (*devatrā*). The plural number is used either because the rule for expressing a genus permits the plural, or because of the multiplicity of individuals, employing a figurative distinction.
What, then, are they?
To this he says: therein, those who have been consecrated are specifically designated—Indra is the king of the gods, Varuṇa of the aquatic creatures.
Soma is the lord of the Brahmins,
Rudra of cattle,
and Parjanya of lightning and the like.
Yama is the kṣatriya among the ancestors (pitṛs), Death is that of diseases and the like, and Īśāna is that of lights; such are the kṣatriyas among the gods.
Following that, it should be understood that [the lineages] beginning with Purūravas were indeed created as being presided over by the divine Kṣatriyas such as Indra and others;

for it was precisely for that purpose that the creation of the divine Kṣatriyas was introduced. Since the Kṣatra was created by Brahmā with preeminence, there is nothing superior to the Kṣatra, even as a controller over the Brāhmaṇa caste.
Therefore, even though he is the cause, the Brāhmaṇa, being situated below the Kṣatriya, attends upon him who stands above. Where? At the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Therein, he places—that is, establishes—the Brāhmaṇa as his own glory, consisting of fame, within the very Kṣatra.
When the king, consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice and seated upon the throne, addresses the officiating priest as "O Brahmin," the priest replies to him in turn: "O King, you are the Brahman.
This is what is meant by the statement: "He thus places that glory in the Kṣatriya alone.
Indeed, this very Brahman is the source of the Kṣatriya.

Therefore, if the king attains or reaches the supreme state characterized by the consecration of the Rājasūya sacrifice, he— being Brahman itself— finally, at the conclusion of the ritual, places himself in his own source; that is to say, he establishes the domestic priest (purohita) before him.

But he who, out of pride in his own strength, harms—that is, injures by looking down upon—his own source, the Brāhmaṇa caste, or a Brāhmaṇa; he reaches his own very womb, he cuts off and destroys his own progeny. Having done this, he becomes more sinful, even more wicked.

Even previously, a Kṣatriya was indeed sinful because of his cruelty; he becomes even more sinful by harming his own offspring through violence, just as in the world one becomes most sinful by harming and insulting someone who is superior and highly esteemed. //11//
Even after the Kṣatriya had been created,
he did not yet become complete.
He created the Viś;
those which are these classes born of the gods, designated by their groups: the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśve Devas, and the Maruts.
He did not become manifold; likewise, the Brahman did not become manifold for the sake of action,
because there was no one to acquire wealth.
He created the *viś* for the purpose of acquiring wealth as a means to accomplish ritual action.
But who is this *viś*?
It refers to those classes born of the gods; here the suffix *-niṣṭhā* is used in its own sense.
The meaning is: "these various classes of gods";
they are "declared," that is, spoken of, "in groups," meaning group by group.
For the common people (*viś*) consist mostly of groups (*gaṇa*); indeed, it is generally when united that they are capable of acquiring wealth, not individually.
The Vasus are a group numbering eight.
Likewise, there are eleven Rudras,
twelve Ādityas,
and thirteen Viśvedevas, who are the offspring of Viśvā.
Or all the gods, the Maruts in their seven groups of seven. //12//
He did not multiply. He created the Śūdra caste, Pūṣan.
This earth, indeed, is Pūṣan;
for she nourishes everything here that exists whatsoever.
He did not become manifold even through the state of being a servant;
he created the Śūdra caste— the Śūdra himself is "Śaudra," with the suffix *aṇ* used in its own sense (*svārthe*) resulting in the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*).
But who is this Śaudra caste that was created?
Regarding "Pūṣan"—he is called Pūṣan because he nourishes (puṣṇāti). But who is this Pūṣan? He specifies it particularly: "This earth is Pūṣan."
He himself provides the etymological explanation: "For this [Earth] nourishes all this, whatever there is. (13)
He did not become more than that;
he emitted from himself that form which is superior, namely Dharma.
This Dharma is the sovereign power of the ruling class (kṣatra);
therefore, there is nothing superior to Dharma.
Thus, even one who is weaker hopes to overcome the stronger by means of Dharma.
As it is with the king, so it is with Dharma; for that which is Dharma is indeed Truth. Therefore, they say of one who speaks the truth, "He speaks Dharma."
Or, when one speaks of Dharma, one speaks of Truth;
for these two are indeed the same thing.
Even after creating the four castes, he did not find rest, because of the fierceness of the *kṣatra* and the resulting fear that it might become unrestrained.
He created that which is a form superior to that; what was it?
Dharma— this very form of the supreme good was created as the sovereign power (kṣatra) of the sovereign power, the controller even of the sovereign power,
more fierce than the fierce, which is Dharma, that which is Dharma.
Therefore, because even the kṣatriya is subject to the governance of dharma, there is nothing higher than dharma;
for by it all are restrained.

How so? It is said: moreover, even one who is weaker, or one who is much weaker, desires—that is, wishes to conquer—by means of the power of dharma even a stronger person, one who is more powerful than himself.

Just as in the world a householder is [subordinate] even to a king who possesses the greatest power, so it is here; therefore, it is established that because Dharma possesses the greatest power of all, it is the controller of everything.
That which is indeed this dharma characterized by worldly convention, being transacted by people in the world—that is truth;
"truth" means accordance with the meaning of the scriptures; that very same thing, when being practiced, becomes what is called dharma.
However, when it is known as the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*), it becomes true.

Because this is so, those standing nearby at the time of legal procedure—who know how to distinguish between the two—say of one who speaks according to the treatise: "He speaks the Dharma," meaning he speaks the well-known worldly principle (*nyāya*).
Likewise, conversely, they say of one who speaks of either the Dharma or worldly convention: "He speaks the truth," or "He speaks that which is not inconsistent with the scriptures.
Thus, that which was stated—both when being known and when being practiced—becomes Dharma itself.
Therefore, that Dharma, characterized by the practice of knowledge, governs all others, including the knowledge of the scriptures.
Consequently, it is the sovereign power even over the ruling class (*kṣatra*).

Thus, the ignorant person, possessing pride in that [Dharma], conceives of distinctions based on the grounds of Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra in order to perform their respective specific duties.
And these, by their very nature, are the causes for eligibility for ritual action. //14//
This very thing is the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among the gods, it became the Brahman through Agni alone; among humans, it became the Brāhmaṇa.
A Kṣatriya by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya by a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra by a Śūdra.
Therefore, among the gods, they desire a world in Agni alone; and among men, in the Brāhmaṇa.
For through these two forms did Brahman come into being.

Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world, it does not benefit him, being unknown to him—just as a Veda that has not been studied, or any other rite that has not been performed.
If indeed even one who does not know this performs a great meritorious deed, it will certainly perish in the end for him.
One should worship the Self alone as the world.
He who worships the Self alone as the world—his work is never exhausted.
For from this very Self, whatever one desires, that one creates.

This fourfold order was created—the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. This summary is for the sake of what follows: that which is the creating Brahman is, among the gods, Brahman itself in the form of Agni and not in any other form.
The Brahmin caste came into being;
among humans, Brahmā became the Brahmins in their own essential form, while among the other castes, he attained various modifications.
By means of a Kṣatriya, he became a Kṣatriya, presided over by deities such as Indra;
by means of a Vaiśya, a Vaiśya; and by means of a Śūdra, a Śūdra.

Since Brahman, as the creator, has undergone modification in the form of the Kṣatriyas and others, while remaining unmodified in the form of Agni and Brāhmaṇas, therefore, among the gods, specifically in Agni, one finds the world— the fruit of action.
The meaning is that they desire [the fruit] by performing action connected with fire;
for it is for that very purpose that Brahman exists in the form of fire as the locus of ritual action.
Therefore, it is logical that having performed action in that fire, they pray for its fruit.

Regarding Brahman among humans—among men, when there is a desire for the fruits of action, there is no dependence on rituals such as fire-offerings and the like; rather, the fulfillment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) occurs simply by the attainment of one's own nature as a member of that particular caste. However, in cases where the fulfillment of the human goal is dependent upon the gods, [the situation is different].
In that very context, there is a dependence on actions connected with fire and so forth.
And from the Smṛti: "A Brāhmaṇa may indeed attain perfection through chanting alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, he is called a Brāhmaṇa who is a friend to all."
Thus [it is stated in] Manu 2.87.
Furthermore, because the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is observed,
it follows that among humans, it is only those who possess the nature of Brahman who desire the world as the fruit of their actions.
For it is because through these two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Fire, which take the forms of the agent and the locus of action—that the Brahman who is the Creator became manifest in its true nature.
Regarding this, some maintain that they desire the world of the Supreme Self (paramātman) within the Fire and the Brāhmaṇa;
however, that is incorrect, because the division of castes was introduced here for the purpose of establishing the domain of ritual action (*karma*) within the context of ignorance (*avidyā*).
And because of the qualification by "another";
for if the word "world" (loka) here referred to the supreme Self alone, then the qualification by "another"— namely, "not having seen his own world"— would be purposeless.
If the "world" under discussion— which is sought after because it is dependent on fire— is distinct from one's own world,
then the qualification "one's own" (svam) is appropriate.
This is because [the passage] aims at the attainment of the world of the Supreme Self (paramātmaloka),
which is not subject to deviation from one's own nature (svatva); whereas that which is produced by ignorance (avidyā) deviates from one's own nature.
And it declares the deviation of those who perform actions, saying, "It surely perishes.
The castes were created by Brahmā for the sake of action;
and that action, known as dharma, governs all as something to be performed and is the means for achieving the goals of human life.
Therefore, if one's own world—known as the Supreme Self—is attained by that very action even though it was previously unknown, why is it made the object of a path?

To this he says: "Now" (*atha*), which serves to set aside the preceding objection; "whoever," indeed, from this adventitious world—which is not one's true nature and is caused by worldly desires and actions, or by the conceit of performing rituals dependent on the sacrificial fire, or by the conceit of performing rituals belonging merely to the Brāhmaṇa caste—[departs].
One's own world, called the Self, is so designated because it is never absent from the nature of the Self;
not having seen [it] as "I am Brahman," one departs— that is, one dies.

Although that [Self] is one's own world, because it is unknown—being veiled by ignorance—it remains as if not one's own; thus, like a common person who completes a numerical count, it does not benefit or protect this [individual], by removing defects such as sorrow, delusion, and fear.
And just as in the world, the Veda, if not recited or studied, does not benefit [one] by making known rituals and other matters, [so too is this Self].
Just as any other worldly activity, such as agriculture, if not performed and thus not manifested by oneself, does not benefit one by bestowing its own fruit;
so too, one's own world—the Self—is not experienced at all unless it is manifested by its own eternal nature through the abandonment of ignorance and the like.
[Objection: But what is the use of protecting for the sake of perceiving one's own world?
Because the attainment of the fruit of karma is certain, and because the karma that serves as the cause for desired fruits is abundant,
the protection resulting from that [karma] will be inexhaustible.
That is not so, because what has been done is subject to decay;
this is what he says: "If here in this saṃsāra, even some great soul who is not a knower of this—being ignorant of his own world according to the method described—"
One who performs great meritorious acts such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and the like, which yield desired fruits, continuously thinking, "By this alone shall my infinity be attained"—

that action of his, belonging to one possessed of ignorance, perishes in the end because it is caused by desire born of ignorance, just like the display of power arising from the delusion of a dream-vision. At the very conclusion, when the enjoyment of its fruit has ended, it is surely exhausted.
Because its two causes— ignorance and desire— are unstable,
the occurrence of destruction and impermanence is established;
therefore, there is indeed no hope for the infinity of the maintenance of the fruits of meritorious actions.

Therefore, one should meditate upon the Self alone as one’s own world— in the sense of "the Self" and "one’s own world," because "one’s own world" is the subject under discussion and the word "own" (sva) is not used here [again]. One should meditate upon it.
As for him who meditates upon the Self alone as his world—what happens to him? It is said: "His work is not exhausted";
this is because of the very absence of work.
Thus, this is a constant restatement (nityānuvāda).
The meaning is that the suffering of saṃsāra, characterized by the exhaustion of karma, is continuous for one who lacks knowledge, but such [suffering] does not exist for him.

"Just as [it is said], 'When Mithilā is burning, nothing of mine burns,' others explain that for the knower who meditates upon his own self as the world (*loka*), karma itself does not perish due to its connection with knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, they indeed conceive of the meaning of the word *loka*—which is inherent in karma—in two ways: one is the world called Hiraṇyagarbha, which is the manifest state and the substratum of karma."
For one who meditates upon that world as being composed of action, defined and limited— it is said that for him who meditates upon it as limited,
for him who perceives the self as consisting of limited action, his karma is exhausted.
For one who meditates upon that very world, which is inherent in action, having brought it to the state of a cause in its undifferentiated condition—
he, because he perceives the Self as consisting of unlimited action, his action is not exhausted. For one who meditates upon that—
because he perceives the Self as consisting of unlimited action— his action does not perish.
This is a beautiful conceptual interpretation, but it is not based on the sacred scripture (*śrauta*).
This is because the Supreme Self under discussion is denoted by the word "one's own world" (*svaloka*);

having introduced the topic with "one's own world," the text then discards the word "own" (*sva*) and substitutes the word "self" (*ātman*), referring back to that very same entity in the statement: "One should meditate upon the self alone as the world."
In this context, there is no occasion at all for the conceptualization of a world as being inherent in karma;

for [the Self] is qualified by the opponent [the Upanishadic teacher] solely as the object of knowledge, as in: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Indeed, he distinguishes it from the worlds produced by sons, ritual acts, and lower knowledge by saying, "This Self is our world."
And [there is the scriptural passage]: "His world is not measured by any action; this is his supreme world.

It is appropriate that these [passages] form a single syntactical unit with those [preceding statements] containing qualifications, because here too the qualification "his own world" (svaṃ lokam) is observed.

If it is argued that the statement "from this [Self] he desires" is improper— given that it is established here that "one's own world" is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and that through meditation upon it one becomes that very Self,
such that whatever one desires is created from this Self— then the mention of a fruit other than the attainment of that Self would be improper.

The meaning is that because he is devoted to the worship and praise of his own world, everything desired is accomplished from that very world; nothing else need be prayed for beyond this, since his desires are already fulfilled, as stated in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23.1: "From the Self comes life-breath; from the Self comes hope."
1) As in other Vedic passages such as these;
or, as before, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the state of being the Self of all.
For if the Supreme Self alone is attained, then the use of the word "Self" in the phrase "from this very Self" is appropriate.
The meaning is "from this very world of the Self under discussion.

Otherwise, he would have stated it with the qualification "from the world of karma in its unmanifest state," in order to exclude both the previously mentioned world of the Supreme Self and the manifest state.
For when the subject here is qualified [in such a way], it is not possible to understand an intermediate state that has not been heard. //15//
Now, this indeed is the Self.

It has been stated that one who is ignorant in this regard—possessing the conceit of caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth—is constrained by *dharma* and, being subject to the performance of rituals for the gods and others, is dependent like a beast.
But what are those rituals, by the necessity of performing which he becomes dependent like a beast?
"Who indeed are those gods and others whom he serves like a beast through their rituals?"—
he elaborates on both of these points:
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.16.
Moreover, this very self is the world of all beings.
In that he offers oblations and performs sacrifices, by that it is the world of the gods;
and in that he recites the prayers, by that it is the world of the seers.
Now, in that he offers to the ancestors, and in that he desires offspring, by that [he serves] the ancestors;
then, in that he provides lodging for men and gives them food, by that [he serves] men;
then, in that he finds grass and water for the animals, by that [he serves] the animals.
Inasmuch as predatory beasts, birds, and even ants subsist upon what is in his house, by that he gains a world for them.
Just as one would surely desire safety for one's own world,
even so do all beings always desire safety for one who knows this.
This, indeed, has been known and investigated.
Now, the word "atha" (then/also) is for the purpose of introducing the statement.
This person under discussion—the householder who is entitled to ritual action, the ignorant one characterized by the aggregate of body, senses, and so forth—is called the "body-self" (*piṇḍātman*);
for he is benefited by all the rites prescribed for the castes, stages of life, and so on.
By which specific actions does he benefit, and for which specific beings is the world [prepared]? It is said: that householder offers oblations (*juhoti*) and performs sacrifices (*yajate*).
A sacrifice (*yāga*) is the renunciation of one's own ownership (*svatva-parityāga*) directed toward a deity.

That very renunciation is itself the oblation (*homa*) exceeding [ordinary] pouring; by that rite characterized as *homa* and sacrifice, which must necessarily be performed, the world of the gods is attained, being dependent upon them like cattle.
Now, as for what he recites—that is, studies his own Vedic lesson (*svādhyāya*) day after day—by that, the world of the seers (*ṛṣi*) is attained.

Now, as for that which he offers and bestows upon the ancestors— such as funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), water, and so forth— and that which he desires offspring, making an effort for the sake of progeny (the word "desire" being intended to indicate actual birth)—
meaning that he procreates offspring— by virtue of those actions, which are obligatory and serve as objects of enjoyment for the ancestors, the world is dependent.
Now, as for the fact that he causes humans to dwell in his house,
and that he gives food to them— whether they are staying or not staying— as seekers,
by that [act] he [shares in] the world of humans.
Now, in that he finds and provides grass and water for animals,
by that he benefits the animals;
and in that the beasts of prey, birds, and ants in his houses subsist upon the fragments of food, the sacrificial offerings, and the rinsing-water of the vessels.
Therefore, this is their world. Because he, by performing these actions, benefits the gods and others, therefore—

just as in the world one who has fallen asleep would desire for his own body (*loka*) well-being (*ariṣṭam*), that is, non-destruction and the non-falling away from his own state of being, out of fear of falling away from that state of being, [he provides] nourishment, protection, and so forth— [so it is here].

In this very way, for one who knows thus—who has conceived of himself as "I am to be enjoyed by all beings" and "in this manner I must necessarily repay [my debt] like a debtor"—all beings, beginning with the gods as previously mentioned, desire his non-harm (ariṣṭi), that is, his non-destruction; they protect him from all sides so that his status as their own may not be lost, just as householders protect their cattle. Thus it was said: "Therefore, that is not dear to them."

This very thing—namely, that the aforementioned rites must necessarily be performed like a debt—is known as such in the section on the Five Great Sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and it has been examined and deliberated upon as a duty in the section on the "Cutting-off" (*avadāna*).
If one knows Brahman, one is liberated from that state of being a sacrificial animal, which consists of the bondage of duty;
for by whom has this person been impelled to proceed as if powerless within the jurisdiction of the bondage of karma?
Furthermore, it is not the case that one has no qualification for knowledge regarding the means to liberation; for was it not said that "the gods protect"?

Certainly, they too protect only those who have ascended to their own domain through the qualification of karma, otherwise there would follow the fallacy of the acquisition of what was not done and the loss of what was done.
But it is not the mere person who has not ascended to the specific qualification;
therefore, there must exist that [impulse] by which one, being impelled, becomes involuntarily turned away from one's own world.
Is it not ignorance that [causes this]?
For one who possesses ignorance proceeds by turning outward; yet even that [ignorance] is not itself the motivator.
For that [ignorance] consists in the non-perception of the true nature of things;
yet it acquires the status of a seed that impels [action], just as blindness is the cause for the inclination to fall into pits and the like.
If this is so, then let it be stated: what is that which is the cause of such inclination?
To this, it is replied: desire (*kāma*) is that which is seeking (*eṣaṇā*).
As the *Kaṭhaka-śruti* states: "The ignorant, abiding in innate ignorance, pursue outward desires," and as the *Smṛti* (the *Bhagavad-gītā*, 3.37) says: "This is desire; this is anger."

37) And so forth; furthermore, in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], it is stated that "all activity has desire as its sole cause. This very point will be demonstrated here in detail, up until the conclusion of this chapter—*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.17.
In the beginning, this world was the Self alone, just one.
He desired: "May I have a wife; then may I be procreated.
May I have wealth; then may I perform ritual action."
This much indeed is desire; even if one were to seek, one would not find more than this.
Therefore, even now, a man living alone desires: "May I have a wife, and may I procreate; may I have wealth, and may I perform ritual acts."
As long as he does not obtain even one of these individually, he considers himself incomplete; such is his incompleteness. For him, the mind alone is the self.
Speech is the wife;
breath is the offspring;
the eye is human wealth.
For one finds that through the eye;
the divine is the ear,
for one hears that through the ear.
The self alone is his action;
for it is by means of the self that one performs action.
This very sacrifice consists of five parts.
The sacrificial animal is fivefold; man is fivefold;
all this that exists here is fivefold.
He who knows this obtains all this. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17.
"In the beginning, this was the Self alone.

In the beginning— that is, prior to the union with a wife— the Self alone existed, characterized as an ignorant seeker of knowledge (*varṇin*) consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects which is one's own nature.
It is designated as the "Self" (ātman);
therefore, there was nothing separate from that Self which could be desired, such as the distinctions of wife and so forth.
He alone existed—He alone, possessed of knowledge, existed as the sole seed of the desire for wife and the rest.

Perfumed by the latent impression of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), which consists in the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) upon his own self of the nature of agents such as the doer, as well as actions and their fruits—an [ignorance] that is innate—he desired (*akāmayata*, i.e., he willed).
How? "May there be a wife for me, the agent, who is the cause for my eligibility for ritual action (*karma-adhikāra*); without her, I am indeed ineligible for ritual action."
Therefore, for the sake of attaining qualification for ritual action (*karma*), there must be a wife;
then I may procreate, that is, I myself may arise in the form of offspring;

then I may possess wealth, characterized by cattle and so forth, which is the means for performing ritual action; then I may perform the ritual action that is the means for achieving both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
I shall perform that action by which, having become free from debt to the gods and others, I may attain their worlds,
as well as those actions intended for specific desires which serve as the means for obtaining sons, wealth, heaven, and so forth.
"Of such extent indeed is desire" means that it is limited by such objects.

For this alone is the object to be desired: namely, wife, son, and wealth—which constitute the "quest for means"—and the three worlds, namely the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods, which are the "quests for results" as the fruits [of those means].
Therefore, that which is the desire for the worlds (*loka-eṣaṇā*) is itself the single desire;
it is the same single desire for truth (*satya-eṣaṇā*), which is twofold in its dependence upon means.
Hence, he will determine later: “For both these are indeed desires” (BU 3.5.1).

Since every undertaking has its purpose in a result, the attainment of worldly desires is already implied; thus, desire is defined as being only this much, only this much. When food is mentioned, satiety is certainly not something that needs to be mentioned separately.
Since eating has that [desire] as its purpose, these two forms of seeking—characterized as the end to be achieved (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*)—constitute desire (*kāma*).
Impelled by this, the ignorant man, quite helplessly like a silkworm, envelops himself; directing himself solely toward the path of action, he turns outward and fails to recognize his own true world.

And likewise in the Taittirīyaka: “One who is deluded by fire, exhausted by smoke, does not recognize his own world. But how is it determined that desires are limited to this extent? Because they are infinite.
Desiring to address the doubt that "desires are indeed infinite," he states the reason: because whether one desires or even does not desire, one would not find—
that is, would not obtain— any further qualification beyond this which is characterized by the means to the fruit.
For in this world, there is nothing to be obtained— whether seen or unseen— that is distinct from the means of attaining results.
Since desire has as its object that which is to be obtained, and since such an object does not exist apart from these [means], it is appropriate to say, "Desire is indeed of this extent."
This is what is meant: desire is this twofold seeking, characterized by means and ends, whether for visible or invisible objects, which pertains to the domain of persons possessed of ignorance;
therefore, the wise man must rise above this.
For it was because he was thus ignorant that the Self previously desired desires.
Likewise, it was so for those even earlier; such is the established order of the world, and thus was this creation of Prajāpati.
He was afraid because of ignorance.
Then, impelled by desire, sporting alone, he desired a woman for procreation; he united with her, and from that this creation came to be—so it has been said.
Therefore, in that creation, even now at this present time, being alone prior to the taking of a wife, he desires: "May I have a wife."
"Then I shall have offspring; then I shall have wealth;
then I shall perform ritual action"—this sentence has already had its meaning explained.
While desiring in this way and striving to accomplish these ends, he does not obtain even one of these aforementioned things, beginning with a wife.
To that extent, he considers himself incomplete and imperfect, thinking "I am not whole.
By the principle of elimination, when he accomplishes all of these [requirements],
then his state is one of completeness.

But when one is unable to achieve completeness, then, for the sake of achieving that completeness for this person who imagines incompleteness, he says: "This very completeness comes about for him in this way. How so?
This aggregate of effects and instruments is divided;
therein, everything else known as effects and instruments follows the lead of the mind (*manas*). Thus, because of the predominance of the mind, the mind itself is the self (*ātman*).
Just as the master of a household is the self of his wife and so forth because he conforms to them— since the fourfold group beginning with the wife follows him—
so too here, the mind is conceived as the self for the sake of completeness.
Likewise, speech is the wife.
Speech is so called because it follows the mind;
"speech" refers to sound characterized by injunctions and the like,
which is grasped, determined, and emitted by the mind through the medium of the ear.
Thus speech is like a wife born of the mind;
and from those two, speech and mind, which stand in the relation of wife and husband, breath is produced for the sake of action;
thus breath is like offspring.
In this context, action characterized by vital breath, movement, and so forth is human wealth, which is the eye.
That wealth is of two kinds: human and other than that;
therefore, he specifies "human" in order to exclude the other kind of wealth.
For cattle and so forth are wealth belonging to humans, perceptible by the eye, and a means for performing ritual action;
therefore, they occupy that [place],
and because of their connection with it, wealth is perceptible by the eye.
For by means of the eye, one finds that human wealth—that is, one perceives cattle and so forth.
What, then, is the other kind of wealth?
It is the divine ear, because its consciousness has the gods as its object.
