Consciousness is divine wealth;
in this context, it is the sense of hearing alone that serves as the object of attainment.
Why? Because by means of the sense of hearing, one hears that divine wealth which is consciousness.
Therefore, that [perception] is indeed the ear.
But what is the action to be accomplished here by these [senses], beginning with the self and ending with consciousness?
It is said: "The self alone"—here, "self" refers to the body.
But how is it that the self stands in the place of karma?
Because it is the cause of karma.
How is it the cause of karma?

Since one performs action with the self through the body, for that very person who previously possessed the conceit of incompleteness, completeness is now attained—just as it exists externally in the form of wife and so forth.
Therefore, this sacrifice is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), accomplished by means of the five; it is a fivefold sacrifice realized merely through perception, even for one who does not perform ritual acts.
But how, then, does this [internal sacrifice] possess the nature of a sacrifice merely through its fivefold perfection?

It is said: because even an external sacrifice is accomplished by means of animals and persons, and those animals and persons are themselves fivefold, due to their connection with the fivefold set beginning with the mind (*manas*), as previously stated.
Thus it is said: cattle, goats, and so forth are fivefold;
man is fivefold. Although he is included among cattle, the separate mention of "man" is because of his distinction as one who is qualified [for ritual action].
What more need be said? All this—the means of action and the fruit—is fivefold.
That is to say, whatever exists—all this is [the fivefold sacrifice]. He who, knowing this, realizes the self as the fivefold sacrifice, attains all this world as his very self. //17//
Thus ends the fourth section, "The Brahmana on Being the Self of All, Beginning with Creation," in the first chapter.
Regarding those seven kinds of food [described] through wisdom,
ignorance has been introduced therein;
in that state, the ignorant person worships another deity, thinking, "He is one, and I am another."

It has been stated that he— who possesses identification with the social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), who is constrained by the duty to perform actions, and who, impelled by desire, performs rites such as the *homa* sacrifice while benefiting the gods and so forth— is the "world" for all beings.
Just as this world was created by each individual through their own respective actions as an object of enjoyment for all beings,
so too did he create all beings and the entire universe as objects of his own enjoyment through the fivefold rites beginning with the *homa*.
Thus, each individual is, according to the nature of his own karma and knowledge, both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment for the entire world;
the meaning is that every person is the agent and the product of everything.
And we shall explain this very point in the section on knowledge, within the Madhu-vidyā, for the sake of realizing the unity of the Self: "Everything is the honey—the effect—of everything."
When he created the world as food for himself through the fivefold optional rite beginning with "He offered," and by means of consciousness,
that entire world, being divided sevenfold according to the relationship of cause and effect, is called the "seven foods" because it is to be eaten.
Therefore, he is the father of those foods;
these mantras are like sūtras for those foods along with their applications, because they reveal them in brief.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.1)
When the Father, through wisdom and austerity, produced the seven kinds of food, he made one common to all; he assigned two to the gods;
he set three aside for himself; and he gave one to the animals.
In that everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.
Why is it that these do not perish, even though they are being consumed all the time? He who knows that imperishability eats food with his very face.
"He goes even unto the gods; he lives upon vigor.
Thus are the verses. BrhUp 1.5.1.
Regarding the phrase "the seven kinds of food," the expression "that which he generated" is an adverbial modifier;
[he did so] by means of *medhā* (insight), *prajñā* (wisdom), *vijñāna* (discernment), and *tapas* (ritual action).
For it is knowledge and action alone that are denoted by the words "wisdom" (medhā) and "austerity" (tapas),
because those two are the subject under discussion;
not other forms of wisdom or austerity.
Because it is not the subject under discussion;
for the fivefold ritual action has wives and so forth as its means,
whereas knowledge is the very thing introduced immediately before in the words, "He who knows thus."
Therefore, one should not entertain the suspicion that intelligence and austerity are meant here;
rather, the remainder of the sentence is: "We shall now explain those seven kinds of food which the Father produced through knowledge and action. //1//
In this regard, because the meaning of the mantras is generally hidden, it is difficult to understand; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa proceeds to explain their meaning:
"That the Father produced seven kinds of food by means of wisdom and austerity... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.2).
"By means of wisdom and austerity, the Father produced that one common [portion] for him," it is said.
This very food which is eaten here is his common portion.
He who venerates this does not turn away from evil.
For this is mixed:
"He assigned two [portions] to the gods," namely the *huta* and the *prahuta*.
Therefore, they offer oblations to the gods and continue to offer them; moreover, they say, "These are the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Therefore, one should not be a frequent performer of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices.
"He gave one to the domestic animals"—
that is milk;
for indeed, both humans and animals subsist on milk first of all.
Therefore, when a boy is born, they first have him lick clarified butter or give him the breast to suck.
But regarding a newborn calf, they say, "From grass!
For upon that [earth] everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.
"In milk indeed all this is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.
Regarding this, they say: 'One who offers oblations of milk for a year overcomes repeated death.
One should not understand it in that way."
On whatever day one who knows this offers the oblation, on that very day he conquers rebirth.
For he bestows all food upon the gods. Why is it that these [foods] are not exhausted, even though they are being consumed at all times?
The person, indeed, is the imperishable; for he produces this food again and again. "He who knows that imperishable," it is said.
The person (*puruṣa*) is indeed imperishable (*akṣiti*).
For he produces this food through every act of thought by means of his ritual actions;
for if he were not to do this, it would surely perish.
"He eats food with his face"—the "face" (pratīka) means the mouth; thus, it means "with his mouth.
"He goes unto the gods, he lives upon strength"—this is a eulogy. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.2)
Regarding that, what is the meaning of the passage, "The Father, by means of wisdom and austerity, produced seven kinds of food"?
He explains it by means of the word *iti*, which serves to illuminate a well-known meaning;
for the meaning of this mantra is indeed well known—this is the sense.
Furthermore, by means of the mantra "yad ajanayat" (that which he generated), which functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*), the fact that the meaning is already well-known is revealed.
Therefore, without even suspecting [any contradiction], the Brāhmaṇa says: "The Father generated [him] through wisdom and austerity.
But how is this meaning already established?

It is said: first of all, the fatherhood of those things beginning with a wife and ending with ritual action—which are the means for attaining the fruits of the worlds—is indeed directly perceived, and it has been stated [in the Veda] by such passages as, "May I have a wife.
And therein, divine wealth, knowledge, ritual action, and a son are mentioned as the creatorship and the means for achieving the worlds that constitute the fruits.
And that which is about to be stated is indeed well-known;

therefore, it is appropriate to say "by means of wisdom" (*medhayā*) and so forth. For the act of seeking (*eṣaṇā*) has as its object the fruit [of action], and this is indeed well-established in the world.
And it has been stated that "desire consists of wife and so forth" by the passage, "This much indeed is desire.
Furthermore, in the sphere of the knowledge of Brahman, because of the oneness of all things, desire is impossible.
By this, it is already explained that the creation of the world proceeds from natural wisdom and austerity that are not based on scriptural injunctions.
Because all [existence] ending with the immobile [plants], which has undesirable fruits, is caused by karma and ignorance (*karmavijñāna*);

however, what is intended here is precisely the relationship of means and end as taught in the scriptures, because the desire for detachment from that [saṃsāra] is intended through the wish to impart the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

For this entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), characterized by the manifest and the unmanifest, is impure, non-eternal, consisting of means and ends, painful, and the domain of ignorance; therefore, the knowledge of Brahman must be undertaken by one who is detached from this.

In that regard, the application of foods through their classification is stated by the mantra phrase "one [portion] of this is common"; its explanation is given by the statement, "this indeed is its common food. Of what is this the food? Of this entire collection of eaters. What is that?
Since this is eaten and enjoyed by all living beings day after day, the Father, having created food, ordained it as common for the sake of all consumers.
He who meditates upon this food—which is common to all, which sustains all living beings, and which is being consumed—becomes devoted to that; such is the meaning.

For in common worldly usage, "worship" (*upāsana*) is observed to mean "devoted application," as in such expressions as "he worships his teacher" (*agurum upāste*) or "he worships the king" (*rājānam upāste*). Therefore, one who is thus occupied—whose primary concern is the maintenance of the body rather than enjoyment, and whose primary concern is not action for the sake of unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—does not turn away from evil, that is, from both kinds of demerit (*adharma*); he is not liberated. And so says the Vedic mantra: "In vain does he obtain food," and so forth.

Smṛti also says: "One should not cook food for oneself alone," "He who eats without giving to these [others] is indeed a thief," and "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of the food," and so forth.
Why, then, does one not turn away from sin?
For this [food] is mixed; indeed, that which is consumed by living beings is their common property, undivided among them.
Indeed, even a morsel of food that is thrown into the mouth of one who eats everything is seen to cause pain to another,
for everyone has a fixed expectation therein, thinking, "May this be mine.
Therefore, it is not possible to swallow even while causing pain to another.

Furthermore, because of such traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) as, "For [the sin of] evil deeds belongs to men," some maintain that the food called *vaiśvadeva* is prepared by the householder day after day; however,
that is not so.

The fact that the food known as *vaiśvadeva* is common to all eaters is not directly perceived in the same way that food being eaten by all living beings is; nor is the scriptural statement, "that which is eaten here," favorable evidence for that [direct perception].
Furthermore, because the food called *vaiśvadeva* is included within the food consumed by all living beings, it is logical that the food of dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and the like is also taken into account.
Since dogs, Cāṇḍālas, and other scavengers are seen even apart from the Vaiśvadeva offering,
the statement "that which is eaten here" is appropriate in that context.
For if that were not perceived,
it would follow— by virtue of the common term— that the father both created it and assigned its specific purpose;
yet it is accepted that he is the creator and the assigner of the purpose for the entire class of food.
Furthermore, it is not logical that there should be no cessation of evil for one performing the rite called Vaiśvadeva as prescribed by the scriptures;
nor is there any prohibition against it;
nor is this act inherently loathsome like the work of a fisherman or similar occupations.
Because it is to be accomplished by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), because of the scriptural declaration of transgression (*pratyavāya*) upon its non-performance,
and because transgression is logically entailed in the other case: "I eat the food that eats [me]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10).
6) From the wording of the mantra:
"He assigned two to the gods" is the mantra phrase, meaning that having created two kinds of food, he assigned them to the gods.
Which are those two? It is said: the *huta* and the *prahuta*. *Huta* is the offering into the fire; *prahuta* is the presentation of the *bali* oblation after having made the *huta* offering.
Because the Father assigned these two kinds of food— the *huta* and the *prahuta*— to the gods,
therefore even now householders offer oblations at the proper times; they offer while thinking, "This food is being given by us to the gods."
The meaning is that they offer oblations and perform the *baliharaṇa* (food-offering).
Now, others say that the two foods provided by the father for the gods are not the *huta* and *prahuta*,
but rather the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
The first position is that [the two refer to] *huta* and *prahuta*, because there is no distinction in their being heard as a duality and because they are extremely well-known.

Although duality is possible for *huta* and *prahuta*, nevertheless, it is more widely established that the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, which are mentioned in the Veda (*śrauta*), constitute the food of the gods.
Because it is illuminated by the mantra;
and when both a subordinate and a primary element are attained, comprehension occurs first regarding the primary one,
and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices possess primacy in comparison with the *huta* and *prahuta* offerings.
Therefore, it is logical that only those two are mentioned in the passage, "He assigned two [portions] to the gods.

Since these two foods called the New and Full Moon sacrifices were prepared for them by their father, therefore, so as not to obstruct their status as being intended for the gods, one who is *iṣṭiyājuka*— one whose habit is the performance of *iṣṭi* sacrifices— [should not perform the *iṣṭi*].
By the word *iṣṭi*, it is said that optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*) are meant; this is the well-known usage in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.
The meaning is that, because of the employment of the suffix denoting habit (*tācchīlya-pratyaya*), [the term] would not apply to one whose primary concern is the performance of optional sacrifices.
"He gave one [part] to the animals"—as for that which was given to the animals, is that food? It is milk.
But how is it understood that animals are the owners of this food? To this he says: "For first, at the beginning, both humans and animals subsist on milk alone."
For it is fitting that "that food is austerity"; otherwise, how could they subsist upon that very thing as a rule at the beginning?
How is it that they subsist upon that very thing at the beginning? It is said: because even today humans and animals subsist by means of that very food.

Just as the father first made the application [of the name], so too, when a boy or child is born, members of the three twice-born classes cause him to lick clarified butter mixed with gold during the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), and afterwards they feed him. For others besides humans— namely, for other animals— they cause the breast to be suckled first, according to their respective circumstances.
Then, when they ask of a newborn calf, "What is the calf's size?
being thus questioned, they say, "He is a grass-eater";
yet even now he does not eat grass.
The meaning is that he is exceedingly young, as he still subsists on milk alone;
and as for the fact that they later consume clarified butter during the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other ceremonies—
And since the others are indeed milk, they subsist on milk in every respect;
and since even clarified butter is a modification of milk, it too is nothing but milk. Why, then, is the seventh [food], being cattle, explained as the fourth?
Because it is a means for performing ritual action (*karman*).
For ritual action, such as the *agnihotra*, has milk and other such things as its means and substratum;
and that ritual action, which is the means, is accomplished by wealth (*vitta*) for the sake of the three kinds of food (*anna*) to be accomplished, which will be described hereafter.

Just as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices were previously mentioned among the [means of] food, therefore, because they belong to the category of ritual action (*karma*), they are taught here in combination with that [other] action. Furthermore, since there is no distinction in their status as means (*sādhana*) and since they are connected in purpose, the immediate sequence [of the text] is not the cause [for their grouping]; moreover, this is for the sake of ease of comprehension in the absence of such an explanation.
For when food items are explained in succession, they are easily understood once they have been explained.
What is the meaning of the statement, "In that everything is established, both what breathes and what does not"?

It is said: in that food, which is the drink of immortality (*amṛta*), the entire world—characterized by the internal (*adhyātma*), the elemental (*adhibhūta*), and the divine (*adhidaiva*)—is established; that is, whatever breathes, moving through the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and whatever does not move, remaining stationary.
Śailādi;
for there, it is explained by the word itself, which indicates what is well-known,
because it is established as being the cause.
And the state of being the cause consists in being inherent in rituals such as the *agnihotra*;

furthermore, hundreds of scriptural and traditional declarations (*śruti-smṛti-vādāḥ*) are established to the effect that the entire universe is of the nature of the transformation of the oblations of the *agnihotra* and other rites.
Therefore, an explanation by means of words is indeed entirely appropriate.
Regarding that which they say in other Brāhmaṇas— "One who offers oblations of milk for a year overcomes repeated death"—

it is said that in a year there are three hundred and sixty oblations, along with seven hundred and twenty [additional ones], which, becoming *yājuṣmatī* bricks, correspond to the days and nights of the year;
thus, they attain the year, Agni Prajāpati.
Having performed it in this manner, one who offers oblations for a year overcomes death again;
the meaning is that, having departed from here and been reborn among the gods, he does not die again. Thus say the declarations of the Brāhmaṇas.
It should not be understood in that way, nor should it be viewed in that way;
for on the very day one offers the oblation, on that very day one conquers recurrent death,
without depending upon a year-long repetition.
Being thus wise, he realizes—
just as it was stated that "all this is established in milk" because everything consists of the transformation of the milk-oblation—
that the nature of the world is attained through a single oblation alone.

This is explained as follows: "He overcomes death again"—that is, having died once and being released from the body by means of the *āviddha* [pierced] state, he becomes the universal self (*sarvātmā*) and does not take up a limited body for the sake of dying again; this is the meaning.
But what is the cause by which one overcomes death through the attainment of the universal self?

Thus it is said: because he offers all—that is, everything—food and what is to be eaten to all the gods by means of casting the morning and evening oblations; therefore, it is appropriate that having made himself consisting of all oblations, having attained a state of oneness with all the gods by becoming the food of all the gods, and having become composed of all the gods, he does not die again. Furthermore, this has been stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "Brahman, indeed, the Self-existent, performed austerity. He then reflected: 'Verily, there is no infinity in austerity.'"

"Come, let me offer myself as a sacrifice in all beings and all beings in myself. Having thus offered himself in all beings and all beings in himself, he attained preeminence among all beings, sovereignty, and lordship.
Why, then, are they not exhausted, even though they are being consumed at all times?

When the Father, having created the foods, assigned them to seven distinct eaters— since their continued existence is dependent upon that [assignment] and occurs perpetually and without interruption— and since it is logical that what is produced must perish, their destruction ought to occur;
yet they do not perish.
Since the world is observed to persist in its very same form without falling away, there must be an inexhaustible cause; therefore, the question arises: why, then, do those [elements] not perish?
The reply to this is: "Food indeed is imperishable.

Just as he was formerly the creator of foods, the father, and the enjoyer through the fivefold rite (*pāṅkta-karman*) by means of wisdom and his connection with wife and so forth, so too those to whom the foods were given, being themselves enjoyers of those foods, are likewise fathers.

Since they produce those foods through intelligence and austerity, this is what is being stated: the person who is the eater of foods is indeed the imperishable, the cause of non-destruction. How is his imperishability established?

It is said: For he, by means of each successive act of cognition—that is, by that specific wisdom arising at each respective time—and by means of actions consisting of the activities of speech, mind, and body, repeatedly and again produces this sevenfold object of enjoyment characterized as the body and its instruments, which consists of the fruits of action; for if he were not to produce this aforementioned sevenfold food, even for a single moment, through wisdom and actions, [it would cease to exist].
Then it would be cut off because it is being consumed, and it would indeed perish through constant depletion;
therefore, just as this person is a consumer of foods continuously, so too does he act according to his wisdom and according to his karma.
Therefore, the Puruṣa is imperishable because of his constant agency;
the meaning is that for this reason, even the foods being consumed do not perish.
Consequently, the entire world—characterized by the means and ends of action, consisting of activity and its fruits—is mounted upon a continuous stream defined by wisdom and action.

Because it is constrained by the continuum of the karmic impressions of many conjoined living beings, it is momentary, impure, and without essence; like the flow of a river or the succession of a lamp’s flame, it is as pithless as a plantain trunk.
Yet, while all views regarding the self—such as those concerning foam, illusion, a mirage, water, or a dream—are being dispersed, it appears as if permanent and substantial.

This is stated for the sake of dispassion: "Whatever one produces with each thought through actions—if one were not to do this, it would perish"—for it is from this [state] that those who are dispassionate must undertake the knowledge of Brahman by means of the Fourth (the *turiya*), as in the passage, "He who knows this imperishability. Since the three other foods to be mentioned later have already been explained on this occasion, the fruit of the realization of their true nature is now summarized: "He who knows this imperishability," that is, the cause of non-destruction...

"The person (*puruṣa*) indeed is the imperishable (*akṣiti*); for he produces this food by means of thought after thought through his actions. For if he were not to do this, it would perish. The meaning of the phrase "he eats food with his face" is now stated: "face" refers to the state of being the mouth, that is, preeminence or primacy. He who knows that the father, the person, possesses the nature of the imperishable in the midst of foods—he eats food, not being subordinate to the food.
Just as an ignorant person is not so, the knower— being non-different from the Self—
is merely the enjoyer; he does not fall into the state of being the object of enjoyment.
"He goes even to the gods; he lives upon vigor"—
that which was said, "he goes even to the gods," meaning he attains the nature of a god, and "he lives upon vigor," meaning he lives upon the nectar of immortality— that is a praise.
There is no other [means] for an unprecedented object. //2//

Those three kinds of food which were introduced as the fruits of the fivefold rite (*pāṅkta karman*) are distinct from and superior to the previously mentioned foods, because they are effects (*kārya*) and because their scope is extensive;
the subsequent text, extending until the end of the Brāhmaṇa, is for the purpose of explaining them.
"He made three for himself":
namely, mind, speech, and breath; these he made for himself.
"I was elsewhere in mind, I did not see; I was elsewhere in mind, I did not hear"—for it is with the mind alone that one sees, and with the mind that one hears.
Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are nothing but the mind.
Therefore, even when touched from behind, one discerns by means of the mind.
Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone.
For this [life] depends on the end; for it is not [independent]. Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—all this is indeed prāṇa.
This self, moreover, consists of that.
Consisting of speech, consisting of mind, and consisting of breath.
Regarding the statement, "He made three for himself," what is its meaning? It is explained as follows: mind, speech, and breath—these are the three foods;
he, the Father, having first created them, made these three—mind, speech, and breath—for himself, that is, for his own sake.
Since there might be doubt concerning them, he says: "There exists, indeed, a mind distinct from the external organs such as hearing."
For this is well known: even when there is a connection between the external sense organ, its object, and the self, one does not perceive the object that has appeared before one;
for when asked, "Did you see this form?", one says, "My mind was elsewhere; with my mind elsewhere, I did not see."
Likewise, when addressed with the words, "Thus you have heard my speech," [the person] says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not hear; I did not hear it.

Therefore, even though the eyes and other senses possess the capacity to perceive forms and so forth, in whose absence the cognition of form, sound, and the like does not occur despite the connection of the eyes and others with their respective objects, and in whose presence it does occur—[that is the Self].
It is understood that there exists another internal organ called *manas*, which is connected to all causes and objects;
therefore, indeed, the entire world sees only with the *manas* and hears with the *manas*, because when that [organ] is distracted, seeing and the other functions do not occur.
The existence of the mind having been established, this is stated for the sake of defining its essential nature: desire (*kāma*) is the longing for sexual union with women and so forth;
resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is the conceptualization of objects as they present themselves, through distinctions such as white, blue, and so on;
and doubt (*vicikitsā*) is knowledge characterized by uncertainty.
Faith (śraddhā) is the conviction regarding actions whose results are not perceived, as well as in regard to providence and so forth; lack of faith (aśraddhā) is the cognition contrary to that;
fortitude (dhṛti) is the sustaining of the body and other faculties when they are sinking.
Lack of fortitude is its opposite;
modesty is shame;
wisdom is discernment.
Fear, terror, and all such things as these are nothing but the mind;
they are the forms of the mind, which is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Another reason for the existence of the mind is stated: therefore, there exists an internal organ called the mind (*manas*), because even when something has been touched from behind while out of the range of vision, one discerns through discrimination, "this is the touch of a hand" or "this is the touch of a tree.
If there were no internal organ called the mind that performs such discrimination, how could such discriminative cognition arise from the skin alone? That [organ] is the mind.
The mind certainly exists,
and its essential nature is understood through its limiting adjuncts.

Here, three kinds of food— which are the fruits of actions and are designated as mind, speech, and breath— are intended to be explained with reference to the self (adhyātma), the elements (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva).

Among those, the mind among speech, mind, and breath—which are internal—has been explained. Now we begin the discussion of speech: whatever sound there is in the world, whether it is manifested by the palate and other organs as characterized by phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth by living beings, or otherwise produced by musical instruments and the like—all such sound is indeed speech (*vāk*).
Thus far, the essential nature of speech has been stated.
Now, its function is described: for this speech is dependent upon and follows after the "end"—that is, the limit of the signified object, the determination of what is to be expressed.

Furthermore, speech itself is not something to be illuminated like the signified object; rather, it is solely the illuminator of the signified object, because its very nature is luminosity, like a lamp and similar things.
For the illumination of a lamp and the like is not illuminated by another illumination;

in the same way, the Śruti avoids the charge of infinite regress by stating that speech itself is not to be illuminated. The meaning is that this [speech] is indeed not an object of illumination, for its very function is to be illuminating.

Now, *prāṇa* is described: *Prāṇa* is the function of the heart that moves through the mouth and nose; it is called *prāṇa* because of its leading forward (*praṇayana*). *Apāna* is the downward-moving function that carries away urine, feces, and so forth; its location is from the navel downwards. *Vyāna* is the function characterized by pervasive movement; it is the junction between *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and it is the cause of vigorous actions. *Udāna* is the upward-moving function, the cause of excellence, ascending movement, and so forth; its location extends from the soles of the feet to the head.

The *samāna* [vital breath] is so called because it leads [the food] equally; it resides in the stomach and is the digester of food and drink. It is the common function (*sāmānyavṛtti*) among these specific functions, connected with the general movements of the body.
Thus, all this aforementioned collection of functions beginning with *prāṇa* is indeed *prāṇa* itself.
That which possesses the function of vital breath (prāṇa) has been described as the internal food;
and its function has been explained precisely by demonstrating the distinctions among those functions.
Thus, the internal foods known as mind, speech, and vital breath have been explained.

Consisting of this, a modification of this, this aggregate of causes and effects—the body—is commenced by these [organs] of speech, mind, and breath belonging to Prajāpati. What is it? It is this "self" (ātman), the physical mass, which is mistakenly identified as the nature of the self by those lacking discrimination.
Having stated generally that it "consists of this," the specific clarification is made that it consists of speech, consists of mind, and consists of breath. //3//
The physical expansion of those very foods belonging to Prajāpati is now described:
these three worlds are indeed they.
Speech indeed is this world; the mind is the intermediate world; and the breath is yonder world.
These three worlds are these very [three]: speech is this world, the mind is the intermediate world, and breath is that world. //4//
Likewise—
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.5–7:
These three Vedas are indeed these very [breaths].
Speech indeed is the Ṛgveda, the mind is the Yajurveda, and the breath is the Sāmaveda.
The gods, the ancestors, and humans are these very ones:
speech indeed is the gods, mind is the ancestors,
and breath is humans.
The father, the mother, and the offspring—these indeed exist.
The mind is the father, speech is the mother, and the vital breath is the offspring.
The sentences beginning with “the three Vedas” (BrhUp 1.5.23) have their meaning straightforward. //5–7//
The known, the object of inquiry, and the unknown— these are precisely that.
Whatever is known is the form of speech.
For speech is the knower;
having become speech, it protects him.
The known, the object of inquiry, and the unknown—these alone [are the forms].
Therein lies the distinction: whatever is known—that is, clearly understood—is the form of speech.
Regarding this, he himself states the reason: for speech is the knower, because its nature is luminosity.
"How could it be unknown when it makes others known? For he will say: "O Emperor, a kinsman is recognized by speech alone" (4.1.2).
This result is stated for one who knows the excellence of speech: speech itself, having become known to him—him who knows the aforementioned glory of speech—protects and sustains him.
The meaning is that his food becomes fit for consumption as if its form were already known. //8//
Likewise:
"Whatever is to be known by means of the mind, that is its form."
For the mind is that which is to be known;
having become that [mind], it protects him.
Whatever is to be desired to be known— that is, whatever is intended to be clearly understood—
all that is a form of the mind.

For since mind is his [the knower's]—being the fruit for one who previously knew the manifestation of the mind—mind protects him by becoming that which is to be known; it attains the state of food precisely through its nature as that which is to be known. //9//
Likewise:
"Whatever is unknown is the form of the vital breath (prāṇa)."
For the vital breath is unknown;
having become the vital breath, it protects him.
Whatever is unknown— that which is beyond the range of cognition and not yet being doubted—

is the form of Prāṇa, for Prāṇa is indeed "unknown," according to the scriptural statement that it is "unexpressed" (*anirukta*). Since the division of speech, mind, and breath is established through the distinction between the known, the object of inquiry, and the unknown, the [passages] beginning with "the three worlds" are merely explanatory statements.
In all cases, because one observes forms such as being recognized and so forth, the restriction must be understood from the statement itself:
"Prāṇa protects him by becoming that"—the meaning is that his food becomes prāṇa precisely in an unrecognizable form.
For even teachers, fathers, and others are seen to provide assistance to their disciples, sons, and so on, while remaining unrecognized and thus causing doubt.
In the same way, it is possible for the mind and the vital breath to be considered food, even though they are subject to doubt and lack clear cognition. //10//
The expansion of speech, mind, and breath with respect to the elemental realm has been explained. Now begins this exposition concerning the divine realm—
*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.5.11.
Of that speech, the earth is the body and this fire is the form of light. As great as speech is, so great is the earth, and so great is this fire.
Of that very speech of Prajāpati which has been introduced as food, the earth is the body and Brahman is the substratum;
the light-form, consisting of illumination, is the instrument and the supported illumination— both of these, namely earth and fire, are indeed the speech of Prajāpati.
In that regard, to whatever extent and by whatever measure speech exists— being differentiated by the internal and external elements—
it is everywhere established as the earth acting as its substratum; to that same extent, it exists as the effect.
This fire, which is to be installed in the form of an instrument, having entered the earth in the form of light, becomes exactly that much; the subsequent portion is the same. //11//
Now, of this mind, heaven is the body;
that Āditya is its form consisting of light.
As far as the mind extends, so far extends the sky, and so far extends yonder sun;
those two united in sexual union,
and from that the vital breath was born.
He is Indra; he is this very one who is without a rival. For a rival is indeed a second [person].
No rival exists for one who knows this. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.12.
Now, regarding this very mind described as belonging to Prajāpati: the sky, the celestial world, is its body—the effect and the support;
and that Āditya, whose form is light, is the instrument—the supported.

In that regard, to whatever extent the mind exists, whether with respect to the self (*adhyātma*) or with respect to external objects (*adhibhūta*), to that same extent—that is, with that same dimension and that same magnitude—is the sky established as the support for the mind, which is the instrument whose form is light.
So great is this Āditya, the luminous form as the instrument to be supported;
these two, Agni and Āditya, are the father and mother in their divine aspect, namely Speech and Mind, and they came together in union— that is, in sexual union— through mutual conjunction.
"With the mind as my father Āditya, and with speech as my mother Agni, I shall perform the action revealed [to me] between the two worlds. Thus [he says].
Then, from the union of those two alone, the vital breath, the wind, was produced for the purpose of movement and action.
He who was born is Indra, the Supreme Lord;
he is not merely Indra, but one whose rival (sapatna) does not exist.
Who, then, is called a "co-adversary" (sapatnana)?
A second person who has approached as an opponent is called a "second adversary.
Even though speech and mind possess this state of being "second," they do not partake in the nature of an adversary.
For those two indeed become subordinate to the vital breath (prāṇa), just as they do within the body (adhyātma).

In this context, the incidental result of the knowledge that there is no rival is this: for one who knows the vital breath as described above—without a rival—there exists no rival or adversary. //12//
Now, water is the body of this vital breath;
its form of light is that moon up there.
Therefore, as great as the vital breath (prāṇa) is, so great are the waters, and so great is that moon.
All these are indeed equal and all are infinite.
Whoever worships them as finite wins a finite world.
Now, he who meditates upon these as infinite wins an infinite world.

Now, of this aforementioned food of Prajāpati— which consists of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) and was previously described as being within the living being— water is the body, that is, the effect which serves as the substratum for the organs.
This moon is of the nature of light, as before.

Therein, to whatever extent the vital breath (prāṇa) exists—whatever its measure it may be within the various internal divisions—to that same extent the waters possess pervasiveness; they are of that same measure.

To that same extent is this moon to be understood as having entered into those waters, acting as the instrument; it possesses an extension that pervades both the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the external elements (*adhibhūta*).
These three foods—namely speech, mind, and breath—were created by the Father through the fivefold sacrificial rite (*pāṅkta-karman*);
by these, the entire world, both internally and externally, is pervaded.
There is nothing else, whether consisting of effects or consisting of instruments, that exists apart from these. Prajāpati, however, is all of these together—

speech, mind, and breath— all of which are equal, identical, and pervasive, remaining pervasively throughout the entire range of living beings, encompassing both the subjective (ādhyātmika) and the objective (ādhibhautika).
For this very reason, they are infinite and persist as long as saṃsāra exists;
for saṃsāra is not understood through the negation of the body and the senses,
since it has been stated that those [entities] consist of the body and the senses.

Whoever worships these as being finite and limited—whether in their form as the internal self (*adhyātma*), or in their form as the elements (*adhibhūta*)—wins a world that is finite and limited in accordance with that very worship;
he is born into something limited and does not become one with their true nature. This is the meaning.

But, on the other hand, he who worships these [elements] as infinite, as consisting of all selves, as having become the self of all living beings, and as undivided—he wins only a world that has an end. //13//
It has been stated that the Father, having created seven kinds of food by means of the fivefold rite (*pāṅkta-karman*), set aside three kinds of food for his own sake;
these very foods,
which are the fruits of the fivefold rite, have now been explained.
In that regard, how, then, is the state of consisting of five parts understood, given that wealth and ritual action are also possible there?
In this context, earth and fire are the mother.
The sun by day is the father;
and that vital breath which is between these two has been explained as the offspring.
In this regard, the undertaking begins with the statement that wealth and action are to be cultivated:
"This very year is Prajāpati, consisting of sixteen parts."
The nights themselves are his fifteen digits;
his sixteenth digit is indeed constant.
By means of the nights alone, he is both filled and diminished.
On the night of the new moon, having entered into all these living beings by means of this sixteenth digit, he is born again from them in the morning.
Therefore, on that night, one should not deprive any living being of its life, even a lizard, out of reverence for this very deity.

"Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 1.5.14: ‘This very one is the year’—this Prajāpati, who consists of the three foods and was previously introduced, is here specifically designated by way of his nature as the year.
‘Consisting of sixteen parts’: he whose constituent parts (kalās) are sixteen; this is the year consisting of sixteen parts, having the form of time and being the self of the year."
And for that Prajāpati, who is Time itself, the nights are indeed his days and nights;
the meaning is that the lunar days (tithis) are his fifteen digits (kalās).

The sixteenth part—the one that completes the sixteen—of this Prajāpati is indeed constant and eternally established. He is filled and diminished by the nights, which are called *kalās*. For during the bright fortnight, the moon, who is Prajāpati, is filled with the lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*); he increases through these accumulating parts until his orb is full on the day of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
By those very digits being diminished, he wanes during the dark fortnight until, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), only one fixed digit remains.

That Prajāpati, whose self consists of the digits, having entered into this entire world of living beings by means of that sixteenth fixed digit which remains night after night on every new moon—whatever water he drinks and whatever herbs he eats; [all that is consumed by him].
Having pervaded all that very universe in the form of herbs and remaining through the night of the new moon, he is then perceived on the following morning as joined with a second digit.
Thus, this Prajāpati consists of five parts.
The day and the sun are the father, the mind;
the earth and the fire are the mother, the speech;
and their offspring is the vital breath.
The lunar days (*tithis*) are the digits (*kalās*), which constitute wealth, because they possess the nature of increase and decrease, just like wealth; and the function of those digits,
which are divisions of time, is to serve as the cause for the transformation of the world.

Thus, this entire Prajāpati has come to be as the fruit of the fivefold ritual (*pāṅkta-karman*), precisely in accordance with that desire: "May I have a wife, then may I procreate, then may I possess wealth, then may I perform rites" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17).
For it is a universal principle even in the world that the effect conforms to its cause.
Because this moon enters into all classes of living beings on this night and exists by means of its fixed digit (*dhruvā kalā*),

for that reason, on this night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), one should not cut off the life-breath of any breathing creature— that is, one should not cause any living being to perish— not even a lizard.
For the lizard is indeed evil-natured and is harmed by living beings by its very nature, being regarded as inauspicious even when merely seen.

Certainly, [killing] has been prohibited; nevertheless, is this statement intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for killing on occasions other than the new moon day, or specifically regarding the lizard? What then?
For the sake of honoring—that is, for the purpose of worshiping—this deity Soma. //14//
That Prajāpati, the year consisting of sixteen parts, is indeed this very person who knows thus.
His possessions alone constitute fifteen parts.
The self alone is its sixteenth digit;
it is filled by wealth and it is diminished by wealth. This very self is the nave.
The rim is wealth;
therefore, even if one suffers the loss of everything, if he himself remains alive, they say, "He has escaped with his rim. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.15)
That Prajāpati, the year consisting of sixteen parts, who was indeed described indirectly, should not be considered entirely beyond perception;
for he is perceived directly as this very person.
Who is "this" one? It is that man who knows Prajāpati—who consists of the three kinds of food—as his own self; he is the person possessing such knowledge.

In what sense is he called Prajāpati? That is now explained: for that person who knows thus, his very wealth—consisting of cattle and so forth—is the fifteen parts (*kalā*), because it possesses the nature of increase and decrease;
and ritual action is that which is accomplished by means of that wealth.
For the sake of his completeness, his own self—the physical body itself—is the sixteenth part, serving as the stable foundation for this knower.
Like the moon, it is filled by wealth and wanes; this is well known in the world.
This is "nabhya," meaning that which is beneficial for the nave (*nābhi*), or that which is fit for the nave.
What is that? It is this body, which is the self (*ātman*).
Wealth is the "felly" (*pradhi*), standing in the place of the outer rim, like the spokes and the rim of a wheel.
Therefore, even if one suffers total ruin—that is, if one is deprived of all possessions, loses everything, and falls into exhaustion—[the self remains].

If he lives by means of the *ātman*, which stands in the place of the nave (*nābhi*), and by means of the outer casing, the *pradhī* (the felly), then he has gone [to ruin]; they say that he is exhausted, just like a wheel deprived of its spokes and rim.
The intended meaning is that if he lives, he is replenished again by wealth, which stands in the place of the spokes and the rim. 15.
Thus it has been explained that through action characterized by the fivefold set (*pāṅkta*) and joined with the divine, wealth, and knowledge, one becomes Prajāpati, who consists of the three foods.
Immediately following this, it was stated that wife, wealth, and so forth constitute the retinue.
In that context, it was understood only in a general sense that the son, ritual action, and the other knowledge are merely means for attaining the worlds.
There is no fixed rule regarding the specific relationship between sons and other such means and the fruit of attaining the world.
Therefore, the subsequent section is composed to state this specific relationship between the means, such as sons, and the result to be achieved: START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16.
Now, there are indeed three worlds: the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods.
This world of men is to be won by a son alone, and not by any other ritual act;
the world of the fathers is won by ritual acts.
Through knowledge, one attains the world of the gods.
Indeed, the world of the gods is the best of all worlds;
therefore, they praise knowledge.
The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the statement. "Trayaḥ, vāva" (there are indeed three) has the sense of restriction;
there are only three worlds fit for the means taught in the scriptures.
It is neither deficient nor excessive.
What are they? It is said: the world of men, the world of the ancestors, and the world of the gods.
Of these, this world of men is to be won, to be conquered, and to be accomplished by the means of a son alone; and how it is to be won by a son, we shall explain further on.
"Not by any other action, nor by knowledge"— this is the completion of the sentence.
The world of the fathers (pitṛloka) is to be won by action alone, characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites, and not by a son, nor even by knowledge.
The world of the gods is attained neither by a son nor by ritual action;
indeed, among the three worlds, the world of the gods is the best and most highly praised.
Therefore, because it is the means to that [world], they praise knowledge. //16//
Thus, there are three means of accomplishment—known as the son, ritual action, and knowledge—which are assigned according to the distinction between the fruits of the three worlds to be attained.

However, the wife is not mentioned separately as a distinct means, because she exists for the sake of the son and ritual action. Furthermore, wealth is not a separate means, because it serves as a means for performing ritual action.
It is well known that the cause for conquering the worlds through knowledge and action occurs precisely by means of the attainment of one's own self.
However, since a son is not of the nature of an action, it is not understood in what manner he can be a cause for conquering the worlds;
therefore, this must be explained, and thus the following section is commenced.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.17:
Now, therefore, follows the transmission.
When he thinks he is about to depart, he says to his son: "Thou art the Brahman, thou art the sacrifice, thou art the world."
That son replied: "I am Brahman; I am the sacrifice; I am the world.
For whatever has been recited, all that is unified as "Brahman";
and whatever sacrifices there may be, all those are unified as "the sacrifice."
Whatever worlds there may be, for all of them, "world" is a single unity. This whole [world] is indeed just this much.
Thinking, "May he, being this whole, not consume me from here," [he offered].
Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed belongs to the world;
for this reason, they instruct him.
When one who knows this departs from this world, he enters into his son together with these very vital breaths.
If he has done anything at all improperly by this [son], the son releases him from all that; therefore he is called "putra.
By means of the son alone, he finds firm support in this world.
Then these immortal deities, the vital breaths, enter into him.
*Sampratiḥ* means *sampradānam* (the act of handing over);
*samprattiḥ* is the name of the ritual action that is about to be described.
For in this manner, the father performs the handing over of his own self-activity to the son.
Therefore, this rite is designated as *sampratti*.
At what time should it be performed?
To this he says: when that father, at whatever time, thinking "I am about to depart" or "I shall die," perceives through a vision of what lies beyond that he is about to die;
Then, having summoned his son at that time, he said: "You are the Brahman, you are the sacrifice, you are the world.
Thus addressed, the son replied;
for he, having been previously instructed, already knew: "This is what must be done by me."
Therefore, it says: "I am Brahman, I am the sacrifice, I am the world"—these three statements.
Considering that the meaning of this is obscure, the Śruti proceeds to provide an explanation.

Whatever indeed has been recited, whatever remains—whether studied or unstudied—all that is unified in this single word "Brahman. The meaning is: "That activity of study which was to be performed by me for so long a time concerning the Vedas—from now on, let that be yours, O Brahman; let it be performed by you."
Likewise, whatever sacrifices were to be performed by me— whether they have been performed or not— all of them are unified in this single term "sacrifice" (yajña); that is,
those sacrifices which had me as their agent.
From this point forward, let them be "you, the sacrifice"— meaning, let them have you as their agent.
Whatever worlds there may be that are to be conquered by me, whether already conquered or unconquered, all of those are unified within this single term "the world" (*loka*).
"From this point forward, my study, sacrifices, conquest of the worlds, and all duties pertaining to ritual action have been entrusted to you;
I am indeed released from the bond of duty regarding ritual action. And the son, having been thus instructed, accepted everything exactly as it was said.
Regarding this, the Śruti, understanding this to be the father's intention, declares: "This much indeed is the extent of all that must be done by a householder;
namely, the Vedas are to be studied and sacrifices are to be performed."
And the worlds are to be conquered.
Let him not think: "May all this—this entire burden dependent upon me—not be cut away from me and placed within his own self, so that he might protect me from departing from this world."
The *laṅ* is used in the sense of the *ḷṛṭ* (future),
because in the Vedic language (*chandas*) there is no restriction regarding time;
for since a son endowed in this way will liberate his father from this world— that is, from the bondage of duties— [the father should perform the rite].
Therefore, the Brahmins say that a son who has been instructed is beneficial to the world and a source of welfare for his father;
for this very reason, fathers instruct their sons, thinking, "May he be one who brings us benefit in the world."

When that father—having thus known this and having entrusted his duties to his son—departs from this world, that is, dies, then at that time he enters his son through these very means already mentioned: speech, mind, and breath; he pervades the son.

Due to the removal of the causes of internal limitation, the father’s speech, mind, and vital breaths enter into everything by means of their own divine forms— consisting of earth, fire, and so forth— just as the light of a lamp enters various separate jars.
Together with those vital breaths, the father also enters,
because the father is essentially constituted of speech, mind, and vital breath.

"I am indeed infinite speech, mind, and breath, expanded through the distinctions of the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth"— thus is the father meditated upon. Therefore, it is rightly said that the father enters into conformity with those very breaths of the son,
for he becomes the Self of all, including the son.
This is what is meant: he whose son has been thus instructed by his father exists in this very world in the form of a son; the meaning is that he should not be considered dead at all.
And likewise, in another Śruti: "This other self of his is appointed for meritorious deeds" (AiU 4.4).

Now, he states the etymological derivation of the word "son" (*putra*): If at any time there remains something unaccomplished by this father— something that ought to be done through his eyes, from the corners of his eyes, or from within— that son releases him, that is, liberates him from all that unaccomplished duty which constitutes an obstacle to attaining the worlds, by himself performing and fulfilling it all.
Therefore, because he protects his father by filling [the gap], he is called "son" (*putra*).
This is the sonship of a son: that he protects by filling the father's deficiency.
Through such a son, even though he has died, the father remains immortal and is established in this very world.

In this way, the father conquers this world of men through his son; he does not conquer the world of the gods or the world of the ancestors through knowledge and ritual action in that same manner, for those two do not attain the status of being causes for the conquest of worlds by depending on any further operation— like a son— beyond the mere existence of their own attainment of form.

Then, once the father has performed the rite of transmission (*sampratti*), these vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—speech and the rest—which are divine, belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha, and immortal, characterized by the nature of non-death, enter him. As to how this occurs, the text will say: "And from the earth [they enter] him," and so forth.
Thus, the Śruti itself has demonstrated that the son, ritual works, and the lower knowledge have as their respective goals the human world, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods.
Regarding this, some eloquent disputants [object], based on the withdrawal of the specific applications stated in the Śruti.
Therefore, it is established that the scriptural teaching regarding debt concerns the unenlightened and not those who know the Supreme Self.
And the text will say: “We shall perform [rites] for whom this Self is not this world” (4.4.22).
Some, however, maintain that even the conquest of the world of the fathers and the world of the gods is indeed a turning away from the world of the fathers and the world of the gods.

Therefore, they maintain that when these three—son, ritual action, and the lower knowledge—are practiced in combination, one turns away from these three worlds and attains liberation through the knowledge of the Supreme Self; thus, they hold that the means such as the son and so forth serve liberation only by way of a succession. To refute even their position, this very subsequent scriptural passage [is given] concerning one who has performed the *sampratti* rite, who possesses a son, who performs rituals, and who knows the science of the threefold food (*tryannātmavidyā*).
It is undertaken for the purpose of demonstrating the fruit;
however, it cannot be said that this very fruit is the fruit of liberation.
Because of the connection with the three kinds of food, because foods are the products of meditation and austerity,
and because of the scriptural observation that "he produces them again and again."
Furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of exhaustion in the passage, "If one were not to do this, it would indeed perish";
because it is logical that the body, being of the nature of light, consists of effects and instruments;
and because of the concluding summary in the passage, "This triad," which identifies it as consisting of name, form, and action.
Nor can it be understood from this very sentence that these three means, when combined, lead to liberation for some, while for others they result in the fruit consisting of the three foods;
for the sentence is exhausted by showing that the means such as sons and so forth result in the fruit consisting of the three foods.
From the earth and from Agni, divine speech enters him.
That indeed is divine speech by which whatever one speaks comes to be exactly so.
From the earth and from fire, divine speech—belonging to the sphere of the deities (adhidaiva)—enters him who has performed the transfer (*sampratti*).
For divine speech, characterized by the earth and fire, is the material cause of all speech;
it is indeed obstructed by internal defects such as attachment and the like.

Upon the removal of those defects in the wise man, it pervades him—just as the breaking away of an obstruction allows water to flow, or as light from a lamp spreads—just as described: "Divine speech entered him from the earth and from fire.
And that divine speech is pure, being free from defects such as untruth and the like.
Whatever he speaks with that divine speech, whether for himself or for another, that very thing comes to pass;
the meaning is that his speech becomes unfailing and unobstructed. //18//
Likewise:
"And from the sky and from the sun, the divine mind enters him."
That indeed is the divine mind by which one becomes truly blissful and does not grieve.
And from the sky and from the sun, the divine mind enters him— that is the divine mind,
because it is pure by its very nature;
with that mind, he becomes nothing but bliss, he becomes nothing but happy.
Moreover, one does not grieve, because of the non-association with the causes of grief and so forth. //19//
Likewise:
"And from the waters and from the moon, the divine breath enters him."
That indeed is the divine breath which, whether moving or not moving, neither suffers nor is harmed.
He who knows this becomes the self of all beings;
as is this deity, so is he.
Just as all beings protect this deity, even so do all beings protect one who knows this.
Whatever grief these creatures suffer, that becomes theirs alone;
only merit goes to him.
Indeed, no evil reaches the gods.
And the divine vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters him from the waters and from the moon.
What are the characteristics of that divine *prāṇa*?

It is said: it is that which moves among the various classes of living beings and does not move—either in the form of the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), or alternatively, moving among mobile beings and not moving among immobile ones.
He does not tremble, nor is he overcome by the fear that arises from the causes of suffering;
furthermore, he does not perish, he is not destroyed, and he does not meet with harm.
He—who thus knows the vision of the Self as it has been described—becomes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all beings.
The meaning is that because he is the self of all beings— thinking "the mind of all beings is mine" and "the speech of all beings is mine"— he becomes omniscient and the doer of all.
In the same way, this primordial deity Hiraṇyagarbha—just so, there is no obstruction whatsoever to his omniscience or his capacity for all-creation.
The word "he" (sa) is a reference to the subject of the illustration.
Furthermore, just as all beings protect, sustain, and honor this deity Hiraṇyagarbha through sacrifices and other rites, [so too is the case with the Lord].
In this very way, all beings protect one who knows thus; the meaning is that they constantly offer him worship characterized by sacrifice and other such acts.

Now, this objection may be raised: it has been stated that he is the Self of all living beings, and if he is the Self who performs the actions and functions of all living beings, he would consequently become connected with the pleasures and pains of all those beings.

That is not so, because [the Self] is of undifferentiated consciousness. For it is observed that those whose consciousness of the Self is limited experience a connection with suffering upon being reviled and the like, thinking, "I have been reviled by this person.

But for this Universal Self, there is no suffering caused by such [an event], because there is an absence of any specific notion of "Self" regarding either the one who is reviled or the one who reviles.

Furthermore, due to the absence of a cause, it is like the suffering at death; for when someone has died, suffering arises in another only because of the thought, "He was my son," or "He was my brother."
It is for the sake of sons and so forth;
in the absence of such causes, even for one who witnesses their death, suffering does not arise at all.
Likewise, for Īśvara as well, because he is of an undivided self and lacks defects such as false knowledge—the causes of suffering like possessiveness—suffering does not arise at all.

This is what is being said: whatever these creatures grieve over, that grief and its cause—the suffering—become joined with them alone along with those very creatures, because their intellects are limited.
But for the Universal Self (sarvātman), with what could it be joined, or from what could it be separated?
However, for him who abides in the station of Prajāpati, only merit—that is, the intended auspicious fruit—is meant by the word "merit," for he has performed unsurpassed merit.
Therefore, he goes only to that fruit [of his actions].
Indeed, evil does not go to the gods; the meaning is that because there is no occasion for the fruit of evil, the suffering that is the fruit of evil does not reach them. //20//

"Thus, all these indeed are equal, all are infinite"— in this way, the meditation on speech, mind, and breath has been taught without distinction, and no specific preference for any one among them has been stated.
Should it be understood exactly thus?
Or rather, when investigated, can any distinction regarding the observance of the vow (*vrata*) and its meditation (*upāsana*) be perceived? To this it is said:
"Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the vow. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21)
Prajāpati created the ritual acts;
once created, they vied with one another.
Speech took up the position, thinking, "I alone shall speak."
"I shall see"—thus is the eye; "I shall hear"—thus is the ear; in this way, the other [faculties] function according to their respective functions.
Death, becoming weariness, took possession of them;
having reached them,
Death held them captive.
Therefore, speech indeed becomes exhausted; the eye becomes exhausted;
the ear becomes exhausted.
Then they could not attain this very one, which is the middle vital breath (*prāṇa*).
They resolved to know it:
"This indeed is the best among us, for while moving and while not moving, it neither suffers nor is harmed."
"Come, let us all take on his very form.
They all took on his very form;
therefore, they are called by this name, "prāṇas."
Indeed, that family in which one who knows this is born is celebrated because of him.
And whoever competes with one who knows this withers away;
having withered away, he finally dies. Thus far with respect to the self (adhyātma). *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.5.21.
BrhUpBh_1,5.21 Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the vow (*vratamīmāṃsā*), which means the deliberation regarding the ritual acts of meditation.
An inquiry proceeds as to which of these vital functions (*prāṇas*) should be maintained as a vow.
In this regard, Prajāpati—indeed, the particle *ha* has the sense of "it is said"—Prajāpati, it is said, having created living beings, [created] the actions and the organs.

Speech and the others—since they are the means for action (*karma*), they are called "actions" (*karmāṇi*)—were created; the meaning is that he brought forth the organs such as speech. Once created, they contended with one another; they engaged in rivalry and competition. How so? Speech took a vow, thinking: "I shall surely speak"—that is, I shall not cease from my own function of speaking—if there be anyone else equal to me in not ceasing from their own function.
Thinking, "Let him too display his own vigor," [he conceives] the eye with the thought, "I shall see," and the ear with the thought, "I shall hear."
In this way, he took possession of other actions and instruments according to their respective functions—whatever action belongs to each, that is "according to its function.
Mṛtyu, the slayer, assuming the form of fatigue (*śrama*), seized those instruments;
how so? He overtook those instruments as they were engaged in their own specific operations.
He manifested himself in the form of fatigue (*śrama*).
And having reached them, Death seized them—that is to say, he caused them to fall away from their own functions.
Therefore, even today, speech (*vāk*), when engaged in its own function, being joined with Death in the form of fatigue, falls away from its own function.
In this way the eye tires,
the ear tires;
yet Death, in the form of fatigue, did not reach nor had he reached this very chief vital breath (mukhya prāṇa).
This which is the middle vital breath (prāṇa)—
even today it proceeds tirelessly in its own function.
Those other organs fixed their minds upon him in order to know him.

"This one among us is indeed the best, the most praiseworthy, the superior, because whether moving or not moving, he neither suffers nor is harmed. Come now, let us all assume his very form; let us recognize this Prāṇa as our self. Having thus resolved, they—
They all became the very form of this [Prāṇa]; they recognized the form of Prāṇa alone as their own self and undertook the vow of Prāṇa, thinking: "Our own vows are not sufficient to ward off Death."

Because by means of the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the other organs possess form—since [the breath] consists of motion and they consist of light; for apart from the vital breath, the nature of motion is not possible elsewhere.
Indeed, they are always observed to be preceded by the activity of motion in their own respective functions.
Therefore, these [organs] such as speech and the rest are designated— meaning they are called— by this name "prāṇa" in this manner.
Whoever thus knows the identity of all the instruments with prāṇa and their state of being denotable by the word "prāṇa," by that very knower indeed, O people of the world, his family is designated.
In whatever family that wise man is born, that family becomes renowned by the very name of "the wise one," such as "the family of Amuṣya" or "the Tāpatya.
This is the fruit for one who knows, as has been stated, the nature of speech and the other organs as being the form of Prāṇa and their designation as "Prāṇa."
Furthermore, whoever competes with one who thus knows the Self as Prāṇa—that is, one who stands in opposition to him—dries up within this very body; he undergoes desiccation.

Having indeed dried up, having reached desiccation, he finally dies at the end; he does not die suddenly, struck down by some external affliction. Thus has been described the vision of the inner Self as Prāṇa; this conclusion of what was said is intended to introduce the demonstration of the divine aspect (adhidaivata).
Now, with reference to the deities:
"I shall surely blaze," thought Agni.
"I shall heat," says the Sun;
"I shall shine," says the Moon;
in this manner, other deities [speak] according to their respective nature.
Just as the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities;
for while the other deities set, Vāyu does not.
This deity, Vāyu, is indeed that which never sets.
Now, immediately following this, the vision concerning the deities—that is, pertaining to the divine—is being stated.
It is investigated as follows: "The observance of which particular deity's vow is more excellent?"
Everything was as it is within oneself:
"I shall indeed blaze," thought Agni;
"I shall burn hot," thought Āditya.
"I shall speak," says the moon;
likewise do other deities according to their respective domains.

As for the internal [self], among these [organs] beginning with speech, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has not been overtaken by death; it has not been displaced from its own function, remaining one whose vow is unbroken by virtue of its own observance of the vow of *prāṇa*.
In this same way, among these deities beginning with Agni, even Vāyu [does not set].
They "set"—that is, they go to their setting or cease from their respective functions—just as the other deities such as Agni correspond internally to speech and the other organs;
however, Vāyu does not set, just as the middle vital breath (prāṇa) does not.
Therefore, this very deity that never sets is Vāyu—this which is Vāyu.

Having thus investigated both with respect to the self (adhyātma) and with respect to the divine (adhidaiva), it is determined: "The vow of the self consisting of Prāṇa and Vāyu remains unbroken. //22//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23 Now,
there is this verse:
"From where the sun rises and where it sets."
Verily, he rises from breath and sets in breath.
The gods made that his law, saying, "He is the same today and he is the same tomorrow.
Whatever these [gods] resolved upon yesterday, that very same thing they do today.
Therefore, one should observe this single vow alone: both when breathing out and when breathing in, [one should think], "Lest evil death should overtake me.
If, however, one should perform it, desiring to complete it, he thereby wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity.
Now, there is this verse, a mantra, which illuminates this very subject:

from which [source] the sun rises—that is, it emerges from the wind (vāyu), and internally, as the eye, it emerges from the vital breath (prāṇa); and where it sets—at the time of the evening twilight for a person, and at the time of sleep, it goes back into the wind and the vital breath.
The gods—the senses such as speech and the deities such as Agni—having deliberated in the past, established that law and maintained the vow of the vital breath (*prāṇavrata*).
The intention is that this very same law is followed by the gods now, will be followed tomorrow, and will continue to be followed in the future as well.
Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa explains the mantra in brief: "Indeed, this sun rises from the vital breath and sets into the vital breath."
"The gods made that law; it is the same today and it will be the same tomorrow"—what is the meaning of this?

It is said: whatever these [deities], such as speech and the others, or fire and the others, undertook as a vow at that time (*amuḥ*) or at that moment (*amuhmin kāle*)—namely, the vow of breath (*prāṇavrata*) and the vow of wind (*vāyuvrata*)—that very thing they do even now, they continue to follow, and they will continue to follow.
Their vow remains entirely unbroken; however,
that which consists of the vows of speech and so forth, as well as the vows of the fires and so forth, is indeed broken,
because at the time of their setting and at the time of their sleep, they are seen to be released into the wind and the vital breath (prāṇa).

Now, this has been stated elsewhere: "When a person sleeps, then speech merges into the breath, the mind into the breath, the eye into the breath, and the ear into the breath. When he awakens, they are born again from the breath alone. This is with respect to the self (adhyātma). Now, with respect to the divine (adhidaivata): when the fire goes out, it merges into the wind; when the sun sets, it enters the wind."

"The moon [is established] in the wind; the quarters are established in the wind; from the wind alone they are born again. Because this very vow—namely, the nature of vibration belonging to both the wind and the vital breath (prāṇa), which is observed by all the gods—is common to speech and the others as well as to fire and the others, therefore another person too should observe this same vow.
What follows from this? One should breathe in—that is, perform the function of inhalation—and breathe out—that is, perform the function of exhalation;
for there is no cessation of the activity of inhalation and exhalation, which are characterized by breathing in and breathing out.
Therefore, one should observe that single vow alone, setting aside the activities of the other senses, lest the evil death, in the form of exhaustion, should reach or seize me.

The word "na" (not) refers to fear: the intention is that one should maintain the vow of breath-control while terrified by the thought, "If I should fall away from this vow, I am already swallowed by death.
If, at any time, one should transgress or fail to undertake the vow of breath-control...
He should desire to complete it, wishing to bring it to its conclusion; for if he were to desist from this vow, his vital breath (*prāṇa*) would be overcome, as would the gods.
Therefore, he must certainly complete it.

Therefore, by means of this very vow—the realization of the Self as Prāṇa—one [perceives] that among all beings, speech and the other [senses], as well as fire and the other [deities], are indeed identical with my own self;

"I am Prāṇa, the Self, the performer of all movement. Thus, by maintaining this vow, one attains either *sāyujya*—the state of union, identity of essence—with this very deity Prāṇa, or *salokatā*—residence in the same world, or being in the same place. This latter result is intended for those whose knowledge is deficient.
"Jayati" means "he attains. //23//
Thus ends the fifth section, "The Seven Kinds of Food," in the first chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya.

All this— the world characterized by the distinction between the means and the end, which was introduced as the object of ignorance, including the fruit that culminates in the attainment of the Self consisting of vital breath (prāṇātman),
as well as its prior state before manifestation, denoted by the term "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta) like the seed of a tree— all this is so.
This world consists of three things: name, form, and action.
Of these names, speech is their *uktha*;
for from it all names arise.
This is their Sāman;
for this is equal to all names. This is their Brahman.
For this indeed bears all names.
"Triad";
what is that triad? It is said:
name, form, and action—these are indeed only the non-Self.
The Self is that which is directly perceived and immediate as Brahman;

therefore, the passage beginning with "the threefold" is commenced for the purpose of causing detachment from this [world]. For one whose mind has not turned away from this non-Self, the intellect does not proceed toward meditating upon the Self alone as the world, thinking, "I am Brahman."
Because there is a contradiction between the outward-turning activity of the external senses and the inward-turning nature of the Self;
and so it is said in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: “The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, and not at the inner Self.
But some wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inward Self with his eyes turned back” (KaU 2.1.1), and so forth.

Furthermore, how can it be possible to conceive that this saṃsāra— which consists of actions, agents, and fruits, and is both determinate and indeterminate— is composed solely of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and karma,
and not of a self (*ātman*)?
To this it is replied: regarding those names as they have been presented, the word *vāk* (speech) denotes the universal of sound (*śabda-sāmānya*).

Since it has been stated, "Whatever sound there may be, that is indeed speech" (1.5.3), the referent of this word *vāk* is the mere universal of sound; this is the *uktha*—the cause, the material source—of these particular names.
