Like a mountain of rock salt from which particles of rock salt [originate],
he said: "For this reason, from this commonality of name, all specific names— such as the divisions of Yajñadatta, Devadatta, and so forth— arise, are produced, and are differentiated,
just as particles of salt arise from a mountain of salt."
Furthermore, the effect is non-different from its cause;
likewise, because particulars are included within the universal, how can there be the relation of universal and particular? This word "sāman" is the universal of these particular names.
It is called *sāman* because of its equality;
the meaning is "commonality," for this [Self] is equal to all names and specific attributes.
Furthermore, because there is no difference in their acquisition of self-nature, there is no difference among particular names.
For whatever acquires its self-nature from something else is seen to be non-distinct from it, just as pots and the like are non-distinct from clay.
How is it said that the acquisition of their own nature belongs to specific names through speech? Because for these [names], the reality denoted by the word "speech" is Brahman, which is their Self;
for from that [Brahman] comes the acquisition of the nature of names, since a self-nature distinct from sound is impossible.
He demonstrates this: "Because the universal sound (*śabdasāmānya*) indeed bears—that is, sustains—all particular sounds as its names by providing them with their own form.

Thus, because the relationship of cause and effect is established, and because the relationship between the universal and the particular is established, and because the provision of their own nature is established, it is proven that particular names are nothing but sound itself.
The same should be applied to the following two [categories] as has been stated. //1//
Now, among forms, the eye is their *uktha*;
for from it all forms arise.
This is their *sāman*;
for this is equal through all its forms.
This is their *brahman*.
For this indeed sustains all forms.

Now, regarding the forms such as white, black, and so forth, the word "eye" denotes the commonality of the objects of sight; that which is expressed by the term "eye" is the generality of form (*rūpasāmānya*), the mere manifesting principle.
For all forms abide in this;
this is their *sāman*.
For this is equal to all forms; this is their Brahman, for it sustains all forms. //2//
Now, regarding ritual actions, the statement "the Self" is their *uktha*;
for from it all ritual actions arise.
This is their *sāman*;
for this is equal to all ritual actions.
This is their *brahman*.
For this indeed sustains all actions;
these three, being real, are this one Self;
and this one Self, being real, is these three.
This very immortal is covered by the real.
Breath indeed is the immortal;
name and form are the real.
By these two, this vital breath is concealed.
Now, it is stated that all specific actions—whether consisting of mental reflection and perception, or consisting of physical movement—are included within the mere generality of action.
How so? The self (*ātman*) is the body common to all specific actions;
because action belongs to the self, it is called the "self" (*ātman*).
It has been stated that "one performs action by means of the self through the body.

And since all action is manifested in the body, therefore—by virtue of being located therein—the term for that [body] refers to action; thus, as before, the mere generality of action, beginning with "the Uktha of all," and so forth.
Thus, this triad consisting of name, form, and action, as previously described, is mutually dependent, the cause of mutual manifestation,
and the locus of mutual dissolution; when combined, like the support of a tripod, it constitutes a single reality.
By what means is oneness with the Self [established]?
It is said: this Self is this body, a collection consisting of the effects and instruments, as explained in the section on the three foods beginning with, "This Self indeed consists of this.
For all this that has been manifested and the unmanifested is only this: name, form, and action.

This very self is indeed one, this aggregate of causes and effects, which exists as the states of the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva). This triad alone is what is called name, form, and action.
This is what will be explained hereafter.

He states the meaning of the sentence "the immortal is covered by the true" as follows: "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the immortal"—that is, consisting of the instruments of perception, it is the inner supporter, the essential self, unborn and imperishable.
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) exist as the body in its state of being composed of effects;

vital breath (*prāṇa*), however, is composed of activity and is the supporter of those two. It is concealed—that is, not made manifest—by these two, which consist of the body, are subject to arising and passing away, and are mortal.
This very reality of saṃsāra, which is the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*), has thus been demonstrated. Therefore...
The fourth chapter is commenced with the thought: "Beyond this, the Self, which is the object of knowledge, is to be realized. //3//
Thus ends the sixth Uktha-Brāhmaṇa in the first chapter.
